The travelers stop partly for the name and partly from surprise at finding any house in those goat-haunted groves.

Other essays follow sheep-shearing, riding in mist, and a magpie over the hill, with scenes where mist thickens to rain-dust and trees seem to lose one another. Black pigs scuttle past a farmhouse and vanish into white air. The book shows Galsworthy's quieter voice, attentive to light, weather, and the small peace of a remote place.
2904-studies-and-essays-quality-and-othe:
John Galsworthy gathered life essays in Studies and Essays: Quality and Others, again under Anatole France's warning that excess is always an evil. The title essay recalls a bootmaker known since the author's youth, who worked with his elder brother in two little shops let into one in a fashionable by-street. Quality, for Galsworthy, lives in work done slowly and well.

Other essays take up the grand jury, threshing, an old-time place, romance, memories, and felicity. One passage protests a woman dying at thirty of a creeping malady she might have checked, had she not spent herself on children and husband. The book rewards readers who enjoy Galsworthy the essayist, humane, observant, and quietly angry at waste.
3020-table-talk-essays-on-men-and-manner:
William Hazlitt collected Table-Talk: Essays on Men and Manners as familiar essays on painting, genius, common sense, and human nature. Volume one includes On the Pleasure of Painting, On Genius and Common Sense, Character of Cobbett, On People with One Idea, On the Ignorance of the Learned, and The Indian Jugglers. Volume two adds a Poussin landscape, Milton's sonnets, going a journey, and coffee-house talk.

Hazlitt's prose turns on worldlings who cannot bear to fritter wealth away in charity, since it would no longer peer in monumental pomp over other men's heads. Even on the point of death, they call such giving madness, waste, and impiety. The essays remain a model of the familiar style, argumentative, personal, and quotable on nearly every page.
3028-the-peterkin-papers:
Lucretia Hale wrote The Peterkin Papers as family comedies about the literal-minded Peterkins, first told to the daughter of the lady from Philadelphia. The first story was accepted for Young Folks, the tales continued in St. Nicholas, and a second edition added The Peterkins at the Farm. Mrs. Peterkin puts salt in her coffee in the opening tale, and the family solves each small crisis with elaborate logic.

A Fourth of July passage has the family driven from sleep by crowing cocks, braying donkeys, horns, cheers, torpedoes, and Chinese crackers from the Antiques and Horribles. In despair of sleep they come down to breakfast. The papers remain a beloved American children's classic, gentle in humor and exact in its portrait of a family that reasons itself into trouble.
3092-the-conquest-of-new-france-a-chroni:
George M. Wrong recounts how France lost North America to Britain. This 1918 volume belongs to the Chronicles of America series from Yale University Press. It covers the long colonial wars of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. Quebec, Boston, Acadia, and Louisbourg are its main prizes.

Wrong moves chapter by chapter through Frontenac and Phips, the Ohio Valley fight, and the expulsion from Acadia. He writes a compact narrative history, not a source collection. General readers get the whole contest in one clear sweep, from coastal raids to a continent changing hands.
311-bunner-sisters:
Two sisters keep a tiny shop near Stuyvesant Square in old New York. Edith Wharton's Bunner Sisters, serialized in Scribner's in late 1916, follows Ann Eliza and Evelina through a shabby basement store. Their sign reads simply Bunner Sisters in blotchy gold.

Customers know the shop's local fame, though strangers cannot guess its trade. A clock, a lover, and a slow decline test the sisters' bond. Wharton writes poverty and devotion without sentimentality. The novella ranks among her most quietly moving works. Wharton wrote the sisters' tragedy from her own New York memories.
3163-birds-and-bees-sharp-eyes-and-other:
John Burroughs gathers his nature essays here, with an introduction by Mary E Burt and a biographical sketch. Birds, bird enemies, and the tragedies of the nests lead the contents. Bees follow, in an idyl of the honey-bee and a study of pastoral bees. Sharp eyes, named in the title, names the gift the whole book celebrates.

Burroughs was born, the sketch notes, just before the wake-robin shows itself in spring. That timing fits a writer who spent a life watching. The essays teach attention: a nest watched daily, a bee followed home, a song traced to its singer. They remain a fine entry to American nature writing, clear, patient, and full of outdoor fact.
3237-the-garotters:
William D Howells writes this farce under the title The Garotters, in an author's edition printed at Edinburgh in 1897 by David Douglas. A note reserves acting rights to the publisher. The first part opens at the window of a woman's apartment in a hotel, with Mrs Roberts, then Mr Roberts, taking the stage in turn. The scene is set for a comedy of manners.

Garotting, the crime of throttling from behind, gives the play its sensational hook, but Howells treats it as farce material. Respectable people, hotel rooms, and sudden alarms drive the fun. The piece shows Howells the dramatist at play, turning a newspaper horror into drawing-room laughter, with dialogue as the chief weapon throughout.
3319-letters-to-dead-authors:
Andrew Lang writes letters to authors who cannot answer in this charming volume. Thackeray and Dickens lead the contents, with Pierre de Ronsard, Herodotus, and an epistle to Alexander Pope. Lucian of Samosata, Maitre Francois Rabelais, and Jane Austen follow, with Master Isaak Walton, M Chapelain, and Sir John Mandeville. Alexandre Dumas, Theocritus, and Edgar Allan Poe join them.

Sir Walter Scott and Eusebius of Caesarea round out a correspondence across two thousand years. Lang writes as a fan, a critic, and a friend, praising, teasing, and arguing with the dead. Lang's letters read one at a time, witty enough to reread, and learned enough to trust.
3421-bramble-bees-and-others:
Jean Henri Fabre collects his essays on wild bees in this volume, drawn from his long Souvenirs entomologiques and translated by Alexander Teixeira de Mattos. The book opens with bramble stems, which peasants cut while trimming hedges and which bees then use as nesting places. Later essays treat the Halicti and other solitary bees, leaving the mason bees to a separate volume.

Fabre watches how each kind of bee digs, builds, stores food, and guards its young. He explains the insects in plain terms, with the patience of a man who spent years in his own field. The volume suits nature lovers who want careful observation rather than theory, and it shows why Fabre earned his name as the poet of insects.
3469-the-hand-of-ethelberta-a-comedy-in-:
Thomas Hardy calls this novel a comedy in chapters, written as a light interlude between his more sober stories. Ethelberta is a young woman of humble birth who has married into a higher station. She must manage suitors, family, and reputation across scenes set in Sandbourne town, its moor and pier, and London drawing rooms. Hardy warns that strict probability was not his aim.

The fun lies in Ethelberta's poise and in the social climbing around her. She keeps her wits while men compete for her hand and her past threatens to catch up with her. Readers who know Hardy only from his tragedies will find a brighter, teasing side here, with the same sharp eye for class and village life.
3690-floor-games-a-companion-volume-to-l:
Herbert George Wells writes a companion to his Little Wars, this time about games played on the floor with simple toys. The jolliest indoor games, Wells says, demand a floor covered with linoleum or cork carpet, where toy soldiers stand up and cities can rise. His list of toys runs to soldiers and civilians, bricks, boards and planks, clockwork railway stock and rails, tin ships, and Easter eggs.

Games include the Wonderful Islands, the building of cities, funiculars, marble towers, castles, and war games, though Wells allows very little of war itself. The book suits parents, teachers, and children who want inventive play from plain materials, and readers who enjoy Wells as a father writing about his sons' games.
373-lay-morals-and-other-papers:
Robert Louis Stevenson gathers essays and papers in this posthumous volume, with a preface by his wife. The pieces range from youth, marriage, and books to travel and moral choice. Many were written in his roaming years, and the preface recalls island days when leprosy touched every port they knew.

Stevenson argues in a warm, personal voice, mixing jest with stern sense. He praises courage, plain speech, and the habit of facing life as it is. Readers who know his tales will find the same mind here, turned to thought rather than plot, and just as keen on style and truth.
3761-this-country-of-ours:
Henrietta Elizabeth Marshall tells the story of America as a chain of tales for young readers. The book moves from early settlements through the colonial years, with governors, founders, and ordinary folk taking turns at the center. One vivid scene shows Boston gone mad with joy as two ships bring orders to proclaim William and Mary, with bells, bonfires, and a great procession to the town hall.

Marshall writes in a plain storyteller's voice, favoring deeds and scenes over dates and debates. Sir Edmund Andros sent home a prisoner marks one turning point among many. The book suits families and young students who want a first narrative of the United States, told as history that reads like a storybook.
386-virginibus-puerisque-and-other-paper:
Robert Louis Stevenson reflects on youth, love, and marriage in the title essay of this set, then turns to books, travel, and talk. He opens with Shakespeare's marrying men and asks why modern lovers fear vows that older folk took lightly. Later essays weigh idleness, talk, and the art of living well.

Stevenson writes with wit and a light, probing touch, never preaching at length. His sentences sparkle, yet his points bite: youth wastes time, love tests pride, and books shape conduct. The volume shows the essayist at his most personal, thinking aloud for readers who like a sharp mind at play.
3953-cinq-mars:
This edition collects all of Alfred de Vigny's Cinq Mars, with prefaces by Charles de Mazade and Gaston Boissier. The life of Vigny traces a reputation of extraordinary ups and downs. First lauded as precursor of French romantic poetry, then sunk in semi oblivion, he was recovered in the last years as a main illuminating force of the nineteenth century. He stands, the preface says, between Musset and Chenier, lyric and philosophic at once.

A tense passage shows the plot's heart, as the Cardinal's guards question Cinq Mars and allow him to advance only with De Thou. The Cardinal Duke says sharply that he has come too late to speak with the king. Then Louis the Thirteenth himself speaks, torn between irritation at his minister and knowledge that he owes him the day's success. Readers who want Cinq Mars whole will find conspiracy, friendship, and a king's divided mind.
399-cast-upon-the-breakers:
Horatio Alger Jr. tells of Rodney Ropes, a schoolboy left to a faithless guardian, in this rags-to-respect tale. Rodney learns his guardian has drained his funds, and he must leave school to earn his keep. Work, friendship, and pluck carry him through hard towns and harder masters.

Alger follows the familiar moral arc: honest toil beats sly schemes, and a true friend proves worth more than cash. David, a poor day scholar, opens the book as Rodney's first ally. The novel charms as a plain, hopeful tale for young readers, where grit and good conduct win out.
404-industrial-biography-iron-workers-an:
Samuel Smiles continues his Lives of the Engineers with this 1863 study of iron workers and tool makers. He traces iron from early smelters and smiths to the furnace masters who built modern British industry. Chapters follow the Forest of Dean, Sussex cannon works, and the shift from wood charcoal to pit coal.

Smiles profiles inventors and mechanics whose toil, thrift, and skill shaped trade and war. Dud Dudley, early coal smelters, and later engineers each get a clear, fact-filled life. The book praises useful work without show, and it still reads as a solid record of how iron made an age.
4218-sisters:
Ada Cambridge's novel Sisters follows a man who dreads a letter from his baby's caretaker, a lady of whom he stands in undignified dread. Mentioning the matter next day, he finds after breakfast a letter forwarded from Five Creeks, her handwriting paling his brown face.

His stout heart flutters at the sight, and he keeps the letter unopened for some time, afraid to know what he already guesses it contains. Cambridge writes Australian domestic life with warmth and humor. Readers who enjoy family novels of the colonies will find a charming, human story.
4274-wives-and-daughters:
Elizabeth Gaskell's Wives and Daughters carries the subtitle An Every-Day Story. It ran in the Cornhill Magazine from August 1864 to January 1866. It appeared in book form in 1866. Gaskell died suddenly in November 1865, having finished all but the last chapter.

The novel is in one sense unfinished, with the editor's notes on her intentions included at the end. The story centers on Molly Gibson, a doctor's daughter, and the families around her. They include the Hamleys, a new stepmother and stepsister, and suitors who complicate her life. Illustrated by George du Maurier, it is often called Gaskell's masterpiece.
432-the-ambassadors:
Henry James follows Lambert Strether, a middle-aged man from Woollett, Massachusetts, to Paris in this major novel. Sent to fetch home a young man lost to Paris charms, Strether instead falls under the city's spell. He urges his charge to live fully, then learns how much that advice costs.

James writes in long, probing sentences that track Strether's shifting mind. Paris salons, gardens, and river towns form the bright ground of his slow awakening. The novel stands as James's great study of American innocence abroad, and of a man who finds his life only as it slips past.
4325-the-new-book-of-martyrs:
Georges Duhamel, a French surgeon and writer, wrote this book of the First World War from the hospitals and wounded towns of France. Translated by Florence Simmonds, its chapters include Throughout Our Land, the story of Carre and Leronudeau, memories of the martyrs, the death of Mercier, Verdun, and nights in Artois.

Duhamel opens with the cry of wounded men echoing from disfigured regions to the mountains, the ocean, and the inland sea. Every French town, he writes, bears wounds and has taken up the duty of easing suffering. The book is a witness to war's human cost, told by a doctor who saw it daily.
4368-flappers-and-philosophers:
F. Scott Fitzgerald collected these eight stories under the title Flappers and Philosophers, dedicating the book to Zelda. The contents include The Offshore Pirate, The Ice Palace, Head and Shoulders, The Cut-Glass Bowl, Bernice Bobs Her Hair, Benediction, Dalyrimple Goes Wrong, and The Four Fists.

The Offshore Pirate opens on a blue Florida sea, beneath a sky blue as children's irises, with golden disks skipping from wave to wave toward sunset. Fitzgerald's flappers, philosophers, and young men of the Jazz Age move through parties, colleges, and resorts. The collection shows his early gift for glamour, irony, and the ache beneath bright surfaces.
4400-hira-singh-when-india-came-to-fight:
Talbot Mundy wrote this First World War adventure in the voice of Hira Singh, telling how Indian soldiers came to fight in Flanders. Mundy dedicates the book to Elmer Davis, through whom he tracked down the hero of the adventures and found the true account better than the newspapers promised. The hero is Ranjoor Singh and his men.

Mundy notes that had the men been Muslims, their feat would have been wonderful enough, but as Sikhs they defied the very nth degree of odds under splendid leadership. The tale follows escape, endurance, and loyalty across enemy lines. It gives a rare Indian voice to the western front, in a story told as Hira Singh himself tells it.
4615-the-upton-letters:
Arthur Christopher Benson published The Upton Letters in 1905, after the letters were returned to him by the widow of the friend to whom they were written. That friend, sorting papers a few days before his wholly unexpected death, had held the bulky packet. He said the letters should be kept together, and that Benson ought to publish them some day. His sudden death gave that unconsidered wish a certain sanctity, and Benson obeyed it.

A few merely personal matters and casual details were left out, but the main substance stands, and the letters appear just as they were written. Benson admits their hurried faults, and hopes their spontaneity makes up for them. Readers get an intimate Edwardian correspondence, full of books, friendship, college life, and daily thought, best read as a portrait of a mind in letters rather than as a formal essay.
472-the-house-behind-the-cedars:
Charles Chesnutt sets this novel of race and passing in post-Civil War North Carolina. A stranger from South Carolina returns to Patesville, where a light-skinned sister and brother live behind cedars, passing as white. Love, a tournament, and a courtship test their secret, while an old judge and loyal friends watch.

Chesnutt writes with quiet irony about color lines drawn by law and custom. The house itself stands for a hidden past that will not stay hid. The novel stands as a pioneering American work on race, identity, and the price of crossing a line society drew in blood.
482-the-woodlanders:
Thomas Hardy sets this novel in the woods and orchards of Wessex, where timber and apple trees rule life. Grace Melbury, back from school, is torn between Giles Winterborne, a loyal woodsman, and Edred Fitzpiers, a charming doctor with a roving eye. Marty South, a girl who cuts her hair for love, watches their fates.

Hardy writes with somber, lyrical prose, letting the woods mirror human hopes. Class, marriage, and pride tangle the four lives toward a bleak end. The novel stands among Hardy's great tragedies of place, where nature endures and people, for all their longing, do not.
4908-five-of-maxwell-s-papers:
Five papers by James Clerk Maxwell gather work on light, color, and vision, including a curious test with the eye itself. The sample paper follows a dark spot that moves with the eye across the blue part of the spectrum. It refuses to pass into other colors. Maxwell traces it to the yellow spot on the retina.

He shows how to observe the effect with blue and yellow glasses, or with slowly turning papers. A quirk of sight becomes measured science in his hands. The papers' subject and method mark their author throughout. Readers with a taste for physics get a window into how a great tester watched his own eyes at work.
4937-hudibras-in-three-parts-written-in-:
Samuel Butler's Hudibras, written in three parts during the late wars, is the great mock-heroic poem of the English Civil War era. Its Presbyterian knight and his squire ride through a world of sects, factions, and learned folly, arguing theology and politics in verse that never quite lets its heroes look heroic.

The edition adds notes keyed by letters in the text, a glossary for Latin phrases, and translations by the transcriber, who warns they may be inaccurate. Butler's satire targets Puritan cant and Royalist bluster alike. Readers get a comic epic that still explains, better than any history, how England laughed at its own revolution.
4947-sisters:
Cherry Strickland, just eighteen, comes home engaged after twenty-one minutes, and this novel follows what that May evening in California sets in motion. She shuts the Strickland house door behind her, breath rising in deep, ecstatic breaths, half afraid the joy inside her might escape into the moonlight.

Her farewell to Martin and her swift run up the path open a story of sisters, suitors, and family feeling, where an engagement is only the beginning of the complications. An author name is absent from the record. Readers get a warm domestic romance about young love tested by kin, pride, and the long business of growing up.
5004-the-motor-boys-on-the-pacific-or-th:
Clarence Young's Motor Boys on the Pacific sends the boys west with Professor Uriah Snodgrass, through bad news, a desperate race, and strange conversations. A motor boat carries them into fog and onto rocks, horned toads furnish comic relief, and news of a brig, a man on the rocks, and Mr. Blowitz's wants drive the plot.

Derelict hunting gives the voyage its purpose: the boys seek wrecked and abandoned vessels along the Pacific coast. Young keeps the pace brisk and the machinery lovingly described. Readers get a boys' motor adventure of sea, fog, and salvage, where a boat's engine matters as much as any hero's courage.
5066-the-whole-family-a-novel-by-twelve-:
The Whole Family, a novel by twelve authors, begins with an engagement that everyone calls pleasant news, and a decision that the father should speak first. William Dean Howells writes the father, newly arrived in the neighborhood, who must address the suitor's father about the match.

Elizabeth Jordan writes the schoolgirl. Bangs writes the son-in-law. Henry James writes the married son. Elizabeth Stuart Phelps writes the married daughter. Edith Wyatt writes the mother. Mary Raymond Shipman Andrews writes the schoolboy. Alice Brown writes Peggy, and Henry Van Dyke writes the friend of the family. Each chapter gives one member's view. Readers get a collaborative experiment in point of view, where one family's engagement looks different from every chair at the table.
5069-the-doctor-s-dilemma-preface-on-doc:
George Bernard Shaw's Preface on Doctors, attached to The Doctor's Dilemma, argues that medicine pays mutilation better than cure. A man who corrects an ingrowing toenail receives a few shillings, Shaw complains. A man who cuts your inside out receives hundreds of guineas. The exception is surgery on a poor person for practice.

Scandalized voices insist the operations are necessary, Shaw concedes, and they may be. But making the doctor judge of that necessity is like making the hangman judge of hanging. The preface ranges over fees, surgery, and professional power with Shavian wit. Readers get Shaw's case against medical monopoly, as provocative now as when it first appeared.
5076-the-spoilers:
Rex Beach's Spoilers opens on an Alaskan harbor agleam with anchored ships' lights, beneath crenelated mountains black against the sky. Glenister drinks cool air tainted with sea scent. The blood of his boyhood leaps within him. He murmurs that this is his country after all, with a hunger for the North in his veins.

Dextry warns him not to expand too strong in one spot, lest mountain air make men drunk, and returns to his pipe's villainous fumes. The novel follows gold-rush claim jumping, love, and fighting in the far north. Readers get a vigorous Alaska adventure, where the country's beauty and its greed contend for the same men.
516-the-silverado-squatters:
Robert Louis Stevenson recounts squatting in a deserted silver mine on Mount Saint Helena in this California memoir. With his wife and stepson, Stevenson camps in the hills above Napa, visiting Calistoga, a petrified forest, and wine country. A hunter's family, sea fogs, and a toll house fill the days.

Stevenson writes with light, keen prose, praising the mountain as the Mont Blanc of its range. Mine tales, toils, and pleasures mix with sharp sketches of neighbors. The book charms as a honeymoon idyll in rough country, where a sick writer found health and a fine tale.
5177-birds-and-poets-with-other-papers:
John Burroughs's Birds and Poets, volume three of his collected writings, joins outdoor sketches with literary essays. Its papers include Birds and Poets itself, a bird medley, April and spring poems. Studies of Emerson and of genius and beauty complete the set, all written with a naturalist's eye for birdsong and season.

Burroughs moves easily from watching a mockingbird to judging a poem. The book shows why he was America's best loved nature writer. Readers who enjoy nature essays will find close observation, gentle humour. The belief that poetry and bird life belong to the same attentive way of seeing the world runs through it.
5222-the-satyricon-volume-05-crotona-aff:
This fifth volume of Petronius's Satyricon, in W. C. Firebaugh's translation, covers affairs at Crotona from chapter one hundred and twenty-five onward. Eumolpus, flushed with success, boasts that no wish of his can be resisted and that his friends can shield any crime, while his companions grow fat on the city's good things.

The volume holds only the Crotona episodes, in which legacy hunting, flattery, and greed drive the comedy to its most cynical pitch. Readers following the novel in order will find here the Satyricon's late satire on wealth and inheritance, told with unflinching humour.
5259-hildegarde-s-neighbors:
Laura E. Richards's Hildegarde's Neighbors, a story for girls in the Hildegarde series, opens with an arrival. It moves through old friends and new, Pumpkin House, Hester's playroom, teas at Roseholme, and good green wood. Later chapters bring a night-piece, a sailing trip, peril by water, Roger the Codger, and a morning hour before goodbye.

Richards writes warm, cheerful stories of girls' friendships and neighbourhood life, with illustrations in the original. The book offers young readers a gentle adventure among new neighbours, where kindness, play, and small dangers shape a happy summer.
5282-the-tales-and-novels-v9-belphegor-a:
Jean de La Fontaine's Tales and Novels continue in this ninth volume, in English verse translation. Its contents are Belphegor, The Little Bell, and The Glutton. Belphegor opens the volume, addressed to Miss de Chammelay, in which La Fontaine places her name with pleasure at the head of his last effusions. A companion record in this library carries the same three tales.

Belphegor tells of a devil sent from hell to learn whether wives are truly the cause of men's damnation, a story La Fontaine handles with wit and irony. Readers get three tales in which devils, bells, and appetites provide the comedy, all in the light verse manner of La Fontaine's tales.
529-knights-of-art-stories-of-the-italia:
Amy Steedman tells young readers the lives of Italian painters in this art history for children. Giotto, Fra Angelico, Masaccio, Botticelli, Leonardo, Raphael, Michelangelo, Titian, and Tintoretto each get a story, with dates and pictures in color. She opens with picture books themselves, asking how art began.

Steedman writes simply, linking each painter's life to a famed work a child can picture. Assyrian carvings, Egyptian walls, and Greek marble set the long road to Florence. The book serves as a friendly first guide to Renaissance art, where masters appear as knights of a shared craft.
5319-pagan-papers:
Kenneth Grahame's Pagan Papers gathers essays on the romance of the road and the rail, loafing, cheap knowledge, the rural Pan, and smoking, among others. Its contents include Non Libri Sed Liberi, Marginalia, The Eternal Whither, Deus Terminus, An Autumn Encounter, The White Poppy. The Lost Centaur completes the list, opening with Pantagruel's voyage to an island whose roads literally go to places.

Grahame, later famous for The Wind in the Willows, writes here as a lover of the countryside and of books. The essays offer readers a gentle, whimsical celebration of walking, reading. The pagan spirit of nature runs through prose that is both learned and light.
5592-the-complete-short-works-of-georg-e:
Georg Ebers's Complete Short Works gathers five shorter pieces: In the Blue Pike, A Question, The Elixir, The Greylock, and The Nuts. The collection opens with In the Blue Pike. There a rough fellow's curse is understood only by a sickly girl and a red-haired woman leading him by a chain like a tame bear. Nuremberg magistrates had earlier had Cyriax's tongue cut out.

The set ranges from wandering singers and pilgrims to fairy tale and romance, showing Ebers beyond his long Egyptian and German novels. Readers get a varied sampler of his shorter fiction, from street crowds to enchanted lakes, in one volume.
5600-the-historical-romances-of-georg-eb:
This omnibus gathers Georg Ebers's historical romances in one great volume, from Uarda and An Egyptian Princess through The Sisters, Joshua, Cleopatra, and The Emperor to Homo Sum, Serapis, and Arachne. Later romances follow: The Bride of the Nile, A Thorny Path, In the Fire of the Forge, and Margery. Barbara Blomberg, A Word Only a Word, and The Burgomaster's Wife join them, with shorter works and the autobiography completing the set.

The collection opens with Uarda, dedicated in verse to a fostering hand that released Ebers from suffering's grasp. Readers get Ebers's whole fictional world in one place, from ancient Egypt and Rome to medieval Nuremberg and besieged Leyden. It suits anyone who wants the novelist entire.
5631-patty-s-suitors:
Carolyn Wells wrote Patty's Suitors, illustrated by E. C. Caswell, as another book about Patty, following the Patty books and the Marjorie books. Contents run from a valentine party and a telephone call through the Hepworths at home. A perfectly good joke, three pictures, and Princess Poppycheek follow, then suitors, a house party, Eddie Bell, and quarantine.

Later chapters bring meeting it bravely, a surprise, Sister Bee, Kenneth, an invitation, Belle Harcourt, May Day, moonlight, and a ride home in the runabout. Wells writes schoolgirl society with humor. Young readers get a lively romance of parties, suitors, and friendship.
5662-the-potato-child-others:
Mrs. Charles J. Woodbury wrote The Potato Child and Others, a small story collection opening with its title tale. Elsie, a tender-hearted little girl, lives a hard and solitary life. When Miss Amanda selects her from the girls at The Home, the motherly matron feels sorry, knowing a kind word goes a great way with Elsie. Miss Amanda, plainly, will speak few words, kind or unkind, yet The Home is more than full.

Other stories include A Story That Never Ends and A Nazareth Christmas. Readers get gentle, old-fashioned tales of children, homes, and kindness, told with sentiment and care.
5707-the-boy-scout-aviators:
The Boy Scout Aviators follows Harry Fleming and Dick Mercer, two boys caught between nations and new flying machines. Harry is an American abroad. He tells Dick that since he cannot be at home, he would rather be where he is than anywhere else. Dick answers with good-humored English teasing about what it means to be American. From that friendly opening, the story moves toward aviation adventure.

Readers get early flying lore mixed with scout ideals: courage, loyalty, and quick thinking under pressure. The book belongs to a wave of boys' adventure fiction that treated airplanes as wonders still fresh enough to thrill. Young readers who enjoy vintage aviation tales will find brisk action and earnest heroes, with friendship carrying the story between flights.
5730-friends-and-helpers:
Sarah Eddy compiled Friends and Helpers in 1899 to teach children to treat living creatures with considerate kindness. Her preface states the aim plainly: children should appreciate the services of man's helpers in the animal world, a lesson she felt many homes left entirely untaught. The book runs in three parts, gathering stories, poems, and lessons about animals that work beside people.

Readers meet horses, dogs, and farm animals as partners rather than tools, with tales that praise patience and gentle handling. The tone is earnest and humane, typical of humane education in its era. Teachers and families will find a useful historical reader on kindness to animals, and children will enjoy stories that ask them to notice the creatures around them.
580-the-pickwick-papers:
Charles Dickens follows Samuel Pickwick and his club through England in this comic classic, his first novel. The Pickwickians travel by coach, attend card parties, shoot badly, fall in love, and land in the Fleet prison over a breach of promise suit. Sam Weller, Pickwick's sharp servant, steals scene after scene.

Dickens writes in rich, bustling prose, mixing farce, ghost tales, and courtroom satire. Eatanswill's election, Dingley Dell's Christmas, and the Fleet's grim humor mark the road. The book endures as a joyful portrait of old England, where a kind, foolish gentleman learns the world by blundering through it.
5803-not-that-it-matters:
Milne gathers light essays in Not That It Matters. They range from the pleasure of writing and Acacia Road to a library and a chase. Superstition, the charm of golf, goldfish, and Saturday to Monday follow. A household book, Milne suggests in a prefatory note, means a book everybody in the house can enjoy, and these pieces aim at that shared pleasure. The pond, a seventeen-year-old, and further domestic subjects follow.

Readers get Milne's gentle, witty prose on ordinary life, where a walk, a game, or a goldfish becomes a small essay. The tone is urbane without being distant, and the humor depends on observation rather than punch lines. Fans of Milne beyond his children's books will enjoy these pieces, and general readers will find a companionable volume for short, pleasant reading.
5829-the-moneychangers:
Upton Sinclair opens The Moneychangers in a business call, as Lucy wants to visit Montague's office to talk business, but he spares her the trouble. Montague calls the next morning at her apartment before going downtown. Lucy shows him her papers there. They include her father's will, a list of his property, accounts, and the rent roll of her properties in New Orleans. Money, inheritance, and power frame the novel.

Readers follow Sinclair's exposé of finance, as personal fortunes meet Wall Street schemes and the men who move markets. The novel favors plot and argument over lyricism, letting documents and deals drive the drama. It suits readers of Sinclair's muckraking fiction, and anyone curious about how early twentieth-century novels indicted American money power.
5848-the-flyers:
The Flyers opens at the Faraway Club on a cold, thick drizzle of an early spring night, with a biting wind sending chills to the marrow. The weather keeps indoors the few hardy members who have haunted the clubhouse since the season opened a week before. Not more than a dozen loyal devotees of open-air sports lounge about the big clubhouse. Three or four figures gather as the story begins.

Readers enter a club tale of fellowship, sport, and the longing for fair weather and far places. The opening favors atmosphere over action, letting drizzle, wind, and club talk set the mood. The book suits readers who enjoy club stories and early twentieth-century tales of friendship, where the promise of adventure hangs just beyond a rainy window.
6015-captain-macklin-his-memoirs:
Richard Harding Davis gives his young soldier's memoirs, with the narrator admitting it may seem presumptuous for so young a man to write his life. Most men wait until they have achieved something or reached old age, but the soldier's trade is hazardous, and tomorrow may not come.

Macklin calls soldiering the noblest profession a man can follow, and his pages run from West Point through Sagua la Grande, moonlit camps, and barrack yards. Davis writes with a reporter's briskness and a soldier's pride. The memoir treats youth, duty, and danger as reasons to set the record down now.
604-gulliver-of-mars:
Edwin Arnold sends navy lieutenant Gulliver Jones to Mars in this early planetary romance, first titled Lieut. Gulliver Jones. Jones, dreaming of steak in a New York slum, is whisked to a Mars of canals, strange folk, and a pale princess he loves, wins, and loses. War, flight, and ruin follow his quest.

Arnold writes in earnest, romantic prose, with Mars as a mirror of earthly longing. The tale predates Burroughs's Barsoom yet shares its wonder. The book charms fans of early science fiction, where a plain lieutenant's love drives him across a world.
6072-the-boy-allies-with-uncle-sam-s-cru:
Ensign Robert L. Drake opens with Jack's adventure, as Frank Chadwick jumps from a chair in a front window and runs to the door of Lord Hastings's London home. A form swings from the sidewalk along the drive, and Frank flings the door open crying Jack, fearing something happened during two weeks of silence.

Jack laughs that he is perfectly whole, though he expected to be gone only a day or two. Frank replies they sail tomorrow night, likely for America, and Jack arrives just in time. The Boy Allies join Uncle Sam's cruisers for wartime service, where friendship and quick action carry the boys across the Atlantic.
6126-quotations-from-georg-ebers:
This volume gathers quotes from Georg Ebers's old tales of Egypt and the ancient world. David Widger picked them out for Project Gutenberg. Readers who know Ebers may check if their best-loved lines are here.

The editor asks for tips on lines to add, since a web book can be fixed fast. The list gives Uarda in five parts and more novels. Each is tied to a Gutenberg number, with tips for finding any quote in full by use of a word search. The book serves fans and students of Ebers, with choice lines kept in one place.
6148-narrative-and-miscellaneous-papers:
Thomas De Quincey gathers narrative and miscellaneous papers in two volumes, opening the first with The Household Wreck, The Spanish Nun, and Flight of a Tartar Tribe. The Household Wreck warns that to be weak is to be miserable, all weakness being suffering and humiliation.

The second volume adds the heavens by Lord Rosse's telescopes, modern superstition, Coleridge and opium-eating, temperance, war, and Kant's last days. De Quincey ranges from frail human tenure of joy to star systems and morals. This collected edition is described from its opening volume onward, without favoring either part.
6180-a-romany-of-the-snows-vol-1-being-a:
A Romany of the Snows continues the personal histories of Pierre and His People, offering the last existing records of Pretty Pierre. Its first volume holds Across the Jumping Sandhills, A Lovely Bully, The Filibuster, and The Gift of the Simple King.

Parker inscribes the tales to Sir William C. Van Horne, whose career belongs inseparably to the far north's life and development. Later volumes promise Malachi, the Lake of the Great Slave, the Red Patrol, and the Going of the White Swan. The first continuation set alone is examined in this entry, while its later continuation sets await separate entries.
6181-a-romany-of-the-snows-vol-2-being-a:
Malachi opens Parker's second Romany volume, as Freddy Tarlton gravely says he'll swing just the same tomorrow, exit Malachi. A door opens on gossips, a man takes the only vacant seat near the fire, stretches hands to heat, and looks at coals with drooping, introspective eyes.

Exit Malachi, he says presently in a soft ironical voice, without looking up, and Tarlton asks Pierre where he sprang from. Pierre answers that the wind bloweth where it listeth, and does not tell where it has been. The Lake of the Great Slave, Red Patrol, and White Swan follow.
6182-a-romany-of-the-snows-vol-3-being-a:
The Bridge House opens Parker's third Romany volume, standing on a wide wall between two small bridges, approaches to a big covered bridge over the Madawaska's main channel. When spring thaws swell the river, flanking channels divide at the house foundations and rustle toward rapids.

From any window one can watch the ugly rushing current, gorged with logs, batter the wall, jostle between piers, and race to rocks, dam, and slide. The Epaulettes, The House with the Broken Shutter, The Finding of Fingall, and Three Commandments follow. This entry takes up the third continuation set by itself, and the other continuation sets are not taken up.
6183-a-romany-of-the-snows-vol-4-being-a:
Little Babiche opens Parker's fourth Romany volume. A narrator corrects the governor: they did not tell you right, for he was with Little Babiche fifteen years, as long as he has known the governor. It was near Noel, the day of the Great Birth, with feastings, grand songs, and many candles.

The governor of the great Company settles back, powerful face seamed by years, hair grey and thick, keen eyes burning under shaggy brows. The Spoil of the Puma, The Trail of the Sun Dogs, and The Pilot of Belle Amour complete the volume.
6184-a-romany-of-the-snows-vol-5-being-a:
The Cruise of the Ninety-Nine opens Parker's fifth Romany volume, with a big gulf yawl a man and boy could manage at a pinch, old-fashioned high bulwarks, lying clean in water. She holds a tolerable record for speed and for other things sometimes considered by the government at Quebec.

The cure named her Ninety-Nine with humor, after telling owner and captain Tarboe the smuggler he came to seek one lost sheep, leaving ninety-nine in the fold at Isle of Days. A Romany of the Snows and The Plunderer complete the volume.
62-a-princess-of-mars:
A Civil War veteran wakes on a dying planet of green warriors and red cities. Edgar Rice Burroughs' A Princess of Mars sends John Carter from an Arizona cave to Barsoom. Lower gravity gives him great strength and leaps.

Captured by Tharks, Carter befriends the chieftain Tars Tarkas and rescues Dejah Thoris, princess of Helium. Arena fights, air scouts, and an atmosphere factory fill his adventures. Love and war pull him between two peoples. The book launched the Barsoom saga. Sequels followed Carter across Barsoom, and the series shaped science fiction adventure for decades.
625-ponkapog-papers:
Thomas Bailey Aldrich gathers notes and essays from Ponkapog, Massachusetts, in this modest volume. Leaves from a notebook, asides, queer names, plot and character, the cruelty of science, and writers and talkers fill the pages. Aldrich chose the Ponkapog name for its modest air, fitting papers that claim no rivalry with great literature.

Aldrich writes with light, polished wit, turning a Kropotkin note on photography into a fantasy of a man photographed out of his good traits. The book charms as a leisurely miscellany, where a New England writer muses on books, folk, and fame without strain.
6354-italian-hours:
Henry James gathers his Italian notes, first collected with other impressions, now placed together for the first time in this November 1909 volume. Venice opens the contents, with the Grand Canal, an early impression, two old houses and three young women, and Casa Alvisi. From Chambery to Milan, the old Saint Gothard, Italy revisited, and a Roman holiday follow, with Roman rides, neighbourhoods, and a notebook from the after season.

A chain of cities, Siena early and late, autumn in Florence, Tuscan cities, and Ravenna close the run. James writes of porticoes at Turin, soft warm air, and the look of the written word itself, which tricks lovers of art into Italian satisfactions on easy terms. The book is travel writing as observation, where a street, a canal, and a facade carry a whole history of feeling.
6361-making-good-on-private-duty-practic:
Harriet Camp Lounsbery, president of the West Virginia State Nurses' Association, writes for graduate nurses on private duty, under the motto not to be ministered unto, but to minister. Though technique changes and teaching grows better, she says, the old problems of private work remain, and young nurses still face them. Her chapters run from nurse and patient, nurse and doctor, and nurse herself, to family, friends, and servants.

Foods and feeding, training school ties, complaints, teaching, convalescence, and waiting days follow, with hints for obstetrical nursing, washing the baby, and the valley of the shadow. Lounsbery advises patience with talkative helpers, never rebuking an amateur nurse harshly, but suggesting gently what would serve the patient more. The book is practical wisdom for a nurse alone in a home, where tact matters as much as skill.
64-the-gods-of-mars:
Edgar Rice Burroughs returns John Carter to Barsoom, the Mars of his earlier romance, twelve years after Carter's strange burial in Virginia. Plant men, a forest battle, and a chamber of mystery open the quest. Burroughs wrote The Gods of Mars as the second Barsoom book, after A Princess of Mars.

Carter seeks Dejah Thoris and Thuvia through corridors of peril, black pirates, and the prison isle of Shador, toward Issus, goddess of life eternal. The novel is fast pulp adventure, with sword fights, air battles, and escapes at every turn. Thuvia and the black pirates widen Carter's world, adding new peoples to the red planet.
6453-the-potiphar-papers:
George William Curtis gathers The Potiphar Papers as satire on fashionable manners. It opens with Goldsmith on parlor splendors and Burke on manners as air we breathe, vexing or soothing by constant, insensible operation. A prefatory letter to the Reverend Cream Cheese sets the tone, with Walton's angler preferring a temperate poor man to a drunken lord. Curtis writes as a watcher of New York society, amused and sharp.

A mid passage argues with Mr. P. about style of living: is his manner inferior to old Mrs. Podge or Mrs. Croesus, and will cutting back make people suspect his affairs? Do not make rash vows, the narrator advises, but go to sleep, recalling Mrs. Croesus said the same to her husband. The papers mock wealth, display, and the fear of seeming poor, in a city where manners are the real currency.
6472-on-the-pampas-or-the-young-settlers:
G. A. Henty sends young settlers to the pampas in a tale whose frontispiece shows the fight with the puma. Mrs. Hardy's resolution opens it, as her husband wonders one evening what he should make of the boys, a train of thought about their circumstances carrying him far. The start, a new life, the pampas, and the settler's home follow, with a tale of the Mexican War told by Seth and continued across two chapters.

Farm work and amusements, neighbourly visits, lost cattle, quiet times, and a steady hand fill the middle, before an Indian attack, terrible news, and the pampas on fire. A mid passage finds captives plotting escape, gnawing through each other's thongs if only their guards would leave them alone ten minutes. Henty writes settler adventure with cattle, fire, and frontier danger.
6625-the-coming-of-the-friars:
Augustus Jessopp, a canon of Norwich, gathers historic essays first printed in The Nineteenth Century, now revised with additions. The title essay on the friars' coming leads to village life in Norfolk six hundred years ago, daily life in a medieval monastery, and the Black Death in East Anglia. A university's building and a prophet of Walnut-Tree Yard close the set.

Jessopp writes as a scholar who loves a good story, with vivid detail on monks, peasants, and plague. His essays make medieval England feel close and human, not distant and dry. The Coming of the Friars is a lively, learned book for readers who like history told with warmth and wit.
6672-the-caesars:
Thomas De Quincey opens on the Roman emperors, whose condition, he says, has never been fully grasped in its unique grandeur. There was but one Rome, he argues, no other city of ancient or modern times matching it in size, and few in display. London, he jokes, should be called a nation, not a city, yet even London cannot match Rome at her height.

A million and a half souls lived in Rome at her peak, a scale that shaped the emperors' lonely power. De Quincey writes with learned fire, mixing history, logic, and high rhetoric. The Caesars is a bold, brilliant essay on empire, power, and the strange fate of men who ruled the world.
6727-england-under-the-tudors:
Arthur Innes writes England under the Tudors in a fourth edition, with a general editor's note on the flood of new historical material. Standard histories, the note says, need revision or even replacement, as monographs, letters, and records pile up faster than scholars can absorb them. Yet few have tried to rewrite history on a large scale.

Innes takes up that task for the Tudor age, from Henry the Seventh to Elizabeth, with a clear, scholarly narrative. His book suits students who want a full, orderly survey. England Under the Tudors is a solid, early twentieth-century history of a dynasty that remade England.
68-the-warlord-of-mars:
John Carter has haunted the Temple of the Sun for six Martian months. Edgar Rice Burroughs' Warlord of Mars, third in the Barsoom series, opens with Carter trailing a shadow toward his entombed princess. Dejah Thoris may live or lie dead below.

Carter crosses the river Iss, the Kaolian road, and carrion caves toward war. New allies join him against yellow men and old foes. Battles, a magnet switch, and a tide of fighting lead to rewards. The novel crowns Carter's long quest on the dying planet. Burroughs's Mars books continued to shape planetary adventure for later writers and filmmakers.
6852-venus-in-furs:
Leopold von Sacher-Masoch's Venus in Furs, in Fernanda Savage's translation from German, was printed in only 1225 copies for private circulation, with type then distributed. An introduction traces Sacher-Masoch from Lemberg in 1836, through law at Prague and Graz, to teaching, then to a full literary life. He edited a Leipzig review, lived in Paris as a Francophile, and died at Lindheim in 1895.

His marriage in 1873 to Aurora von Rumelin, who wrote as Wanda von Dunajew, mirrors the novel's own tangle of love, power, and surrender. The tale that follows is frank, strange, and famous. Venus in Furs is a landmark erotic novel, best read with its history in mind.
6865-four-years:
William Butler Yeats looks back on 1887 to 1891, when his family had lately come from Dublin to settle at Bedford Park in London. The red brick house, its garden under a great horse chestnut, and streets shaped by Pre-Raphaelite taste set the scene for a young writer finding his place. He recalls the gap between the suburb's high ideals and its plain daily life, from shops that looked common to a church he never liked.

Friends, talk, and art fill these years, as Yeats measures the hopes of his circle against small letdowns close at hand. The memoir moves through rooms, streets, and gatherings rather than through great public events. It keeps returning to how a place can stir the mind even while it fails its promise.
6876-the-british-association-s-visit-to-:
Lady Rayleigh gathers letters on the British Association's 1884 visit to Montreal, a meeting planned long in advance for a far city. The introduction, drawn from the Times, notes that the Dominion government and Canadian men of science had chosen presidents and fixed steamship and rail deals. Excursions were planned, and full guidance was drawn up for members before the ships sailed.

Much of that readiness is credited to the High Commissioner, Sir Charles Tupper, and his zeal for the visit. The letters that follow record the crossing, the welcome, and the work of the sections. They give a private view of how a great body of British science carried its yearly meeting across the Atlantic to Canada.
6901-the-happy-adventurers:
Lydia Miller Middleton tells a tale she calls strictly true, of children who find adventure in building, digging, and play. The chapters name their games one by one: a little house built by small hands, a cherry garden, a duke's nose hunt, a miracle, grape gathering, and a fateful stone. A Kipling verse at the head claims little has changed in the building trade since things were made.

Grannie opens the story with the old saying that woes cluster, and the children answer trouble with pluck and humor. Illustrations catch moments like a wish for a bridge to a brother and a watch kept on a kangaroo. The book keeps a warm, homely tone, and it ends as it began, with the joy of making.
6914-the-last-of-the-huggermuggers:
Christopher Pearse Cranch tells a giant story of Little Jacket, a boy who longs to go to sea. Luck at sea, good and bad, brings him to shore and then to the giant Huggermugger, whose boot becomes his strange shelter. He escapes from the shop of Kobboltozo, learns to use the giant in travel, and at last leaves the giant's island with friends.

Later chapters bring Mister Nabbum, Zebedee and Jacky plotting together, and a return voyage to the island. The Huggermuggers appear in a new light at Huggermugger Hall, while Missus Huggermugger grows thin and fades and the giant's sorrows deepen. Cranch mixes fairy tale wonder with jokes about size, pride, and home.
6984-the-pothunters:
Wodehouse's Pothunters opens with Tony Graham looking up from his bag as a voice asks where it has seen a face before. Allen's arrival sets the school tale moving, and the contents promise patient perseverance producing pugilistic prodigies, thieves breaking in to steal, and certain revelations. A mutual friend, a literary banquet, and Barrett's exploring lead to a sleuth hound and Mister Thompson's inquiries.

The sports, an interesting interview, and Sir Alfred's scoring give way to a long run, explanations, and the disappearance of J Thomson. A search follows, whether he be above the ground, and the affairs of various persons are wound up at the close. Wodehouse mixes school sport, theft, and detection with light humor.
6991-across-the-years:
Eleanor Porter gathers stories across the years, reprinted by leave from the Ladies Home Journal, Ainslee's, the Century, Harper's Bazaar, and other magazines. The contents list When Father and Mother Rebelled, Jupiter Ann, the Axminster path, Phineas and the motor car, and the most wonderful woman. The price of a pair of shoes, the long road, a couple of capitalists, and the bridge across the years follow.

Later tales give a summons home, black silk gowns, a belated honeymoon, and the giving thanks of Cyrus and Huldah. When Father and Mother Rebelled opens a month before Christmas, with Lyddy Ann hearing the news. Porter writes New England life with warmth, humor, and a keen eye for small revolts of the heart.
6995-ghosts-i-have-met-and-some-others:
John Kendrick Bangs meets ghosts with humor in this collection, dedicated to choice spirits everywhere. The contents list ghosts that haunted him, the mystery of his grandmother's hair sofa, the mystery of Barney O'Rourke, and an exorcism that failed. Thurlow's Christmas story, the Dampmere mystery, and Carleton Barker first and second follow, with illustrations by Newell, Frost, and Richards.

Captions catch the tone: grotesque attitudes no one ever saw, a thing grinning in a chair, a friendly spectre standing by, and a flight madly through wainscoting. Bangs tells of gold and silver ware in the Elysian fields, empty chairs, and cooking sherry drained to the dregs. The book is a comic ghost book, where dread gives way to laughter.
7044-in-the-courts-of-memory-1858-1875-f:
L de Hegermann Lindencrone draws In the Courts of Memory, 1858 to 1875, from contemporary letters of court life. Illustrations name Madame Charles Moulton, the Fay house at Cambridge, Emperor Napoleon the Third, Empress Eugenie, and composer Auber. Facsimiles show letters from the Duke de Morny, Jenny Lind, and Liszt, with signatures and answers from Merimee, Metternich, Napoleon, and Eugenie to Madame Moulton's questions.

Views of Compiegne and Pierrefonds, their music hall and hall of fetes, and the hall of heroes set the stage. Elihu Washburn and Raoul Rigault appear among the figures of the age. The letters carry readers into Second Empire salons, concerts, and courts, through the eyes of a woman who lived among princes and artists.
7053-pages-from-a-journal-with-other-pap:
Mark Rutherford gathers pages from a journal with other papers in this 1901 Unwin volume, second impression. The contents open with a visit to Carlyle in 1868, then early morning in January, March, June, August, and the end of October. November, the break up of a great drought, and Spinoza follow, with a supplementary note on the devil, injustice, and time settling controversies.

Later papers treat talking about troubles, faith, patience, an apology, and belief, unbelief, and superstition. Judas Iscariot, Scott's use of the supernatural, September 1798, and notes on Milton lead to the morality of Byron's poetry and Byron, Goethe, and Matthew Arnold. Rutherford writes a quiet, reflective journal of reading and conscience.
7082-lives-of-the-necromancers:
William Godwin writes Lives of the Necromancers as an account of the most eminent persons in successive ages who claimed magical power or had it imputed to them. Published in London in 1834, the book aims to exhibit a fair picture of human credulity, which Godwin holds cannot fail to teach salutary lessons. One view of the subject, he argues, teaches a useful pride in the abundance of our faculties.

Without pride, he insists, man is of little value, since pride stirs great undertakings and the secret persuasion of extraordinary talents. Footnotes, numbered in sequence and moved to the end, support the narrative. Godwin's lives run through magicians, prophets, and pretenders, showing how wonder and fraud shaped ages before science.
72-thuvia-maid-of-mars:
Carthoris, son of John Carter, loves Thuvia of Ptarth, but custom and war stand between them. Edgar Rice Burroughs' Thuvia, Maid of Mars, fourth in the Barsoom series, opens in the royal gardens where a suitor presses his case. Thuvia is soon swept into slavery, treachery, and a war between cities.

Chapters carry her through phantom bowmen, the Jeddak of Lothar, and the hall of doom. Carthoris fights green men and white apes to reach her, aided by the bowman Kar Komak. A glossary of Martian names and terms closes the volume. The romance keeps Burroughs's Mars vivid with duels, escapes, and strange cities.
7304-the-life-of-captain-matthew-flinder:
Ernest Scott, professor of history at the University of Melbourne, tells the life of Captain Matthew Flinders, who died one hundred years before this book's 1914 publication. Within forty years Flinders discovered a very large area of what is now an important region of the earth. He took part in stirring events memorable in modern history, and applied a vigorous, original mind to knowledge with useful results.

Scott adds that Flinders was the victim of circumstances peculiarly unfortunate, whatever way they are stated, and bound to win sympathy from any reader who takes the trouble to understand them. Portraits, maps, and facsimiles support the text. The biography honours an explorer whose charts outlived his troubles.
742-editorials-from-the-hearst-newspaper:
Arthur Brisbane, the leading editorial voice of the Hearst newspapers, gathers his daily pieces on politics, business, and American life at the turn of the century. Brisbane wrote for millions, in short, punchy paragraphs. Brisbane edited Hearst papers in New York, where his column reached millions daily.

The editorials show Hearst journalism at its most confident, urging reform, praising progress, and scolding power. Historians of the press value the volume as a record of what ordinary readers were told, day after day. His plain style, short sentences and bold claims, set the tone for popular journalism.
7422-roman-holidays-and-others:
W. D. Howells published these travel sketches in 1908, after a lifetime of writing about Europe and America. The journey begins up and down Madeira, passes through Spain, and comes ashore at Genoa. Naples and her joyful noise, Pompeii revisited, and a week at Leghorn follow, with Pisa and Genoa again before the close.

The title piece, Roman Holidays, sits at the center: Rome seen not as a museum but as a living city on holiday. Howells writes as a familiar visitor, amused by crowds, ruins, and modern streets in the same paragraph. The book ends with Eden After the Fall, a wry coda. It is travel writing for readers who like their ruins mixed with people.
7504-tom-of-the-raiders:
Austin Bishop's Civil War story follows Tom with the Second Ohio into one of the war's boldest strokes. The chapters map the adventure: the raiders start, Tom is arrested, Tom goes alone, Tom arrives at the Beeghams', and on to Chattanooga and Marietta. Then the train is captured, and the race begins.

Pursuit, speeding northward, fighting with fire, and fighting the river follow, as Tom and his companions run for the Tennessee line with the enemy after them. Morgan Dennis's illustrations picture Tom feeding logs into the flames. The book is a boys' tale of the great train raid, told at full gallop, ending with Tom reporting at headquarters.
7509-the-logbooks-of-the-lady-nelson-wit:
Ida Lee, author of The Coming of the British to Australia, gathered the logbooks of the Lady Nelson in one volume. The little Australian discovery ship's story comes with the journal of her first commander, Lieutenant James Grant of the Royal Navy. Sixteen charts and illustrations from the originals in the Admiralty Library accompany the text. Lee dedicated the book to her grandfather, William Lee, one of Australia's pioneers.

Grant's story is paraphrased in places, since he sometimes writes in diary form under date headings and sometimes inserts the date into his narrative. The Lady Nelson's voyages, undertaken for discovery, make her logbooks of more than ordinary interest. The volume preserves the working record of early Australian coastal exploration, in the words of the men who sailed it.
7542-quotes-and-images-from-the-novels-o:
Georg Ebers, the German Egyptologist turned novelist, wrote historical romances once read across Europe, and this volume collects short passages and pictures from them. Portraits and illustrations introduce the novels: Uarda, Cleopatra, Margery, Homo Sum, the Recluse, and In the Fire of the Forge. Any passage can be searched to find its full context in the eBook below.

Read together, the passages sketch Ebers's moral world: Egypt and Germany, ancient and modern, seen through private choices. First impressions, small joys, timely words, and the claims of honor recur across them. The pictures help a new reader tell the novels apart. It is a pleasant way into Ebers: short, vivid samples before choosing a romance to read whole.
776-hermione-and-her-little-group-of-ser:
Don Marquis creates Hermione, a fashionable young woman who takes up every serious thought of the day and talks it to death. Her little group of thinkers meets to discuss art, souls, and the new psychology, with great earnestness. Marquis created Hermione for the New York Sun, where her chatter delighted readers.

Marquis writes the sketches as Hermione's own chatter, and the comedy lies in her confident misuse of big ideas. The book satirises a whole generation of drawing-room intellectuals, and its heroine remains delightfully unaware. Her group, earnest and vague, mirrors real drawing-room fashions for Bergson, Freud, and souls.
7762-wanderers:
Knut Hamsun's Wanderers, translated by W. W. Worster, joins two volumes, Under the Autumn Star and A Wanderer Plays on Muted Strings, under one title. Its center is Knut Pedersen from the Northlands, through whose eyes the fates of Captain Falkenberg and his wife slowly unfold.

Worster's introduction calls the books close to diaries, mirroring Hamsun's moods and known life events with unusual candor. Read with the sequel The Last Joy, they form a psychological record as much as a story, tracing a wanderer's mind through autumn roads and muted music.
7766-a-dog-of-flanders:
Louisa de la Ramee, writing as Ouida, tells of Nello and Patrasche in A Dog of Flanders, with color pictures by Maria L. Kirk. A Flemish boy and a big Flemish dog, both orphaned and poor, share a hut a league from Antwerp, among pastures, cornlands, and poplar lines.

Their bond, closer than brotherhood, grows from a shared rescue and daily toil pulling a cart. Nello draws with charcoal and dreams of art, while Patrasche pulls beside him. The tale is a tender classic of loyalty, poverty, and a child's hope, known to readers far beyond Flanders.
781-sinking-of-the-titanic-and-great-sea:
Logan Marshall edited this account of the Titanic's loss and of other great sea disasters, written soon after the event. The Titanic, the largest and finest steamship of her day, struck an iceberg on her maiden voyage, 600 miles southeast of Halifax, with more than 2,300 souls aboard. The book tells of the collision, the boats, and the rescue.

Other chapters gather wrecks and heroics from the age of steam, with portraits of captains, crews, and passengers. Marshall writes for a popular audience, with a moral eye on pride, speed, and the lack of boats. The book is a vivid, if partisan, record of how the world first learned of the disaster, and why it shocked the age.
7856-the-cheerful-cricket-and-others:
Jeannette Marks's The Cheerful Cricket and Others, pictured by Edith Brown and dedicated to her nephew Henry Douglas Bacon, tells insect tales for children good and bad, big or little. The cheerful cricket runs anxiously through grass, while Mrs. Cricky hunts food for Chee, Chirk, and Chirp.

Other stories bring a slothful toad, sullen caterpillar, green inch worm, mean spider, noisy fly, dizzy moth, honest ant, walking stick, ladybug, and tuneful hummingbird. A marsh grass vesper quartette sings late at night. Through small creatures, Marks teaches cheer, work, and kindness.
7932-brook-farm-historic-and-personal-me:
John Thomas Codman wrote these memoirs of Brook Farm, the famous community founded near Boston in the 1840s. His chapters trace the movement from its Transcendentalist beginnings under George Ripley, through its reorganisation on Fourierist lines, to its industrial period. Along the way he describes Ripley, Charles Dana, Margaret Fuller-era friends, and Nathaniel Hawthorne, who lived at the farm.

Codman writes as a participant, mixing the community's constitution and daily rules with personal memories of work, walks, and wild flowers. The book is therefore both a history and a first-hand account of an American experiment in shared living. It remains a key source for anyone studying Transcendentalism, utopian communities, or Hawthorne's early circle.
7941-mrs-day-s-daughters:
Mary E. Mann set this English provincial novel in the household of Mrs William Day, opening at a New Year's party that dances into the small hours. The chapters that follow trace the Day daughters, Bessie and Deleah among them, through an office disaster, family misfortune, and the suitors, neighbours, and callers who crowd a market-town social world. Names like the Manchester man and the importunate Mr Gibbon hint at the comedy and worry mixed into the plot.

Mann writes with a keen eye for class, money, and reputation in a small community, where one setback can unsettle a whole family. The novel moves between drawing room, tea-party, and office, and its interest lies in how ordinary people recover their footing. It is a warm, observant example of the late Victorian domestic novel at its most readable.
7994-the-crayon-papers:
Geoffrey Crayon, Gent. , the pen name of Washington Irving, gathered these miscellaneous papers under his familiar byline. They range widely: Mountjoy, or passages from the life of a castle-builder; the Great Mississippi Bubble, a time of unexampled prosperity; Don Juan as a spectral research; Broek, or the Dutch paradise. Sketches in Paris in 1825, including the Tuileries, Windsor Castle, and the field of Waterloo; American researches in Italy; and early experiences of Ralph Ringwood, plus Seminole traditions.

The collection shows Irving in his most roaming mood, mixing travel, history, legend, and humour. Each paper stands alone, so the book can be dipped into anywhere. For readers who know The Sketch Book, it offers more of the same urbane pleasure, and a reminder of how widely Irving travelled in search of stories.
8004-the-bible-king-james-version-book-4:
Numbers, the fourth book of the Bible, takes its name from the censuses that open and close it, counting Israel's tribes in the wilderness. Between the counts lies forty years of wandering: complaints about food, rebellion against Moses, the report of spies who feared Canaan, and the death of the generation that left Egypt. Only Caleb and Joshua, of that generation, will enter the land, and the book ends with Israel camped across the Jordan.

The book is frank about a people's failures, showing how fear and grumbling delay promise. Its laws about priests, vows, and inheritance sit inside a travel story that never quite arrives. In the King James Version, Numbers reads as a long, honest middle chapter: between deliverance and home, with a whole generation lost on the way.
8110-lincoln-letters:
Abraham Lincoln's letters, published by the Bibliophile Society, are presented as so characteristic of the man and so self-explanatory that they need no comment. The editor notes philosophical admonitions to Lincoln's brother Johnston written on the same sheet as a letter to his father, and an unequivocal order to the Attorney-General. Endorsed on a pardon request, showing how promptly Lincoln despatched affairs during the most turbulent scenes of the Civil War.

The letters range from family counsel to presidential orders, and their plain, direct style is Lincoln's own. Readers meet the president without a biographer's filter: patient, humorous, and decisive. For students of Lincoln, the volume is a compact source, and for general readers, a moving introduction to his character in his own words.
8140-lectures-of-col-r-g-ingersoll-volum:
Robert G. Ingersoll's first volume of lectures gathers his famous freethought orations, including Gods, Ghosts, Hell, Individuality, Humboldt, Which Way, The Great Infidels. Talmagian Theology, and The Mistakes of Moses, with his answers to the clergy and his oration at his brother's grave. The lecture on Gods opens with his claim that an honest god is the noblest work of man, and that each nation creates a god resembling its creators.

Ingersoll, the Great Agnostic, drew huge crowds with eloquence, humour, and moral argument against orthodoxy. His lectures made freethought respectable in Gilded Age America, and his defence of reason still reads with force. For readers interested in American religious debate, this volume is the essential Ingersoll, in his own rousing voice.
8154-revolutionary-heroes-and-other-hist:
James Parton, author of lives of Horace Greeley, Andrew Jackson, and Benjamin Franklin, wrote these historical papers for the Historical Classic Readings series, number ten. His subjects include General Joseph Warren, Captain Nathan Hale, Washington's spies, Robert Morris, Valley Forge, John Jay, John Adams, Fisher Ames, and the Pinckneys. Parton himself was born in Canterbury, England, in 1822, brought to America at five, and educated in New York.

The papers are short, vivid lives and episodes from the Revolution, written for schools and general readers. Parton was a popular biographer, and his sketches favour anecdote and character over theory. For students of the Revolution, the volume offers an old-fashioned but engaging gallery of its heroes, in the style that once taught American history.
8157-esther-waters:
George Moore published Esther Waters in 1899, opening with a young woman of twenty on a railway platform, watching a receding train. She wears a faded yellow dress and a black jacket too warm for the day. And beside her lies an oblong box tied with rope, while the bundle she carries bulges with dead weight. From that arrival, the novel follows Esther, a servant girl, through work, seduction, single motherhood, and the struggle to keep herself and her child respectable.

Moore wrote with the frankness of French naturalism, refusing to soften Esther's hardships or to condemn her. The novel's power lies in its heroine's endurance and in its picture of domestic service and horse-racing society. It remains one of the great English novels of working-class life, and Moore's most humane book.
8231-the-world-english-bible-web-numbers:
Numbers, in the World English Bible, opens with Yahweh speaking to Moses in the wilderness of Sinai, in the Tent of Meeting, in the second year after the Exodus. Commanding a census of Israel by families and fathers' houses, every male from twenty years old and upward able to go to war, numbered by divisions with a head of each tribe. Lightly reformatted from ebible. org by Martin Ward, the book follows the wilderness wanderings that give it its name.

The modern version keeps the counts, camps, and complaints in order, so the forty years of delay read as a coherent journey. Numbers here shows a people learning, through failure, toward the promised land. For readers working through the Pentateuch, this rendering makes a long book easier to follow.
8377-the-water-ghost-and-others:
John Kendrick Bangs, the American humorist, gathers ghost stories with a comic twist in this volume. Contents include The Water Ghost of Harrowby Hall, The Spectre Cook of Bangletop, and A Speck on the Lens. A Midnight Visitor and The Ghost Club follow, along with the literary remains of Thomas Bragdon. Bangs treats the supernatural as a chance for jokes rather than terror.

His ghosts complain, cook, and join clubs, and the humor lies in treating them as ordinary, tiresome company. Readers who like ghost stories without dread, in the vein of Bangs's popular humorous fiction, will find the book light and clever. It is a good introduction to a writer who made the afterlife funny.
8424-mohun-or-the-last-days-of-lee-and-h:
John Esten Cooke presents this novel as the final memoirs of Colonel Surry of Eagle's Nest, a staff officer serving in Virginia, and it tells the last days of Robert E. Lee and his paladins. Two crossed swords hang over the mantel in Surry's quiet study, and the prologue turns from that peace to the closing campaigns of the Civil War.

Cooke, a Confederate veteran and prolific novelist, wrote the Surry books as romantic history, loyal to Lee and his circle. Readers meet the Army of Northern Virginia in its final months, through a staff officer's eyes. The novel is a Southern romance of the war's end, best read with its sympathies understood as those of its time and author.
8485-books-fatal-to-their-authors:
P. H. Ditchfield gathers stories of books fatal to their authors, dedicating the volume to John Walter of Bearwood. His preface, addressed to the book lover, admits a risk. To record the woes of authors and discourse on fatal books seems to court the displeasure of the fickle mistress who presides over authorship. The chapters that follow tell of writers ruined, imprisoned, or killed for their books.

Ditchfield, an antiquary and clergyman, writes literary history as cautionary tale, with anecdotes of censorship, libel, and martyrdom. Readers who love books about books will find a morbid, fascinating collection. It reminds writers that words once had sharper consequences, and that fame could be fatal.
8495-the-life-of-st-frances-of-rome-and-:
Lady Georgiana Fullerton wrote The Life of St. Frances of Rome, with lives of Blessed Lucy of Narni, Dominica of Paradiso, and Anne de Montmorency, and an introductory essay on the miraculous life of the saints by J. M. Capes. The authorities for the histories are set out at the start, grounding the lives in sources.

Fullerton, a Catholic convert and novelist, writes saints' lives for Victorian readers, with devotion and narrative skill. Frances, a Roman wife and mystic, anchors the volume, and the other lives show women of faith in different centuries. Readers get hagiography in the nineteenth-century manner, earnest and edifying, and a window onto Catholic devotion.
8546-two-summers-in-guyenne-a-chronicle-:
Edward Harrison Barker, author of Wayfaring in France and Wanderings by Southern Waters, wrote Two Summers in Guyenne as a chronicle of the wayside and waterside, with maps and illustrations. Contents follow the upper Dordogne, across the moors of the Corrèze, in the viscounty of Turenne, and on through the villages and rivers of southwestern France.

Barker writes travel as slow walking and boating, with attention to churches, doorways, and local life, like the abbey church at Beaulieu pictured at the head. Readers get Edwardian travel writing at its most leisurely, for a region less visited than Provence. The book suits armchair travelers and walkers planning a Dordogne tour.
8547-pirke-avot-the-sayings-of-the-jewis:
Pirke Avot, the Sayings of the Jewish Fathers, gathers the ethical teachings of the rabbis in the Mishnah, and this edition transliterates Hebrew letters in brackets, spelling them out where needed. A transcriber's note explains the method, so readers without Hebrew can follow the text, with rare additional notes also in brackets.

The sayings themselves are short and practical: on study, character, community, and the world to come, passed from master to disciple. Jews read Pirke Avot on Sabbath afternoons between Passover and the New Year. Readers new to rabbinic literature get a welcoming doorway, with the Hebrew kept visible beside the English.
8604-the-house-of-atreus-being-the-agame:
Aeschylus wrote the three tragedies gathered here about the cursed house of Atreus, in E. D. A. Morshead's English version. Agamemnon returns from Troy to be murdered by his wife; his son Orestes avenges him in The Libation-Bearers. And in The Furies, the avenging spirits pursue Orestes until Athens itself must judge him. An introductory note sketches Aeschylus, born at Eleusis in 525 BC, soldier and playwright, dead in Sicily in 456 BC.

Together the plays trace blood guilt from one generation to the next, asking whether revenge can ever end without law. Gods, ghosts, choruses, and courts all take part in the argument. The trilogy remains the foundation of Western tragedy. This plain translation lets a new reader follow its stark plot and fierce poetry without a scholar's apparatus getting in the way.
8697-guns-and-snowshoes-or-the-winter-ou:
Captain Ralph Bonehill sends four boy hunters into winter camp in this Boy Hunters series volume, also billed as the outing of the gun club. The contents promise a quarrel in the snow, snowballing with results, an explosion, chickens and mince pie, a dismaying discovery, and a first night in camp. Bonehill, author of Four Boy Hunters and the Flag of Freedom series, knew his young audience well.

Snowshoes, guns, tracking, and camp craft fill the chapters, with mishaps and rivalries keeping the fun moving. The boys learn to work together, handle firearms with care, and endure cold nights outdoors. It is straightforward Edwardian boys' adventure, wholesome and brisk, and a good window onto the outdoor books that taught a generation of American boys to romanticize winter camping.
8934-the-forest-lovers:
Maurice Hewlett wrote this romance of the Middle Ages, set in a green, half-magical England of knights, hermits, and outlaws. Its hero, Prosper le Gai, rides out into the forest and falls in love with a lady tied to a holy thorn and a strange vow. Around them move a dark knight, a charcoal-burner, and folk of wood and road.

Hewlett writes in a rich, old-style voice, full of chases, sanctuaries, and sudden turns, yet the heart of the book is love tested by vows and peril. It was a popular success in its day and still pleases readers who like their romance steeped in forest shade and medieval color.
8992-the-blockade-runners:
