Jules Verne wrote this short novel in French in 1871 as Les forceurs de blocus, and N. d'Anvers turned it into English. It tells of the Dolphin, one of the fastest ships of its day. The Dolphin dares to run the Union blockade of the American South during the Civil War. Speed and nerve are its whole game.

First paired with A Floating City, the tale mixes sea detail with wartime risk, as captain and crew dodge guns and weather to reach port. Verne keeps the action tight and the stakes clear. The novella still reads as a brisk sea yarn from the age of steam and blockade.
9177-the-royal-game-of-the-ombre-written:
Printed in London in 1665 for Thomas Palmer, this manual teaches Ombre, a Spanish card game whose name means The Man. The player who takes the game cries, I am the Man, and Spaniards boast their Ombre beats the French game Beste as a man beats a beast. The form taught here is called Renegado.

Three players use a pack stripped for the game, and the manual sets out its rules in order. The British Library copy, Jessel 1249, preserves its old spelling. The book is a treasure for card players and historians of games, a glimpse of Restoration play.
9188-aboriginal-american-authors:
Daniel Brinton, anthropologist and member of learned societies in Philadelphia and abroad, wrote this chapter in the history of literature in 1883. Its subject is aboriginal American authors and their works, especially those in native languages. A new introduction notes its fitness for an age seeking history from the Indian point of view.

Brinton, known for The Myths of the New World and American Hero Myths, treats native writers as authors, not curiosities. He lists their books and languages with scholarly care. The book remains a pioneering survey, dated in language yet valuable for recovering Native voices in print.
9372-songs-out-of-doors:
Henry van Dyke published these outdoor songs in 1923, in four parts. Of Birds and Flowers gives the veery, the song-sparrow, and the Maryland yellow-throat, with sea-gulls of Manhattan and an angler's reveille. Of Skies and Seasons adds spring in north and south, Indian summer, and a snow-song. The Grand Canyon and God of the Open Air follow.

Wayfaring psalms in Palestine close the set, with the heavenly hills of Holland recalled. Van Dyke sings nature as a spiritual home. The book remains a pleasant volume of verse for walkers, birders, and lovers of open air.
9406-government-by-the-brewers:
Adolph Keitel, who spent thirty years inside the brewing trade, wrote Government by the Brewers as a fierce attack on that trade. He argues that brewers bought votes, bent laws, and fed crime through the saloon, all to guard their profits. The book belongs to the Prohibition fight, when reformers sought to ban drink by law. Keitel writes as an insider turned foe, naming firms and tricks.

Chapters claim beer is a habit-forming drug, not a mild temperance drink, and that saloons bred vice, broke homes, and staged crime. He tells how brewers backed cabarets, fought distillers, and spent millions to sway elections. A reader gets a raw, one-sided brief for Prohibition, useful for grasping how bitter and personal the drink war had grown.
9461-the-foolish-lovers:
St. John Ervine wrote this Irish novel in 1920, dedicated to his mother, who asked for a story without bad words, and to Mrs. Hannay, who asked for one without sex. Its epigraphs praise love as discovery. The tale opens with Ulster pride: ask an Ulster man who are Ireland's proudest people, and he answers, the Ulster people, of course.

Ask a Ballyards man who are Ulster's proudest, and a child would know: the Ballyards folk. Ervine builds a comedy of pride, love, and village honor from that boast. The novel remains a witty, warm Irish tale, clean in language and rich in character.
9501-concerning-cats-my-own-and-some-oth:
Helen M. Winslow wrote Concerning Cats in the early 1900s, a fond book about cats she knew and cats of fame. Winslow, editor of The Club Woman, opens with her own Pretty Lady, a quiet, lordly cat of fine manners. Later chapters take up other people's cats, historic cats, cat clubs, cat shows, and cats in verse and art. The book speaks to cat lovers in a chatty, warm voice.

Chapters range from high-bred cats in America to cats in England, cat hospitals, and the speech cats use with us. Winslow mixes true tales with lore on breeds, care, and shows. A reader gets a gentle, old-style celebration of feline grace, and a glimpse of how cats first won clubs, prizes, and a place in print.
9613-the-young-buglers:
G. A. Henty wrote The Young Buglers, a boys' adventure of the Peninsular War. Tom and Peter Scudamore, the most popular boys of their age at Eton in 1808, enlist as buglers and sail for Portugal. Chapters follow a coaching adventure, a tough customer, and a fall overboard, then the passage of the Douro and Talavera. Madrid, Busaco, and Albuera mark the campaign's course.

Later chapters bring Ciudad Rodrigo, Badajos, Salamanca, Vittoria, and Toulouse, with traps, rescues, and just-in-time escapes. Henty writes with brisk, factual verve for boys. A reader gets a rousing war tale for the young, rich in marches, battles, and schoolboy pluck.
9853-the-mystery-of-the-four-fingers:
Fred M. White wrote The Mystery of the Four Fingers in 1908, a detective tale of a lost mine and phantom gold. Chapters open with a black patch at the Great Empire Hotel in high London season, then a first finger, a lift, and a puzzle for Venner. A white lady, a missing person, and a house next door deepen the case. Felix Zary and Fenwick move the plot.

Later fingers, a prodigal's return, and a mouth of the net lead to nemesis and explanations, closing in a peaceful sunset. White writes with brisk Edwardian suspense. A reader gets a lively mystery of fingers, gold, and ghosts, from the author of The Crimson Blind.
9993-captivating-mary-carstairs:
Henry Sydnor Harrison's novel, first published under another name in February 1911, opens with a chief conspirator securing a pal. The pair embark upon a crime, arrive in Hunston, fall in with a stranger, and tangle themselves in local politics and other matters.

Mary Carstairs herself, captivating as the title promises, sits at the center of the plotting, while Varney meets a galling rebuff and Peter marches on. Harrison writes a light, comic romance of schemes gone sideways. Readers get a cheerful tale of rogues, small towns, and love arriving where it is least expected.
a-bundle-of-letters:
Henry James builds his tale entirely from letters, in the 1887 Macmillan edition used here. The first comes from Miss Miranda Mope of Bangor, Maine, writing home to her mother from Paris on September 5th, 1879. She is boarding in a French pension with a lively set of fellow lodgers, and she reports on all of them.

Other pens join in: a young Englishman, a German musician, a French poet, and the sharp Miss Vanderbank, whose letters judge the rest. Each writer sees the same small society differently, and the comedy comes from the gaps between accounts. James, still young, practices here the art of character shown through voice that fills his later novels.
a-dog-of-flanders:
A Dog of Flanders, first published in 1872, is a short novel by Ouida, the pen name of Marie Louise de la Ramée. Ouida wrote many popular novels of adventure and romance, and also stories for young readers. This tale, set in Flanders in Belgium, became the best loved of them.

The story follows Nello, a poor and gentle boy who dreams of becoming a painter, and Patrasche, the great dog who shares his life and work. Their bond carries the book through hardship and rejection toward its famous sad ending. It is a story about loyalty, poverty, and unrecognized talent, and it has moved readers for more than a century.
a-prince-of-swindlers:
A Prince of Swindlers, first published in 1900 by Guy Boothby, presents the adventures of Simon Carne, one of literature's first and greatest gentleman rogues. Carne predates both Hornung's Raffles and Leblanc's Arsène Lupin, the two famous gentleman thieves who followed him. The British Viceroy first meets Carne while traveling in India and, charmed, invites the reclusive hunchbacked scholar to London.

Little does society guess what the invitation brings among them. Carne's London career of elegant swindling forms the heart of the book, as the supposed scholar turns his charm and learning to crime. Boothby builds the rogue's double life into a portrait of a prince among swindlers, admired and dastardly at once.
a-princess-of-mars:
Edgar Rice Burroughs wrote this adventure novel as the supposed manuscript of Captain John Carter, a Virginia soldier who is mysteriously carried to Mars. The foreword, written in a family voice, presents Carter as a strange, ageless uncle. On Mars, called Barsoom by its people, Carter's Earth muscles give him great strength and leaping power. Captured by green Martian warriors, he wins standing by combat.

The contents list twenty-eight chapters of escapes, duels, and air battles. Carter meets Dejah Thoris, a red Martian princess held captive, and her cause pulls him through the wars of rival cities. Sola, his guard, tells her own sad history along the way. The book launched the Barsoom series and helped define planetary romance.
a-romany-of-the-snows-vol-1-being-a-cont:
A Romany of the Snows, Volume 1, by Gilbert Parker, continues the personal histories of Pierre and His People and calls itself the last existing records of Pretty Pierre. Parker's Pierre is a French Canadian half breed wanderer of the North West, gambler, philosopher, and witness to other men's tragedies. This first volume prints four of his tales, and its contents page maps the whole five volume gathering ahead.

Across the Jumping Sandhills opens the set, followed by A Lovely Bully, The Filibuster, and The Gift of the Simple King. The stories move between Hudson's Bay country, mining camps, and the borderlands where Canadian and American law both run thin. Parker was a Canadian who made his career in London. He writes the North as a moral climate. Cold, distance, and hunger strip men to what they are. Pierre, who has seen everything twice, narrates without surprise.
a-romany-of-the-snows-vol-2-being-a-cont:
A Romany of the Snows, Volume 2, by Gilbert Parker, gives Pretty Pierre five more northern tales. Parker opens with Malachi, in a room of gossips calmly predicting that a man will swing tomorrow. The door opens, the condemned man's friend Pierre steps to the fire, stretches his hands to the heat, and repeats the sentence himself in a soft ironical voice: Exit Malachi. The wind, Pierre says, does not tell where it has been.

The Lake of the Great Slave and The Red Patrol take the tales onto the water and the mounted police trails of the far North. The Going of the White Swan and At Bamber's Boom close the volume among river drivers and their booms of trapped logs. Parker's North West gives a hanging, a drowning, and a log jam the same weight of fate. Pierre's shrug there is a philosophy earned at forty below.
a-romany-of-the-snows-vol-3-being-a-cont:
A Romany of the Snows, Volume 3, by Gilbert Parker, places Pretty Pierre among the river drivers of the Madawaska. Parker opens The Bridge House with a building set on a wall between two small bridges, above channels that divide at its foundations. Spring floods batter the wall with logs, and a man can step from the back door into the river itself. The house was once a tavern, and the drivers who loved it were its true parish.

The Epaulettes, The House with the Broken Shutter, and The Finding of Fingall follow, with Three Commandments in the Vulgar Tongue to close. Soldiers, deserters, and river men pass through Parker's Ottawa valley, where French and English Canada meet on the drives. The Bridge House itself, rock like among the currents, stands for the book's method: fix one spot where wild lives converge, and let the river bring the stories past.
a-romany-of-the-snows-vol-4-being-a-cont:
A Romany of the Snows, Volume 4, by Gilbert Parker, opens with a Christmas tale told to power. In Little Babiche, Pretty Pierre faces the governor of the great Company, the Hudson's Bay chief, whose grey head and seamed face carry long solitary years in the northern fastnesses. Pierre corrects the record about a man he has known fifteen years, and promises the strange truth of a thing that happened at Noel, the day of the Great Birth.

At Point o' Bugles, The Spoil of the Puma, The Trail of the Sun Dogs, and The Pilot of Belle Amour complete the volume. Parker's tales keep returning to witnesses: men who were present, who knew, and who set a governor or a reader straight years later. The North of these stories is governed from fur trade posts and remembered in firelight, and its justice arrives, when it arrives, as testimony.
a-romany-of-the-snows-vol-5-being-a-cont:
A Romany of the Snows, Volume 5, by Gilbert Parker, closes the Pretty Pierre records with the longest tale in the set. The Cruise of the Ninety-Nine follows a big gulf yawl, handy enough for a man and a boy, with high old fashioned bulwarks and a tolerable record for speed. Her captain was Tarboe the smuggler. He named her after a parable. The parish priest came seeking the one lost sheep. Tarboe replied that he was the ninety nine, needing no repentance. He offered the cure his excellent smuggled brandy.

A Romany of the Snows and The Plunderer fill out the volume. Parker ends his northern cycle on salt water. Customs officers wink there, and priests drink with their parishioners.
across-the-years:
Eleanor H. Porter gathers eighteen stories reprinted from magazines such as the Ladies' Home Journal, Harper's Bazaar, and the Century, as her contents page records. The titles sketch her world. They include When Father and Mother Rebelled, Jupiter Ann, and The Price of a Pair of Shoes. The Bridge Across the Years, A Belated Honeymoon, and When Aunt Abby Waked Up follow.

The first story opens a month before Christmas with old Samuel Bertram sighing to his wife Lyddy Ann. Porter's people are elderly couples, country girls, and tired workers, and her plots turn small sacrifices into glad outcomes. The author of Pollyanna writes here for adults, with the same faith that gladness is a duty and a medicine.
addams-twenty-years:
Jane Addams published Twenty Years at Hull-House in 1910, looking back on the settlement house she co-founded in Chicago in 1889. Hull-House stood in a poor immigrant ward on Halsted Street. Addams lived there among her neighbors for decades.

She describes the neighbors who came: Italians, Greeks, Jews, Bohemians, each with old-country ways and new-world troubles. Hull-House offered classes, a nursery, art, and help with jobs and law. Addams also traces her own growth toward labor reform and peace work. The book helped invent American social work and remains its founding memoir.
bandelier-delight-makers:
Adolph Bandelier founded much of Southwestern archaeology in the United States. His novel The Delight Makers first appeared in 1890, here in a 1918 edition. He set the tale among the Pueblo peoples in the age before Spain came.

Bandelier builds daily life from the ruins and records he knew best. Corn fields, clan rites, hunts, and feuds fill the prehistoric village. A young hero moves through custom, duty, and secret plots. Few novels of the ancient Southwest rest on such deep field knowledge. Science wears the dress of story here, with rare skill and care throughout.
barchester-towers:
Anthony Trollope returned to Barchester in Barchester Towers, and the cathedral town is asking who will be the new bishop. The answer is Dr. Proudie, whose wife rules the palace and whose chaplain, Mr. Slope, schemes to rule the diocese. Against them stand Mr. Harding, the gentle ex-warden of Hiram's Hospital, the old dean and chapter, and the whole habit of Barchester life.

Chapters promise war, receptions, and Slope versus Harding, while the Stanhope family, including the fascinating Signora Neroni, stirs the drawing rooms. Trollope treats church politics as high comedy with real stakes: livings, sermons, and souls. This second Barsetshire novel made the series famous, and Mrs. Proudie remains one of fiction's great commanding wives.
billy-baxter-s-letters:
William J. Kountz Jr. of Pittsburgh wrote himself into these comic letters as Billy Baxter, a young blade writing home to his friend Jim. Billy reports a Minnesota hunting trip where he cannot open his borrowed gun, then moves through society calls, courtship, and a jaunt to New York. The letters first appeared as advertising booklets for a Pittsburgh distributing company and sold by the thousand.

Kountz died in August 1899, not yet thirty-two, and his brother gathered the letters as a tribute. Billy's slang, boasting, and sudden collapses of dignity drive the jokes. Read as a period piece, the book catches American young-man humor just before the twentieth century, pleased with itself and quick with a wisecrack.
birds-and-bees-sharp-eyes-and-other-pape:
John Burroughs's nature papers are collected in this volume, which opens with a biographical sketch of the author and an introduction by Mary E. Burt. The sketch fixes his beginnings: born at Roxbury in the Catskills on April 3, 1837, and raised on his father's farm. He was schooled in district schools, and drawn from the first to the essay form. The contents then divide into birds, bees, and other papers.

Bird Enemies and The Tragedies of the Nests give the bird section its edge; nesting is a dangerous business. An Idyl of the Honey-Bee and The Pastoral Bees turn to the hive and the bee-keepers. Sharp Eyes, the title piece of the remaining papers, trains the reader's own observation. Burroughs writes as a walker and watcher, and the book is meant to send its readers outdoors with better eyes.
birds-and-poets-with-other-papers:
John Burroughs's Birds and Poets, volume three of his collected writings, opens with a preface dated at Esopus-on-Hudson in March 1877. Burroughs explains that he has coupled outdoor nature sketches with chapters of a literary kind. Audubon, he argues, had the eye and heart of a poet though not the tongue. The title essay follows.

Touches of Nature and A Bird Medley carry the field observation, with April and Spring Poems for the turn of seasons. An essay on Emerson honours his master, and The Flight of the Eagle closes on Walt Whitman. Burroughs had championed Whitman when America mostly scorned him. His method is the naturalist's eye turned on books: close, patient, and affectionate. The volume helped found the American nature essay as literature, neither science nor sermon but a walk with a companionable mind.
bramble-bees-and-others:
Jean-Henri Fabre wrote the essays in Bramble-Bees and Others from his patient studies of wild bees in southern France, translated here by Alexander Teixeira de Mattos. Fabre collected the pieces from his Souvenirs entomologiques, leaving the mason-bees to a separate volume. His subjects live in bramble stems, reeds, and old walls. Careful watching, not laboratory theory, drives every chapter.

Opening essays follow bramble-dwellers and the Osmiae, a family of solitary bees. Fabre then asks how a mother bee controls the sex of her eggs. Leaf-cutters, cotton-bees, and resin-bees each get a chapter. Two closing groups study the Halicti, small bees with parasites and portresses. Readers get exact natural history written like storytelling, where an insect's nest becomes a small household with work, danger, and design.
brentano-aus-der-chronika-eines-fahrende:
A wandering scholar's chronicle gives Brentano his frame in Aus der Chronika eines fahrenden Schuelers, presented in German. The traveling student moves through a Germany of inns, roads, and chance meetings. Youth and freedom breathe through the fragmentary tale, part picaresque and part meditation.

Episodes gather like entries in a travel diary, warm with the poet's verbal music. The open road itself becomes the hero's teacher, as in so many Romantic daydreams. Melancholy underlies the charm; wandering also means never quite arriving. Brentano left the work in a loose, songlike form that suits its subject. Readers who love the Taugenichts spirit will feel at home here.
bunner-sisters:
Edith Wharton wrote Bunner Sisters in 1892, though it waited until 1916 for book publication. Ann Eliza and Evelina Bunner keep a tiny shop in a poor New York street, selling notions and mending, and live together in the room behind it. A clock bought for Ann Eliza's birthday brings Mr. Ramy, the clockmaker, into their lives, and both sisters quietly hope for the marriage that would change everything.

He marries the younger, Evelina, and the tale that follows is one of slow ruin: a drug habit, poverty, a lost child, and a return too late. Wharton tells it with pity and a steady eye. The tale is an early proof of the power she later brought to The House of Mirth.
calamities-and-quarrels-of-authors: Calamities and Quarrels of Authors, Isaac D'Israeli's literary history. The authors' fights. This book preserves that work. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care.
captain-macklin-his-memoirs:
Captain Macklin: His Memoirs, by Richard Harding Davis, pretends to be the life story of a young American soldier of fortune. Davis gives his narrator a West Point opening and a frank excuse for writing young: soldiering is hazardous, and tomorrow might not come, so the record must be made now. Walter Appleton Clark illustrated the volume, and the frontispiece shows a cavalry farewell, a captain crying God bless you to his horse.

Macklin's road runs from the Military Academy through revolutions and filibustering expeditions in Central America, the world Davis reported as a correspondent. Camp moons, barrack yards, and cabin fights fill the illustration list. The memoir form lets Davis string his war reporting into one swaggering career. It is half confession and half recruiting poster. The narrator calls soldiering the noblest profession a man can follow. Then he sets out to prove the price of believing it.
cast-upon-the-breakers:
Horatio Alger Jr opens Cast Upon the Breakers with schoolboy Rodney Ruland, a star boarder whose rich guardian pays all his bills. Rodney soon learns the money is gone, spent by that faithless guardian, and he must leave school and earn his living. The first chapter sends his friend David off to learn the carpenter's trade instead.

Rodney heads west, guards a casket of his dead mother's jewels on a train, loses it to thieves, and works his way up through honesty and luck. Alger's formula is complete here: a boy cast on the world, tempted, tested, and rewarded. Young readers of the 1890s made such tales bestsellers, and this one shows why.
catherine-memoirs:
Catherine the Great wrote her memoirs in French over many years, and they surfaced long after her death in 1796. The German princess had come to Russia as a bride and seized the throne from her husband in 1762. Her own account stops before that coup.

She describes the court of the Empress Elizabeth, her loveless marriage to Peter, and her reading of the French thinkers. Intrigue, loneliness, and ambition shape her rise, told in a cool, observant voice. The memoirs break off in 1759, before the seizure of power. Even so, they remain the key source for her early life.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbreviators:
The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on abbreviators describes those who shorten a long work into an abstract, tightening its words and sentences. Abbreviation took two forms: a single letter for a single word, and a mark standing for a word or phrase, both common among the Romans.

Emperor Justinian forbade abbreviations in the Digest and later in all writings, but the ban was not universally obeyed, and abbreviators kept the practice for convenience and interest, especially at Rome. Early Christians used abbreviated writing as an easy, safe way to communicate and guard secrets from enemies. In time the Apostolic Chancery adopted it as curial style, further dropping diphthongs and punctuation marks.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-acts-of-the-m:
Acts of the Martyrs, strictly speaking, are the official records of early Christian martyrs' trials, made by court notaries. In a wider sense the title covers all narratives of a martyr's trial and death. The entry classifies them with care. Official reports of interrogatories survive in few numbers, like the Acta Proconsulis for Cyprian, and reach us only in editions shaped to edify the faithful. The Passio Cypriani and Acta of the Scillitan martyrs typify this class.

Non-official records by eyewitnesses or contemporaries form a second class. It includes the Martyrium of Polycarp, with its pious fancy, and the Acta of Perpetua and Felicitas, most famous of all, holding autograph notes of Perpetua and Saturus. The letter of the churches of Vienne and Lyons on their martyrs belongs here too. Later classes, legends and romances, demand sharper criticism.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-algiers:
Algiers, ancient Icosium, is an archdiocese covering Algeria province in French Africa, with Oran and Constantine as suffragans. Missions rose in 1632, and an apostolic vicar soon followed. Late in the seventeenth century he oversaw Tunis's pro-vicar and Tripoli's prefect. The second-century Icosium see died under the Arabic conquest and revived in 1838 as Aix's suffragan. Dupuch was its first bishop until 1845, Pavy served from 1846 to 1866, and Lavigerie became its first archbishop in 1867.

The church honours Mercedarian confessors, including thirteenth-century Peter Armengaud at Algiers, and venerates Raymond Lully, dead at Bougie in 1325, and Geronimo, buried alive at Algiers in 1569. At the end of 1905 the diocese counted 230,843 European-born inhabitants besides the army, 8 first-class and 101 second-class parishes, 25 vicariates, and 24 auxiliary priests.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-angers:
Angers, anciently Andegavum, is a diocese covering Maine-et-Loire in France. It was a suffragan see of Tours under the old regime and the Concordat. The first known bishop is Defensor, who in 372 opposed Saint Martin's nomination at the Tours election. The legend of an earlier bishop Auxilius belongs to the Saint Firmin cycle, against Angevin tradition before the thirteenth century.

Early names include Saint Maurilius, hermit of Chalonnes, who stood against idolatry and died in 427, and Thalassius, bishop in 453, who left a brief compendium of canon law. Modern bishops include Cardinal de la Balue, caged by Louis XI from 1469 to 1480, the Jansenist Henri Arnauld, Freppel, and Mathieu, later cardinal and academician. The twelfth-century cathedral of Saint Maurice, without side aisles, shows Angevin architecture. Medieval Angers held six great monasteries, including Saint Aubin and Saint Serge. In 1905 the diocese counted 514,658 inhabitants and 543 parishes and vicariates.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-anglican-orde:
This article treats the validity of orders conferred in the Church of England. In Catholic belief, Holy Order is one of the seven sacraments, giving the priesthood's powers to consecrate the Blessed Sacrament and administer Confirmation, Penance, and Extreme Unction. Holy Order has three degrees, bishops, priests, and deacons, with bishops holding the priesthood in full, able to exercise and transmit it. Only a bishop ministers Holy Order, and validity requires his valid consecration and a rite keeping all Christ's essentials.

From the start, Catholic writers attacked the Edwardine Ordinal for an insufficient rite. The article traces the debate through the Parker succession and Rome cases, where re-ordination was the practice. Leo XIII's Bull Apostolicae Curae pronounces Anglican ordinations absolutely null and void, on defect of form and defect of intention. The Bull caused excitement in England, and Anglicans showed no disposition to accept its arguments or decision.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-annals-of-the:
The Annals of the Four Masters are Ireland's most extensive ancient annals. They run, nominally at least, from A.M. 2242 to A.D. 1616. Entries, bare early, grow fuller as the Annals progress, and towards the end become almost like history. The principal compiler was Michael O'Clery of Donegal, a trained antiquary and poet who joined the Franciscans at Louvain. Father John Colgan sent him back to Ireland to collect saints' lives. Many lives he copied from Ireland's old vellum books are preserved.

The name comes from the four compilers, most learned masters in antiquarian lore. Written in archaic language, difficult even then except for the learned, the Annals give reigns, deaths, genealogies, and dates. They cover high-kings, provincial kings, chiefs, and family heads, men of science, historians, and poets. They record saints, abbots, bishops, and dignitaries, and the foundation and occasional overthrow of countless churches, castles, abbeys, and convents.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-apostolic-exa:
Apostolic examiners, named by the Apostolic See for work in Rome, were instituted by Pius V in 1570 to examine candidates for holy orders and confessors. Chosen by the pope, they swear before the cardinal vicar. Under a constitution of Alexander VII in 1662, examinations for orders take place in the vicariate before at least three examiners. Only after consulting the pope may the vicar dispense a candidate, except for tonsure, the first clerical rite, which one examiner may test privately.

All candidates, whether tied to Rome or not, must pass this examination. Anyone in Rome four months or more who plans to return must face examination in the vicariate before receiving orders elsewhere, on pain of suspension. Canons of St. Peter's are examined by their cardinal archpriest. The entry is a precise guide to how Rome guarded entry to the priesthood.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-apostolic-exp:
Apostolic expeditors are officials who handle the sending of bulls, briefs, and rescripts, papal documents, issuing from the Apostolic Chancery, Dataria, Sacred Penitentiaria, and the Secretariat of Briefs. In a narrow sense they are laymen approved by the Dataria, after examination, to act as agents for bishops and others before the Dataria or Chancery. They count as members of the Roman court. They are not solicitors, who merely prepare documents as assistants to procurators, and from procurators or agents in general.

An expeditor deals more with matters of favour, privileges, and dispensations than with cases in litigation, and the Dataria and Chancery do business only with authorized agents of this kind. Their office is to draw up and sign needed documents, receive the answer, and forward it, for a fixed fee per transaction. The entry opens a window on the paperwork engine behind papal government.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-apostolic-let: Apostolic letters carry two meanings in this short entry. First, they are the letters of the apostles to Christian groups or to those in authority. They are the Pauline epistles, including the letter to the Hebrews, together with the seven general epistles of the other apostles. Second, they are documents issued by the pope or under his name, such as bulls and briefs, the formal and less formal papal letters that govern, teach, or grant favours.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-assessors:
Assessors, in church law, are learned persons whose task is to advise a judge with whom they sit in trying cases. They are called assessors since they sit beside the judge, from Latin assidere. They must examine documents, consult precedents, and explore laws for points bearing on the case at issue.

A judge overburdened with business or conscious of inexperience in law may voluntarily take assessors, or superior authority may assign them. Assessors should be beyond suspicion of partiality, with conceded learning, and if a judge's acts are appealed, they make unexceptionable witnesses. As advisers, not judges, they hold no jurisdiction and bear no public character, attending trials in a private capacity, though they may take part in examining witnesses and evidence.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-berengarius-o:
Berengarius of Tours, an eleventh-century teacher condemned for his views on the Eucharist, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born at Tours about 999, he died in 1088 after study at Chartres under Fulbert, whose anxiety over his pupil's bold opinions already showed. As head of the school of St. Martin at Tours, his fame drew students from far away.

His teaching held that the bread and wine of the altar are figures and memorials of Christ's body, not that body itself in the sense later defined. Lanfranc attacked him, councils at Rome and Vercelli condemned him in 1050, and repeated retractions followed. The entry traces a brilliant mind caught in the age's fiercest doctrinal fight.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cahors:
Cahors covers the whole French department of Lot, once under Bourges, then from 1676 under Albi, and after the Revolution restored in 1822 to near its old bounds under Albi. Tradition sends Saint Martial to Cahors in the first century. The first bishop known to history is Saint Florentius, correspondent of Saint Paulinus of Nola at the end of the fourth century.

Its bishops include Saint Rusticus, murdered in office, his brother Saint Desiderius, steward of King Dagobert, and Guillaume de Cavaillon, who joined the Albigensian crusade. Cahors gave birth to Jacques d'Euse, who became Pope John XXII in 1316. The Venerable Alain de Solminihac, bishop from 1636 to 1659, ranks among the great reformers of the seventeenth-century French clergy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-canonical-hou:
A canonical hour is each fixed portion of the Divine Office the Church appoints to be said at set hours. The term came from Jewish custom into early Christian speech, and Acts shows prayer named by its hour. Once the observance turned from optional to obligatory for certain classes by church canons, each portion took the name canonical hour, and the whole day's prayers took the name canonical hours. The term spread even to the prayer book itself, the book of hours.

The Rule of Saint Benedict is among the oldest documents using the phrase, and it passed into common speech by the next century, as Saint Isidore of Seville shows. The Breviary article treats the Office's parts, their origin, and their history. The duty itself binds daily, at least in private, all clerics in holy orders, all beneficiaries, and religious bound by rule to choir.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-catholic-orde:
The Catholic Orders of Foresters were three fraternal insurance societies built on the plan of the Foresters' courts. The first, the Massachusetts Catholic Order of Foresters, was organized on 30 July 1879 by members of Boston's St. Vincent de Paul Society. By January 1909 it counted 235 courts and 27,757 members, nearly ten thousand of them women, with $27,757,000 of insurance in force.

A second body, the Catholic Order of Foresters of Illinois, followed in Chicago in 1883, moving from a flat one-dollar death assessment to a graded system after an 1895 convention. It had paid over ten million dollars in death claims by 1908. A Women's Catholic Order of Foresters, founded in Chicago in 1892, counted 54,350 members with courts across many states.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-john-:
An encyclopedia life of Charles John Seghers, the Belgian-born bishop who became known as the Apostle of Alaska. Born at Ghent in 1839 and left an orphan while still young, he was raised by uncles, trained at Louvain, and ordained a priest in 1863. Within months he sailed for Vancouver Island, where he spent a decade working among settlers and native peoples before becoming bishop there.

Seghers twice crossed into Alaska, setting up missions along the Yukon and on the island's west coast, then served briefly as Archbishop of Oregon City. He gave up that higher post to return to Victoria and resume the Alaskan work, founding missions at Sitka and Juneau in 1885. On a fifth northern trip he was murdered by a travelling companion, and his remains were later moved to Victoria.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-christian-bro:
An entry on the Brothers of the Christian Schools, a society of male religious who take no holy orders. They devote themselves to the Christian education of youth, above all poor children and artisans' sons. Founded at Reims in 1680 by Saint John Baptist de La Salle, then canon of the city church, it runs any boys' school except one teaching Latin. Its chief work is free elementary schooling.

De La Salle was moved by the ignorance of the people in knowledge and religion. He built the institute almost without a set plan, first steadying a congregation for poor girls, then backing a layman's schools for poor boys. The entry warns against thinking the Church neglected popular schooling before him, citing councils from Vaison in 529 to Trent in 1547 that ordered free teaching of the poor. It then traces the brothers' spread, rule, and schools.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cistercian-ab:
Villers, on the borders of Villers and Tilly in Brabant, was the first Cistercian monastery in that territory. In April 1146 twelve monks and five lay-brothers went from Clairvaux to Boverie, sent by Saint Bernard under Abbot Lawrence. After more than a year of discouragement they moved about three miles to a better site and raised a modest oratory and dwelling. Local nobles gradually came to their aid.

Abbot Charles, from 1197 to 1209, laid the foundations of the great church, finished only about 1300. By the mid-thirteenth century Villers stood at its height, with over a hundred monks and three hundred lay-brothers, and more than fifty of its members are honoured as saints or blessed. Later, sovereigns claimed the choice of abbots, unworthy prelates intruded, and political disorder once drove the whole community away for nearly twenty years.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cistercian-si:
The first Cistercian house for women was founded at Tart in the Diocese of Langres in 1125. Its sisters came from the Benedictine monastery of Juilly, with the help of Saint Stephen Harding, Abbot of Citeaux. Tart founded Ferraque in 1140, Blandecques in 1153, and Montreuil-les-Dames in 1164. In Spain the first house was Tulebras in 1134, followed by Las Huelgas de Burgos, Alfonso the Eighth of Castile's 1187 foundation and the most celebrated of all.

Eighteen French abbesses held their first general chapter at Tart in 1190, but Trent's cloister decrees ended the chapters and visitations. Reforms followed: Jeanne de Courcelles restored Tart's discipline and moved it to Dijon in 1625, while Angelique Arnauld reformed Port-Royal, suppressed by royal order in 1710. After the Revolution, Dom Augustin de Lestrange rebuilt the sisterhood as Trappistines, who returned to France in 1816. By 1908 the Reformed nuns held twenty-one houses with about two thousand religious.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-co-consecrato:
Co-consecrators assist the presiding bishop in consecrating a new bishop. Church rule strictly requires two assistants, three bishops in all. Missionary countries, where gathering so many proves impossible, may use two priests as assistants with Holy See leave. In the present Roman Pontifical the assistants help place the Gospels on the elect's shoulders, join in laying hands on his head, and say over him Accipe Spiritum Sanctum. The consecrator alone says the Eucharistic prayer, the essential form of the rite.

So it was in ancient Western rites, where the words are a late medieval addition. In earliest times as many bishops as possible gathered, with the comprovincials at least taking part under the metropolitan. Since that proved impracticable, Nicaea enacted choice by all his province's bishops. If necessity or journey length prevented it, at least three bishops could proceed with written permission of the absent.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-covenanters:
This historical entry explains who the Covenanters were: the Scots who subscribed the National Covenant of 1638 and the Solemn League and Covenant of 1643. Though the covenants as national bonds ended with Cromwell's conquest, a remnant kept them alive after the Restoration.

At stake was a struggle for supremacy between king and Kirk over who should decide Scotland's religion. Charles I sought to impose bishops and a new liturgy, while Presbyterians held that the Kirk, not the crown, governed the Church. The entry traces that clash from the Reformation under Knox and Melville through persecution and resistance, drawing on standard histories of the Scottish Kirk.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-crutched-fria:
This entry describes the Crutched Friars, or Crossed Friars, a mendicant order that reached England in the thirteenth century from Italy. There they were called Fratres Cruciferi. They first appeared at a Rochester diocesan synod in 1244, bearing papal documents and asking leave to settle. Each friar carried a wooden staff topped by a cross and wore a red cloth cross on his habit.

Their rule was that of Saint Augustine, and their habit, first brown or black, was changed to blue by Pius II. They founded eight or nine English houses. The first stood at Colchester or Reigate in 1245, and London followed in 1249, lending their name to the district still called Crutched Friars near Tower Hill. Their claimed first-century founding by Saint Cletus is treated as uncertain.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-david-teniers:
An art entry untangles two Flemish landscape painters both named David Teniers, father and son. The elder was born at Antwerp in 1582 and died there in 1649. He trained under his brother, entered Rubens's school for a time, and studied under Elsheimer at Rome. He returned in 1606 to paint landscapes, rural sports, and classical scenes.

The younger was born at Antwerp in 1610 and died at Brussels in 1694. He far eclipsed his father. Likely trained in his father's studio, he married Anne Brueghel in 1637, with Rubens at the wedding. After her death in 1656 he married Isabel, daughter of Brabant's council secretary. Rich from both marriages and picture sales, he bought a chateau and served as court painter. The Louvre alone holds nearly forty of his works.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-definitors-in:
A canon law entry describes definitors in religious orders, generally the governing council of an order. Usage varies: with Dominicans, all sent to represent provinces in a general chapter are definitors, and Cluniacs had a similar rule, though Benedictines normally have none. Franciscans, Carmelites, and Augustinian Hermits elect definitors in general and provincial chapters to assist superiors in government.

In that case definitors act as a kind of executive committee for the chapter, subject to its legislation. Strictly so called, they hold a decisive vote in congregation equal to the superior's, unlike mere consultors such as the Jesuits have. No superior may act in weightier matters without their vote. A definitor votes only when present, must speak candidly in conscience even against the majority, yet must sign the minority report after the vote.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dimissorial-l:
Dimissorial letters, from the Latin for letters of dismissal, are papers a church superior gives his subjects for use outside his own bounds. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry explains their proper sense, letters by which a bishop or regular prelate lets his man be ordained by another bishop. The name is also stretched to cover testimonial and commendatory letters for traveling clergy.

Letters of excorporation, by which clerics pass from one diocese to another, belong to the same family. The entry sets out when such letters are required and when they are merely fitting. For readers of canon law, it offers a compact guide to the paper trail that lets priests cross diocesan lines in good order.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-diocesan-cons:
In American dioceses, a group of priests serves as the bishop's official advisers, under the name of diocesan consultors. Together they stand in for the cathedral chapter found elsewhere under church law. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry traces their start to the Second Plenary Council of Baltimore in 1866. The Third Plenary Council of 1884 made them a diocesan council and fixed their rights and duties.

They number six, or at least four, where possible, and hold office for three years with renewal allowed. The entry sets out how they are chosen and what matters call for their counsel. It gives American readers the rules of a body that stands close to the bishop in governing his diocese.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dominique-bou:
Dominique Bouhours was a French Jesuit author born at Paris on 15 May 1632. At sixteen he entered the Jesuits, then taught grammar and rhetoric in Paris, Tours, and Rouen. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry notes his works against the Jansenists, above all two letters to a lord of the court and to the gentlemen of Port-Royal. They won wide circulation and set him among the leading critics of the seventeenth century.

He also turned the New Testament into French, a version often reprinted. English readers know him best by his lives of Saint Ignatius from 1679 and Saint Francis Xavier from 1682, both translated at London. His Art of Criticism, on thinking well in works of wit, appeared in London in 1705. He died in 1702.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ecclesiastica:
Ecclesiastical letters are publications of church authority, above all of popes and bishops, sent to the faithful in letter form. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry notes that synods also issue them, but popes led the way, using the primacy to lay down laws for the whole Church and for single persons. Such letters went out on the pope's own motion or on appeal from synods, bishops, or single Christians.

Apart from the epistles of Peter, the first example is the letter of Pope Clement the First to the Corinthians, written when grave dissension split that community. Few papal letters survive from the first three Christian centuries, and the entry traces the growth of the form. It cites Laurentius and Sagmuller on a genre that carried church government by post.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-familiars:
Familiars were lay people attached to a religious house as servants. They lived under the regular prelate and shared in the house privileges. These included absolution, Easter Communion, and the last sacraments in the house. The term covered household staff and servants, not friars or monks.

The Council of Trent set rules for ordaining such household members. A man needed three years' residence in the house and a benefice before ordination. The article explains how familiars differed from oblates and servants. It also notes their share in the community's spiritual goods and prayers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-family-of-rue:
The Rueckers were celebrated organ and keyboard builders of Antwerp. Hans Rueckers, who died in 1640 or 1641, joined the Guild of St Luke. His spinets used two keyboards coupled together to sound an octave apart. His son Andreas, born in 1579, carried on the family workshop.

Andreas the Younger became a maker of world renown in his own turn. Rueckers instruments reached wealthy buyers across Europe, including England. Some were later broken up so that their painted lids could be sold. The article values their sweet tone, fine craft, and painted decoration.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-flanders:
Flanders is a low, flat land by the North Sea, once flooded at high water. Its poor soil was made fertile by careful farming; flax, hemp, linen, and dairy goods lead its trade. The county was founded in 864, when Baldwin Iron Arm received the land from Charles the Bald. Baldwin's successors ruled a county split between a French fief and an imperial fief.

Later counts added lands, granted privileges to communes, and joined the crusades. Baldwin IX became the first Latin Emperor of Constantinople and died fighting Bulgarians in 1205. Countess Jeanne ruled wisely through her husband's captivity after Bouvines in 1214. On Margaret's death in 1279, Hainault went to the Avesnes children and Flanders to the Dampierres.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-forty-martyrs:
The Forty Martyrs were soldiers put to death for their faith at Sebaste in Lesser Armenia during the persecution of Licinius after 316. The earliest account is a homily by St. Basil of Caesarea, preached on their feast only fifty or sixty years after the event. Forty soldiers who had openly confessed their Christian faith were condemned to stand naked on a frozen pond through a bitter night. Warm baths stood nearby to tempt anyone who gave in.

One man yielded, but a guard who saw a strange brightness over the sufferers declared himself a Christian and took his place, keeping the number at forty. At dawn their bodies were burned and the ashes thrown into a river, yet Christians gathered the remains, and relics spread widely. Churches rose in their honour, and their feast is kept on 9 March in both the Greek and Latin churches.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-fossors:
Fossors, from the Latin for diggers, were the grave diggers of the Roman catacombs in the first three or four Christian centuries. Once the Church resolved to bury its dead in cemeteries reserved for Christians alone, it needed workers to cut the underground galleries. Those workers soon ranked among the lower clergy, a rise in standing that the entry contrasts with the low esteem of pagan burial workers, the vespillones.

By the fourth century their corporation could sell burial plots, and the work also covered tomb decoration, so some fossors were painters or sculptors as well. The entry cites named fossors at Cirta in 303, a fresco of the fossor Diogenes with pick, sack, and lamp, and a second-century painting in the catacomb of St. Callistus. Fossors also kept unauthorized people out of liturgical gatherings held in the cemeteries for martyrs.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-four-crowned-:
The Four Crowned Martyrs, the Quatuor Coronati, are a group venerated at the catacomb of Sts. Peter and Marcellinus on the Via Labicana outside Rome, where pilgrims came to their grave. Their story is tangled. Five sculptors from the quarries of Pannonia, named Claudius, Nicostratus, Simpronianus, Castorius, and Simplicius, refused to carve a statue of Aesculapius for a pagan temple, though they had made other pagan images. They were drowned in leaden caskets in the River Save toward the end of 305.

Later a Roman legend told of four Christian soldiers martyred at Rome for the same refusal. Because their true names were unknown, Pope Melchiades ordered them honoured on 8 November under the sculptors' names. A basilica on the Caelian Hill, first mentioned in 595, still stands as their titular church, and about 850 Pope Leo IV moved relics there from the Via Labicana. Both groups are commemorated on 8 November.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-foxe-s-book-o:
John Foxe, born at Boston in Lincolnshire in 1516 and educated at Oxford, wrote the vast Protestant martyrology known as Foxe's Book of Martyrs. An extreme reformer under Edward VI, he fled to Germany in Mary's reign, worked for the printer Oporinus at Basle. He published a large Latin folio in 1559 tracing persecution from Wyclif to Cranmer. Back in England he translated and enlarged it as Acts and Monuments, published in 1563.

The book grew through editions in 1570, 1576, and 1583, and five more within a century. By 1684 it reached three folio volumes, packed with documents, letters, and woodcuts of martyrs' sufferings. Convocation ordered copies kept in cathedrals in 1571, and it became beloved in Puritan and Low Church homes. Yet the entry judges Foxe untrustworthy with evidence, sometimes mutilating documents, and notes that Catholic critics attacked him in his own day.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-franz-karl-mo:
Franz Karl Movers, born at Koesfeld in Westphalia on 17 July 1806 and died at Breslau on 28 September 1856. He was a German exegete and scholar of Scripture and eastern languages. Schooled at Koesfeld and Munster, he studied philosophy, theology, and eastern languages at Munster Academy under Laurenz Reinke and was ordained at Paderborn in autumn 1829. He continued eastern studies briefly at Bonn, tutored for Baron von Geyr at Rath, became pastor at Berkum in 1833. He became professor of Old Testament exegesis at Breslau, extraordinary in 1839 and ordinary in 1842.

His studies include critical work on the biblical Chronicle in 1834, on the Greek and Hebrew recensions of Jeremiah's prophecies in 1837, on passages illustrating the Old Testament canon in 1842. His essays in theological journals included articles in the first Kirchenlexicon.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-fredegis-of-t:
Fredegis of Tours, an Anglo-Saxon monk of the ninth century, studied under Alcuin first at York and then at Charlemagne's court. Known in the palace school by the name Nathaniel, he followed his teacher to Tours and succeeded him as abbot there in 804, keeping his ties to the emperor. He died at Tours in 834 with a name for deep learning.

Besides poems, Fredegis wrote a short letter-treatise asking whether nothing and darkness are real things, a question raised by their use in the opening of Genesis. He answered yes, arguing from authority and from reason, though his view never won general assent. The entry values the piece for its early use of the logical method that later grew into scholastic debate.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-free-thinkers:
Free-thinkers are people who take no religious teaching on authority and rest belief on reason alone. The Catholic Encyclopedia entry defines free-thought as an extreme form of private judgment, the idea that each mind must judge doctrine for itself. A free-thinker accepts only what he feels he can prove and gives assent to nothing else.

The name arose among the English Deists, and Collins gave the movement its label in a 1713 Discourse of Freethinking. But the entry finds the same spirit far earlier, in classical scoffers at old myths and in medieval schoolmen who reasoned revelation away. From the Deists onward, it says, free thought spread from learned studies into the wider public mind.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-g-henry-woute:
G. Henry Wouters, a Belgian historian born at Oostham in 1802, taught church history at Liège and Louvain for over forty years. He became professor of moral theology at Liège in 1829, then moved to the restored Louvain in 1834 as professor of church history, holding the chair until 1871. He drew on Baronius, Pagi, and Noël Alexandre.

His three-volume Compendium of Church History, issued in 1842 and 1843, won wide fame and became a classic handbook in many lands. A four-volume set of dissertations followed between 1868 and 1872, meant to treat disputed questions down to Trent, but it stopped at the fourteenth century. Wouters saw church history as a helper science to theology.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gemblours:
Gemblours, a suppressed Benedictine monastery nine miles from Namur in Belgium, was founded about 945 by Saint Guibert. Guibert, aided by Erluin, a canon turned monk, built it for Saint Peter and the martyr Exuperius on the river Orneau. Kin challenged the gift as fiscal land, but Otto I, pleased by their defense, confirmed the house by diploma in September 946.

Erluin, its first abbot, was beaten by reform-hating monks of Lobbes in 958 while trying to renew that house. Under Olbert, abbot from 1012, discipline returned, a new church rose in 1022, and a rich library grew. Thietmar's age saw the chronicler Sigebert, whose world chronicle from 381 to 1111 Anselm continued to 1136, with Gottschalk carrying on its abbots' history.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henri-count-o:
French historian Henri, Count of Boulainvilliers, born in 1658, pioneered the history of France's institutions as a long plea for feudalism against monarchy. A soldier until his father's death in 1697 forced him into estate research, he argued, saturated with aristocratic conviction like Saint-Simon, that conquering Franks divided Gaul among themselves as free peers. The king was a mere magistrate to settle disputes.

Crusade mortgages let wealthy commoners buy fiefs and corrupt the nobility. Ignorant lords handed justice to clerks who became the robe nobility, and Capetian kings gathered fiefs, dazzled lords into courtiers, freed communes, and packed the States General with clergy and freed serfs. Written for his grandchildren and published after his death, his works found their school only in the last twenty-five years, in Fustel de Coulanges and his followers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-herbert-golds:
Herbert Goldsmith Squiers, an army officer and diplomat born at Madoc in 1859, was educated at several academies and Fordham University. He became a second lieutenant in 1877 and served with the 7th Cavalry at Wounded Knee before resigning in 1891. In diplomacy he was second secretary at Berlin in 1894 and first secretary at Peking in 1898, where Archbishop Favier received him and his family into the Church.

During the siege of the legations in 1900 Squiers served as chief of staff under Sir Claude Macdonald, who with the Russian minister called his services invaluable amid exaggerated racial feeling. He was thanked by Britain and by President McKinley. As minister to Cuba from 1902 and to Panama from 1906, his tact and firmness helped settle questions of those early days. His health broken by eight years in the tropics, he died in London in 1911, leaving burses for Catholic students and a collection of Chinese porcelain.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-holy-orders:
Holy Orders is the sacrament by which grace and spiritual power for church offices are conferred. Order first means the right arrangement of things, giving each its proper place, as Augustine defines it. It then came to mean rank itself, applied to clergy and laity, and later restricted to the hierarchy and the ranks of the clergy. It also names the outward action, ordination, by which clergy rise to that rank.

Tertullian and early writers already used the word in this sense, often with a qualifying adjective. The entry traces how Christ founded the church as a supernatural society with ordered ministry, and how the sacrament's nature, matter, and effects were understood across the ages. Readers find the theology of ordination set out from its scriptural roots to its developed form.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hospitallers:
Hospitallers were religious who served the sick and poor in the hospitals of the medieval West, the Maisons-Dieu or Hôtels-Dieu. Men and women lived under one roof, followed the Rule of St. Augustine, and vowed perpetual chastity and service to the sick. Paris's Hôtel-Dieu stood out above all houses.

There, in the early 1600s, Mère Geneviève Bouquet opened a novitiate and began the custom of taking a saint's name. The congregation survived the Revolution and the disorders of 1830. Military orders of the Crusades likewise cared for the sick, aided by women's communities under the same rules, such as the Hospital Sisters of St. Lazarus and the Hospitaller Sisters of St. John of Jerusalem, founded for pilgrims.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-imposters:
This entry rounds up shady figures too slight for their own articles, yet too notorious or disruptive in Church life, through lies or base conduct, to skip outright. Christ warned in the Gospels that men would use pious show to hide wicked plans.

He told hearers to watch for false prophets in sheep's clothing who were inwardly ravening wolves. He also said false Christs and false prophets would arise, working signs and wonders to mislead even the elect if they could. Other New Testament writings strike the same note: false prophets abroad in the world, lying teachers yet to come among the people. The Didache and Justin Martyr, writing about A.D. 150, show these warnings coming true early.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-institutes-of:
Looking after the sick in their own homes is the chief aim of this society, second only to the personal holiness of its members, as its constitutions put it. Its nursing sisters care for sick people at home, rich and poor alike, nursing the poor for nothing while those who can pay do so. Sixteen houses stood in France; Ireland had four, England one, the United States two, and Belgium one.

Paris kept the motherhouse, where Archbishop de Quélen started the Bon Secours sisters in 1822. Pope Pius IX gave them formal approval in June 1875. The sisters dressed in a black habit, a white frilled cap, and a black veil. The Paris congregation, the first of France's nineteenth-century home-nursing congregations, is taken up here before the others.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-irish-confess:
Persecution in Ireland between about 1540 and 1713 fills this long martyrology, opening with Henry VIII's break with Rome. Local acts set up the king's church supremacy, abolished papal jurisdiction, and suppressed religious houses, with the act against the pope in force from 1 November 1537. Its penalties were terrible, the entry says, and the license of enforcers worse.

Within little more than a year the Bishop of Derry told Paul III a grim tale. The king's deputy and his men were burning houses and wrecking churches. They were robbing and killing unoffending people. They were murdering priests who prayed for the pope or kept his name in the Mass. Torture awaited preachers who would not deny papal authority. The entry then names confessors and martyrs across nearly two centuries of that pressure.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-japanese-mart:
No people in church history offer annals as glorious, or a martyrology as lengthy, as Japan's people, this entry claims at its outset. In January 1552 St Francis Xavier noted the early converts' proselytizing spirit. He wrote that he saw them rejoicing in successes, showing ardent zeal to spread the faith and win pagans they met to baptism. He foresaw obstacles blocking faith's progress in certain provinces, above all the absolutism of daimyo lords, then very independent of the Mikado and in revolt against his supreme authority.

In Hirado province, where Xavier made a hundred converts, six years later 600 pagans were baptized in three days. Yet a Christian woman, the proto-martyr, was beheaded there for praying before a cross. In 1561 a daimyo forced Christians into new trials. The entry follows Japanese Christianity from Xavier's hopeful start through persecution toward the great martyrdoms of Nagasaki and beyond.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-pierre-m:
Jean-Pierre Minkelers, inventor of illuminating gas, was born at Maastricht in 1748 and died there in 1824. At sixteen he went to Louvain, studied theology and philosophy at Falcon College, and became professor of natural philosophy there in 1772.

When ballooning gripped scientists, the duke of Arenberg set a committee to find the best balloon gas, and Minkelers served on it. Heating oil sealed in a gun barrel in a forge, he drew off a remarkably light gas, best for balloons, and published his memoir in 1784. His pupil records that he also lit his workshop with it, an early hint of gas lighting.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-judaizers:
The Judaizers were Jewish Christians in the early Church pressing Gentile converts to accept circumcision and the Mosaic Law. At first the apostles and their converts still kept Jewish customs and ate no unclean food. They worshiped in the Temple, looking from outside like one more Jewish sect.

When the Gospel reached Gentiles, the question turned sharp: must converts take the Law, or may Jews relax the barriers that kept them apart? Most Palestinian Jews favored imposing the Law, yet the entry argues that neither forcing circumcision nor treating Gentiles as second-class could serve a Church meant for all nations.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-kafirs:
Kafir was a name Arab traders of the East African coast gave to nearly all South Africa's natives. It means unbeliever; the peoples themselves do not use it, distinguishing their many tribes instead. The legal list runs from Zulu, Basuto, and Bechuana through Pondo, Fingo, Griqua, Damara, Koranna, Bushman, and Hottentot. Nearly all speak Bantu, whose Kafir group divides into Xosa, Zulu, Tabele, and Mfengu.

Jesuits and Dominicans evangelized these peoples' ancestors from the fifteenth to the eighteenth centuries, but converts relapsed when the missionaries were driven out. The Zulu chief Chaka's wars at the start of the nineteenth century are said to have killed over a million people. Wars with the British and Dutch followed until 1879. South of the Zambesi there were then some five million natives. A South African commission of 1903-1905 held that only Christian faith and morals could raise their standard of conduct.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lay-brothers:
Lay brothers were religious given wholly to manual labour and a monastery's secular business, distinct from choir monks devoted to the divine office and study. They appear under names like fratres conversi, laici barbati, and illiterati.

Their origin is disputed. Mabillon credits St. John Gualbert at Vallombrosa about 1038. Yet Fonte Avellana about 1000 already set religious servants apart for manual work. Camaldoli about 1012 certainly had brethren apart from choir monks. Early Benedictine monks, mostly not clerics, all laboured by hand. By the eleventh century study had grown, more monks held orders, and illiterate recruits crowded in. Hired servants needed ordering into the family. Cistercians, Carthusians, Grandmont, and most later orders all kept lay brothers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-liturgical-co:
Liturgical colours are the hues the Church assigns to vestments and altar drapery, matched to the feast or season of the day. The entry takes up their number, the garments they touch, how binding they are, how old the usage is, and what each colour is meant to signal.

Since Pius V the Roman Rite has used five: white, red, green, violet, and black, with rose on two Sundays alone. White marks feasts of the Lord, of Mary, of angels, and of non-martyr saints. Red marks martyrs, apostles, and the Passion. Green fills ordinary time, violet marks Advent and Lent, and black marks mourning and funerals.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-louis-adolphe:
Louis Adolphe Thiers was a French statesman and historian, first president of the Third Republic, born at Marseilles in 1797 and dead at Paris in 1877. As editor of the Constitutionnel he rose in the liberal press, and his ten-volume History of the French Revolution made his literary name.

Le National, founded by Thiers, Mignet, and Carrel in 1829, helped topple the Bourbons in 1830, and Thiers served often as minister under Louis-Philippe. His twenty-volume history of the Consulate and Empire followed, and after 1848 he swung toward church interests, backing the Falloux school law and the Roman expedition. In 1871 he became chief of state and president.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mendicant-fri:
Mendicant friars belong to religious orders that, by vow of poverty, gave up ownership not only singly but also in common, unlike monks, living by their own work and the faithful's charity. Hence the name begging friars. Four great mendicant orders survive from the Middle Ages, recognized by the Second Council of Lyons in 1274. They are the Order of Preachers, the Friars Minor, the Carmelites, and the Hermits of St. Augustine.

Later congregations won the same privilege, and the Council of Trent granted all mendicant orders except the Friars Minor and Capuchins the freedom of corporate possession. The entry sketches first the mendicants' origin and character, then the opposition they met. Roots are plain. After the investiture struggle, ill will toward church property lingered. Arnold of Brescia preached that propertied monks and clerics could not be saved, and John Valdes founded the Poor Men of Lyons, with similar sects following.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-minor-orders:
Minor Orders, in Latin Ordines Minores, are the lower degrees of the hierarchy, as opposed to the major or sacred orders. At present the ranks of the clergy are entered by the tonsure, after which all the orders are received in succession without omission. As a general rule ecclesiastics no longer remain in the lower orders. Clergy in higher orders now perform those liturgical tasks, as with exorcism, or layfolk do, as with singing and altar service.

In earlier times, appointment to any task reserved to churchmen marked one's entry into the clergy. The article surveys the four minor orders, porter, lector, exorcist, and acolyte, with the subdiaconate once counted among them, tracing their origin, functions, and the ceremonies of conferral.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-modeste-demer:
Modeste Demers, the Pacific Coast apostle of North America, was the first Catholic missionary to most Indian tribes across Oregon, Washington, and British Columbia. He was born at St. Nicholas, Quebec, on 11 October 1809 and died at Victoria, British Columbia, on 21 July 1871. His parents, Michel Demers and Rosalie Foucher, were upright French Canadian farmers.

Sensitive in conscience and deeply drawn to religion, the young Demers chose the priesthood, learning first on his own and then at Quebec's seminary. Bishop Signay ordained him on 7 February 1836, and he spent fourteen months in parish work. He then headed for the Pacific Northwest, where he worked among natives and settlers and in time became the first Bishop of Victoria.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-music-of-vesp:
The Music of Vespers deals with the texts sung at evening prayer: antiphons, psalms and hymns that change with feast and season. They follow the Ordo wherever public recitation of the Canonical Hours is obligatory. The Second Plenary Council of Baltimore in 1868 ordered complete vespers on Sundays and feasts wherever possible after the Roman fashion, never replaced by other devotions.

To spread the practice, the council ordered Gregorian chant rudiments taught in parish schools so congregations could join ministers and choir in song. A rescript of 1882 banned the custom of singing only some verses of psalms, and the Third Plenary Council of 1884 commanded integral psalms wherever vespers are performed. The entry then surveys chant books, harmonisations and the practical problems of preparing changing antiphons.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nevers:
Nevers is a diocese covering the Department of Nievre in France. Suppressed by the Concordat of 1801 and united to Autun, it was restored in 1823 as suffragan of Sens, taking parts of the former dioceses of Autun and Auxerre. Gallia Christiana names Saint Eladius, healed in Clovis's reign by Saint Severinus, as its first bishop.

Duchesne counts Tauricanus, present at Epaon in 517, as the first authentic bishop. Several later bishops are venerated as saints, including Arey, Agricola, and Jerome, who rebuilt the cathedral for martyrs Quiricus and Julitta. Notable bishops include the future cardinal Pierre Bertrandi, who defended church immunities against barons in 1329 to 1330. Charles de Bourbon, whom the Leaguers wished to make King of France as Charles X, also held the see.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nicholas-taci:
A Franciscan scholar of Scripture from the Low Countries, Nicholas Tacitus Zegers worked at Louvain in the first half of the sixteenth century. Trained in Greek and Hebrew, he took over the chair of biblical explanation there in 1536 and gave it up in 1548 to write full time.

Zegers left many books, with notes on all the New Testament books and corrections to the New Testament text. He also made a kind of concordance and translations of devotional works from Flemish and French into Latin. He died at Louvain in 1559. His Greek and Hebrew learning set his criticism apart in an age when such judgment was rare.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-non-jurors:
The Non-Jurors were Anglican clergy and laity who in 1689 refused to swear allegiance to William and Mary. Their episcopal leaders, Sancroft of Canterbury with Turner, Lloyd, White, Thomas, Ken, Lake, and Cartwright, faced suspension by August and deprivation by the following February if they held out.

Most held out and lost their sees, joined by some four hundred clergy including Hickes, Collier, Kettlewell, and Nelson. Though five bishops had resisted James II, they would accept William only as regent, not as king, and their schism shaped Anglican life for decades.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-notre-dame-de:
Notre-Dame des Ardilliers, a shrine at Saumur in France, centers on a statue found by a spring in 1454. A monastery Charlemagne founded there fell to Normans, and its last monk kept only a statue of Our Lady in a cave by the spring, the image later recovered and honored.

Miracles at the spring, whose waters were held healing, led to a chapel dedicated in 1553, enlarged notably by Richelieu, and entrusted to Oratorians in 1614. Louis XIII, Anne of Austria, and Marie de' Medici numbered among its pilgrims, and Sulpician founders sought inspiration there.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-order-of-prea:
The Order of Preachers, or Dominicans, joins friars, sisters, and lay penitents under Dominic's preaching mission, and this entry covers all three branches. Dominic's preaching in Languedoc against Albigensians led Innocent III's letters of 1205 to shape a new kind of apostolic preacher, patterned on the apostles.

Legislation for friars and sisters grew together, and the historical survey follows foundations, studies, missions, and the Inquisition's shadow. The entry details constitutions, government, habit, and the order's schools, saints, and missions across eight centuries. The order’s legislation grew closely with its history, a point the entry stresses.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pamiers:
Pamiers is a French diocese covering the department of Ariege, suffragan of Toulouse. Joined to Toulouse by the Concordat of 1801, it rose again by the Concordat of 1817. The new diocese took effect only in September 1823. It united old Pamiers and Couserans with most of Mirepoix and Rieux and a deanery of Alet. A 1910 decree restored the titles of Couserans and Mirepoix.

Tradition names Saint Antoninus, born near Pamiers and martyred in his home country, as first apostle of the region. His abbey, founded about 960, passed to Girona in 1034 and to Cluny in 1060. Roger II of Foix built a castle on the site called Appamia, whence Pamiers. Boniface VIII raised the see by bull of 23 July 1295, named Bernard Saisset its bishop, and fixed bounds carved from Toulouse, despite the Toulouse bishop's opposition.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-parochial-reg:
Parochial registers are the five books a pastor must keep to know his flock: baptisms, confirmations, marriages, deaths, and a census of souls. Trent's command that a shepherd know his subjects, plus the historical weight and legal proof of public records, grounds the rule. Set forms govern entries, and every public paper must show place, date, and nature of the act, officiant, parties, witnesses, and official signature.

Church law adds parentage and parish for each person, the officiant's office, and full detail to remove doubt over validity or form. A baptism entry thus notes legitimacy, birth date, and names given, plus private, conditional, or supplied ceremonies where they apply. Foundlings' entries record where, when, and by whom they were found, with apparent age, and later pages cover corrections, secrecy, and custody of the books.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-patrician-bro:
The Patrician Brothers, or Brothers of Saint Patrick, were founded by Daniel Delaney, Bishop of Kildare and Leighlin, at Tullow in County Carlow, on the Purification feast in 1808. Their aim was religious and literary schooling for youth and instruction of the faithful in Christian devotion. Catholic Ireland was just emerging from penal-law times, when procuring Catholic schooling for a child counted as treason.

Young and old alike thus lacked teaching, and Delaney chose seven Sunday-school catechists as the new order's nucleus. Under his own training and his successor Doyle's direction, the congregation took root as a diocesan body. Daughter houses spread through Ireland, and bishops invited the brothers to Australia and India, where several foundations rose. Later pages follow their schools, rules, and growth.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-paul-melchers:
Paul Melchers was Cardinal Archbishop of Cologne, born at Muenster in Westphalia on 6 January 1813 and dead at Rome on 14 December 1895. He read law at Bonn from 1830 to 1833, practised briefly at Muenster, then studied theology at Munich under Klee, Goerres, Windischmann, and Doellinger. Ordained in 1841, he served at Haltern village, became seminary vice-rector in 1844, rector in 1851, cathedral canon in 1852, and vicar-general in 1854.

Pius IX made him Bishop of Osnabrueck in 1857 and Archbishop of Cologne in 1866. There he laboured zealously and launched the annual Fulda meetings of German bishops in 1867. Though he always taught papal infallibility, he judged its definition untimely, saying so with thirteen bishops in 1869. At Vatican I he voted against it on 13 July 1870, yet refused to join fifty-five others in a protest departure, and later submitted fully.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-paulist-fathe:
The Paulist Fathers are a community of priests for missions and apostolic works, above all winning converts to Catholic faith. Founded at Rome and New York in 1858 by Isaac Thomas Hecker, with Augustine Hewit, George Deshon, Francis Baker, and Clarence Walworth, they had all belonged to the Redemptorists. Suspected of disloyalty and accused of disobedience, they sought to explain themselves to their superior general, and Hecker, reaching Rome in 1857, was expelled from the Redemptorists three days later.

Appeal to the Holy See failed to win approval of the expulsion, and at their own request the priests were dispensed from vows and formed the new community. Propaganda letters warmly commended Hecker and his fellows to American bishops. Long before, Hecker felt distinct intimations that he was set apart to lead his country's conversion in some conspicuous way, and he told many, singly and together, of those supernatural visitations.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-penitential-o:
Penitential orders were religious congregations bound to harsh works of penance, or to helping others atone for grave faults. This Catholic Encyclopedia survey names the great families first. They run from Capuchins and Carmelites to the Third Orders of Dominic and Francis and the Sisters of the Good Shepherd, each treated under its own heading. It then lingers on smaller and stranger communities that fit the same pattern.

Hermits of St. John the Baptist in Navarre lived eight to a hermitage in silence and mortification, wearing rough brown habits and heavy wooden crosses. A French reform of hermit life under Michel de Sabine admitted only men of proven character and delayed final vows until age forty-five. The survey closes with the Polish and Bohemian Order of Penance of the Holy Martyrs, whose origins writers disputed back to Pope Cletus.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-peter-donders:
Peter Donders was a Dutch missionary to lepers in Suriname, born at Tilburg in 1807. A childhood wish for the priesthood survived factory work and service in a college, where a benefactor's help finally let him study at Herlaar.
