Sachiko Tsuruta of the Smithsonian Astrophysical Observatory and A G W Cameron of Goddard's Institute for Space Studies wrote this study of neutron star cooling. Neutron stars are the dense remains left after a supernova explosion. Soon after birth, such a star is extremely hot. The authors calculate how its heat fades with time.

New X-ray sources in the sky had raised fresh interest in these objects. One idea was that the X-rays came from hot neutron star surfaces. Earlier calculations suggested a star could still be millions of degrees hot at some age. This work tests that picture with its own cooling calculations.
nasa-tm-19650019136-automatic-extensomet:
C D Hooper, at Marshall Space Flight Center, designed an automatic extensometer and described it in a June 21, 1965 memorandum. An extensometer measures how far a material stretches. This one was built for elastomers, rubber-like materials that can stretch a great deal. It records the stretch directly on the testing machine's chart.

Hooper says the device measures accurately from no stretch to ten times the starting length. It needs little skill to operate. Because the process is semi-automatic, labs can match each other's results more closely. That repeatability matters when stretch data decide whether a seal or hose is fit to fly.
nasa-tm-19660030633-analysis-of-cadmium-:
Eugene R. Stroup, of NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland, wrote this September 1966 report on a small charge-measuring device. The device is the cadmium-cadmium coulometer, which tracks electric charge passing through it. Stroup examines its use for controlling the charging of nickel-cadmium batteries built for spacecraft.

The report sums up two years of coulometer work at Goddard. Coulometers were designed and built there, then put through design, forming, and accelerated tests. Sections cover leakage, the signal the device gives, impedance, electrolyte, and separators, followed by systems tests. Stroup reports that the devices proved acceptable for controlling spacecraft battery charging. Two manufacturers, he adds, showed they could build and deliver them.
nasa-tm-19680010860-cryogenic-positive-e:
Raymond F. Lark, at the Lewis Research Center in Cleveland, tested plastic films at brutal cold in April 1968. The films form expulsion bladders inside propellant tanks. A bladder flexes to push fuel out when gravity cannot. At liquid hydrogen temperatures, most plastics turn stiff and brittle.

Lark's programs twisted and flexed single and layered films hundreds of degrees below zero. Thin Mylar films proved the most flexible of those tested. The report gives the links between cycle life, film thickness, and the number of layers. Tank designers used such data to pick bladder materials that would not crack in service.
nasa-tm-19700017709-x-radiation-in-binar:
Klaus Schocken of the Marshall Space Flight Center wrote this report on March 13, 1970. It reviews what was known about X radiation from binary stars. Binary stars are pairs of stars that circle each other.

Schocken sums up the known traits of close binary stars and old novae from published sources. Old novae are star systems that flared up brightly in the past. He then takes up a binary system as his main case. Reviews of this kind gave astronomers a shared picture of odd X-ray sources. They also pointed to what new observations should test.
nasa-tm-19720007838-diatomic-gasdynamic-:
Robert L McKenzie of the Ames Research Center wrote this December 1971 memorandum, NASA TM X-62,099, on diatomic gasdynamic lasers. A gasdynamic laser expands hot gas very fast through a nozzle. The rapid cooling traps molecules in excited states, which can then emit laser light. McKenzie modeled how vibrating two atom molecules relax during that expansion. Small imperfections in their vibration pattern turned out to matter greatly.

His numerical model followed anharmonic oscillators, whose energy steps are uneven. For gases like carbon monoxide, that slight unevenness built up. It caused large overpopulations of the upper vibration states. Those overpopulations are exactly what a laser needs to work. Mixed gas recipes could sharpen the effect further.
northup-twelve-years:
Solomon Northup was a free Black musician and farmer in New York when kidnappers drugged him in 1841. Sold into slavery in Louisiana, he spent twelve years on plantations before friends traced him. His account appeared in 1853, the year of his rescue.

Northup describes cotton and sugar work, overseers, and fellow enslaved people with precise, calm detail. He names places and owners, and court records later backed his story. That makes Twelve Years a Slave the best documented American slave narrative. Its cool tone makes the cruelty it reports hit even harder. A white editor, David Wilson, helped ready the tale for print that year.
not-that-it-matters:
A. A. Milne gathered Not That It Matters as a book of light essays, listed here by title. The Pleasure of Writing opens the contents, then Acacia Road and My Library. Superstition, The Charm of Golf, and Goldfish follow. Saturday to Monday and The Pond keep the tone easy and domestic.

Later essays praise autumn, daffodils, and lunch, and mock a household book. A Day at Lord's, By the Sea, and At the Bookstall take Milne outdoors. Signs of Character, Intellectual Snobbery, and Smoking as a Fine Art show his targets. On Going Dry and A Misjudged Game close the sampled list. Small subjects, handled with grace, are the point.
old-and-new-masters:
Robert Lynd published this book of literary essays in 1919. He writes about major poets, novelists, and critics of the past. The contents name Dostoevsky, Jane Austen, and Henry James. Other essays treat Wordsworth, Keats, Browning, and Pope. Irish and modern writers also receive close attention.

Lynd judges each writer with warmth, wit, and clear taste. He asks what makes a book live for later readers. Essays on Yeats, Shaw, and Chekhov sit beside older masters. Some pieces split into two or three short studies. The book suits readers who enjoy lively literary talk.
on-the-pampas-or-the-young-settlers:
George Alfred Henty wrote this adventure for young readers. A fight with a puma fronts the book as picture. Chapter one gives Mrs. Hardy's bold resolution to emigrate. The family then starts for a new life abroad. Later chapters reach the pampas and a settler's home.

A tale of the Mexican War fills two chapters. Farm work, games, and neighborly visits follow the settling. Gauchos, cattle work, and frontier dangers fill the story. Henty blends excitement with sturdy, practical values. Generations of boys learned geography from his tales. Seth then goes on with his tale of that same war. His long tale fills two full chapters of the book.
one-of-ours: Willa Cather's 1922 Pulitzer winner: Claude Wheeler, the Nebraska farm boy, finds meaning in the Great War. Tender, tragic, and beautifully written, it is her most controversial novel. A great American war book. Cather's war scenes rank with the finest in American fiction.
our-boys-entertaining-stories-by-popular:
Our Boys: Entertaining Stories by Popular Authors is an illustrated gift book for children, published in Akron, Ohio, in 1904. Its title page rounds up a slate of popular magazine writers for the young — George Cary Eggleston, Mary E. Wilkins, Frances A. Humphrey, Margaret Eytinge, Mrs. A. D. T. Whitney, and Mary D. Brine among them — in a volume profusely illustrated, as the period liked its juveniles.

The book opens in verse, with Clara Doty Bates's The Cat-Tail Arrow. Little Sammie whittles a bow shaped like half an O and sighs for an arrow light enough to fly to the treetops; a cat-tail reed suggests itself. The poem sets the anthology's tone: outdoor boyhood, small inventions, and rhymes and stories made to be read aloud in a lamplit parlor.
pagan-papers:
Kenneth Grahame wrote Pagan Papers before The Wind in the Willows made him famous. The contents promise The Romance of the Road and The Romance of the Rail. Non Libri Sed Liberi, Loafing, and Cheap Knowledge follow. The Rural Pan, Marginalia, and Of Smoking close the range. These are essays for a countryman stranded in the city.

The Romance of the Road opens with Rabelais. Pantagruel visited an island whose roads literally went to places. Grahame's real-life answer is the Ridgeway of the North Berkshire Downs. Join it at Streatley, where it crosses the Thames. It strikes away from the habitable world at once. A broad green ribbon of turf, it keeps the highest ridge. No village tempts it aside for a yard.
pages-from-a-journal-with-other-papers: Pages from a Journal with Other Papers is by Mark Rutherford. That was the pen name of William Hale White. T. Fisher Unwin published this second impression in London in 1901. The hosted sample shows the title page and contents only. A Visit to Carlyle in 1868 leads the contents. Journal entries for January, March, June, and August follow. Pieces on Spinoza, Injustice, Faith, and talking about our troubles complete it. No essay text appears in the sample.
pardners:
Rex Beach's Pardners collects tales of the Alaskan gold country. Beach had written The Spoilers and The Barrier. Ten stories fill the contents. The Mule Driver and the Garrulous Mute appears. So do The Colonel and the Horse-Thief and The Thaw at Slisco's. Bitter Root Billings and North of Fifty-Three close the range. The title story opens the book in a tent.

Joyce, its narrator, announces that most quotations need fixing. Marriages, the old saying claims, are made in heaven. Joyce insists the saying meant pardnerships. A true pardnership is the sanctifiedest relation that grows. Just then the camp dogs erupt outside. Joyce dives through the tent flap to arbitrate. Beach's Alaska runs on that mixture: philosophy, profanity, and dogfights.
parish-papers: Norman Macleod's Parish Papers appeared in 1863. Macleod was a Doctor of Divinity and one of Queen Victoria's chaplains for Scotland. He dedicated the papers to his parishioners of Loudoun, Dalkeith, and the Barony. The hosted sample shows the title page, dedication, and contents only. Thoughts on Christianity leads, asking what Christianity is and who Jesus was. Thoughts on the Final Judgment and on Future Life follow. Future Punishment and What After Death? close the range. No essay text appears in the sample.
patty-s-suitors: In the hosted sample, only the front matter of Patty's Suitors, the title page and table of contents, with no chapter text visible. The title page names Carolyn Wells and E. C. Caswell as illustrator. The contents open with a Valentine party and move through a house party, a quarantine, May-Day, and moonlight, with chapters named Eddie Bell, Kenneth, and Belle Harcourt. Those chapters mark the social round in which Patty's suitors appear.
phaethon-loose-thoughts-for-loose-thinke:
Charles Kingsley's Phaethon, dated 1852, is subtitled Loose Thoughts for Loose Thinkers. Two friends lounge by a clear limestone stream in a park, fishing badly on a lovely morning. Templeton confesses he has been dreaming instead of fishing; the narrator has sat up all night writing after a talkative evening.

The talk of that evening runs on, in dialogue, while the flies rise and the keeper despairs of them. Kingsley uses the fishing idyll to carry arguments about faith, doubt, and the Church. The book is a conversation piece: theology in waders, with the Severn hills in view.
piano-mastery-talks-with-master-pianists: In the hosted sample, only the front matter of Piano Mastery, the title page and the start of the contents, with no talk text visible. The title page names Harriette Brower and promises talks with master pianists and teachers, an account of a Von Bülow class, hints on interpretation by William Mason and William H. Sherwood, and sixteen portraits. The contents open with a prelude and Paderewski, then Ernest Schelling on the hand of a pianist and Sigismond Stojowski on mind in piano study.
pindar-odes-myers:
Pindar of Thebes was the greatest lyric poet of ancient Greece. Ernest Myers translated his surviving victory odes into English. The odes celebrate winners at the Olympic, Pythian, Nemean, and Isthmian games.

Each ode weaves the victor's praise together with myth and moral warning. Pindar warns athletes that glory is brief and pride draws divine anger. His language is dense, soaring, and famously hard to follow. Chariot owners, wrestlers, and boy boxers all receive the same lofty treatment. Myers helps modern readers through the thickets of allusion. These poems defined how Greece praised excellence in public.
pirke-avot-the-sayings-of-the-jewish-fat: Joseph Isaac Gorfinkle's edition presents Pirke Avot, the Sayings of the Jewish Fathers. It is the third volume in a Library of Jewish Classics series, after works by Zunz and Hyman Hurwitz. The sample held for this entry holds the transcriber's comments, not the sayings themselves. Those notes say the source book printed all of Pirkei Avot in Hebrew with vowels. That Hebrew text is left out of this e-text, and Hebrew words appear in brackets in transliterated form. Footnotes were moved to follow the passages they belong to.
podcast-joerogan-Xr0jaqT8eRs:
Jay Anderson joins the Joe Rogan Experience for episode 2430 for a full-length conversation. The entry keeps the show's standard shape: one guest across hours of open talk with Rogan, with the transcript holding the whole session as it aired.

The value of such entries is the record itself, the guest's views and stories in his own words rather than in clips cut by others. Readers can follow the exchange from start to finish and judge the ideas whole. The episode stands in the library as a complete sitting with the day's guest, filed for listeners who want nothing trimmed away.
podcast-joerogan-nMBFf1SIBRs:
Benjamin Franklin is the unlikely star of this Joe Rogan Experience segment about skeletons found in a London basement. Franklin lived in the house for years while serving as a colonial agent. When workers dug into the cellar, they found human bones buried under the floor.

Rogan and his guest sort through why the bones were there. The leading account points to an anatomy school run by Franklin's friend, who used bodies for study and buried the remains in secret. They weigh that sober story against darker rumors. It is a short, strange detour into the hidden side of a founding father.
ponkapog-papers:
Thomas Bailey Aldrich gathered his miscellaneous notes and essays as Ponkapog Papers, explaining the odd title in a note from Redman Farm, Ponkapog, in 1903. Ponkapog, a little Massachusetts settlement under the Blue Hills on an old Indian reservation, has no illusions about rivalling great centers. Aldrich claims the same modesty for his papers, with alluring alliteration as a further excuse. The book is dedicated to Francis Bartlett.

Contents promise a notebook's variety: leaves from a notebook, asides, an essay on Tom Folio, queer surnames, a note on Rostand's L'Aiglon. Plot and character, the cruelty of science, Leigh Hunt and Barry Cornwall, Decoration Day, writers and talkers, and the case against early rising. Aldrich, poet, editor of the Atlantic, and author of the Story of a Bad Boy. Writes here as a gentleman at leisure, and the slightness he apologizes for is exactly the charm his readers bought.
primavera-poems-by-four-authors:
Thomas B. Mosher of Portland, Maine, published Primavera in 1900 from his press at 45 Exchange Street. A volume of poems by four authors, issued with the care for type and paper that made Mosher's books collectible on sight. An epigraph from Guarini's Pastor Fido gives the book its name and season: spring, youth of the year. Beautiful mother of flowers and new loves, returns, but the serene days of the speaker's joys do not return with her.

The opening poem refuses the Muse outright: no Muse will I invoke, for she is fled. Sitting breathing yet all but dead, she who dreamed of gods in Tempe's golden air and deemed heroic Greece could never die. The four poets of the volume, young men of the 1890s little magazine world, mourn and celebrate that fled muse between them. Primavera is the American aesthetic movement in one small garland.
quiet-talks-with-world-winners: Quiet Talks with World Winners, by S. D. Gordon, is shown here by its contents alone. Part one, World-winning, treats the master passion, the Master's plan, the need, the present opportunity, the pressing emergency, the past failure, and the coming victory. Part two, Winning Forces, names the church, each single believer, Jesus, the Holy Spirit, prayer, money, and sacrifice. The opening talk, The Master Passion, breaks into heads that run from the earliest Calvary picture to Jesus' world-passion.
quotations-from-georg-ebers: Quotations from Georg Ebers is one of David Widger's quotation volumes, drawn from the Project Gutenberg edition of Ebers's collected historical novels. The pages shown give Widger's editor's note and the start of his contents. He invites readers who know the novels to check whether their favorite passages are listed and to send additions. The contents begin with the ten volumes of Uarda and the volumes of An Egyptian Princess, each tied to its source file.
quotes-and-images-from-the-novels-of-geo:
Quotes and Images from Georg Ebers is prepared by David Widger. It combines a list of the novelist's pictures with quotations from across his historical novels. The pictures include his portrait. They include Uarda, Cleopatra, and Margery. Homo Sum appears too, with a recluse in The Fire of the Forge. The quotations are set in alphabetical order.

The sayings carry Ebers's sententious, storyteller's voice. A noble mind can never swim with the stream, a first impression is often a final one, and a small joy makes us forget a heavy grief. A live dog is better than a dead king, a well-to-do man always gets a higher price than a poor one, and a knot can often be untied by daylight.
raabe-elderflowers:
Fragrant blossoms of early summer give Raabe's novella Elderflowers its name and its mood, in this English translation. Small-town German life again supplies the scene, where ordinary people carry quiet burdens. Dignity and humor, Raabe's twin signatures, mark the way his characters bear them.

Tender, observant, and gently melancholy, the tale shows the author at his most characteristic. Old attachments stir as the elderflowers bloom, and the past leans into the present. Nothing is forced; feeling gathers like scent on warm air. Readers new to Raabe will find a compact sample of his gifts. Those who know him will recognize the beloved hand at once, unhurried and kind.
records-of-a-family-of-engineers:
Robert Louis Stevenson turned from tales to his own stock in this family record, issued by Chatto and Windus of London in 1912. The book opens with an introduction on the surname itself. Stevenson traces its many old spellings across Scotland, from the Firth of Forth to the Firth of Clyde.

Place names, parishes, and landholders carry the name through the centuries, then it fades from the land rolls. Stevensons of Hirdmanshiels rode in raids, served as jurors, and stood bail for neighbors before their line died out. Stevenson finds still others in Parliament and in burgh life, a stock that later rose in works of building and light.
red-saunders-pets-and-other-critters:
Henry Wallace Phillips gathered tales of animals in this book, published by McClure, Phillips of New York in May 1906. Phillips was already known for Red Saunders and Mr. Scraggs, and the pieces had run in magazines from 1902 onward. A frontispiece shows a pet its owner calls lovely, though the picture is noted as missing here.

The contents open a section called The Pets, with tales named Oscar's Chance, Per Charley, and Billy the Buck. A buck, at least, is a creature with a will of its own. Phillips writes of ranch and town animals with the dry humor of his Saunders stories, in short pieces made for magazine readers.
revolutionary-heroes-and-other-historica:
James Parton's historical papers on heroes of the American Revolution form number ten of a series of classic readings. A title-page list names his subjects: General Joseph Warren, Captain Nathan Hale, and Washington's spies. Valley Forge, John Adams, John Jay, Robert Morris, and Fisher Ames stand in the same list.

An introduction sketches Parton's own life first. Born at Canterbury, England, on February 9, 1822, he was brought to America at five and schooled in New York. He taught, wrote for the Home Journal, and made his name with a life of Horace Greeley in 1855. Lives of Aaron Burr and Andrew Jackson followed, built from original sources.
richard-lovell-edgeworth-a-selection-fro:
Beatrix L. Tollemache, the Hon. Mrs. Lionel Tollemache, edited this selection from the memoirs of Richard Lovell Edgeworth, issued by Rivington, Percival of London in 1896. A short poem of her own, Life Is An Inn, stands before the text, signed with her initials. Guests at life's inn, she writes, pay nothing when they depart.

Her first chapter tells how she found the Memoirs in a second-hand bookshop and found the book full of interest. Edgeworth, father of a large family and a man of projects and inventions, tells his own life in the extracts that follow. Tollemache's other books, verses and a Swiss translation, are listed on the title page.
roman-holidays-and-others:
W. D. Howells published these travel sketches with Harper and Brothers in 1908, illustrated, after a voyage to Italy. Up and Down Madeira opens the contents, and Two Uptown Blocks into Spain follows. Ashore at Genoa and Naples and Her Joyful Noise bring the ship to Italy.

Pompeii Revisited and the title piece, Roman Holidays, stand at the book's centre. A Week at Leghorn, Over at Pisa, and Back at Genoa trace the return along the coast. Eden After the Fall closes the list. The first sketch finds Madeira's cliffs and cataracts richer than any theatre drop-curtain Howells had seen, on a tearful mid-January afternoon.
roscoe-twenty-five-years:
Roscoe told his own story in Twenty-five Years in East Africa in 1921. The memoir covers his mission work and research in Uganda. A young missionary grows, across its pages, into a famed scholar.

Travel, danger, and close watching mark his slow path to trust. He shows how a people's respect is earned, not merely claimed. The human tale behind his great Baganda study stands clear here. Readers meet the man inside the classic work of East African studies. Adventure and patient science share the road in his warm, plain telling. The memoir explains the trust that made his great study possible.
rouen-its-history-and-monuments-a-guide-: Theod. Licquet, a member of the Royal Academy of Rouen, wrote Rouen, Its History and Monuments, a guide for strangers printed at Rouen in 1840. The book was cut down and translated from the French by M. D. G. It comes with a map of the town and five views, and it sold for two francs. The title page also lists two French works then in the press, one on the parliament of Normandy and one on the abbots of Saint-Ouen.
rough-stone-monuments-and-their-builders: T. Eric Peet wrote Rough Stone Monuments and Their Builders, issued in London and New York in 1912. Peet is named as a former scholar of Queen's College, Oxford, and as lately Craven Fellow at Oxford and Pelham Student at the British School at Rome. A view of Stonehenge from the south-east faces the title page.
roundabout-papers: William Makepeace Thackeray wrote the Roundabout Papers, a set of short essays gathered here under one title. The contents list On a Lazy Idle Boy, On Two Children in Black, On Ribbons, and On Some Late Great Victories. Other pieces include Thorns in the Cushion, On Screens in Dining-Rooms, Tunbridge Toys, De Juventute, and On a Joke I Once Heard from the Late Thomas Hood.
russia-as-seen-and-described-by-famous-w:
Esther Singleton edited and translated Russia As Seen and Described by Famous Writers, issued in New York in 1909 by Dodd, Mead and Company, with many pictures. Singleton is named as author of Turrets, Towers and Temples and A Guide to the Opera. A view of Moscow faces the title page. In her preface she calls the book a companion volume to Japan, following the same general plan. It aims to present, in small compass, a fairly full view of the great Muscovite power.

The plan moves in a set order. A short account of country and race comes first, then a brief review of history and religion, with the rites and ceremonies of the Greek Church. Regions, cities, and fine buildings follow, then pieces on manners and customs of rural and town life.
salute-to-adventurers: John Buchan wrote Salute to Adventurers, headed with the year 1915. A picture captioned 1798 Edinburgh faces a long verse dedication to Major-General the Hon. Sir Reginald Talbot. Buchan tells him he tells of old Virginian ways, and asks who is more fit to scan the tale than a man who knew the eager horse of Sheridan in far-off days. The verses recall sullen meads of fate, tattered scrub, and blood-drenched sod where Lee bent to the storm of God.
sea-and-shore-a-sequel-to-miriam-s-memoi:
Mrs. Catharine A. Warfield published this novel in Philadelphia in 1876 as a sequel to her earlier Miriam books. Warfield had already won readers with The Household of Bouverie and Monfort Hall. A verse motto about a proud ship facing its last hour fronts the title page.

Warfield continues the family story begun in Miriam's Memoirs and Miriam's House. The publisher sold each of her novels in one cloth volume for a dollar and three quarters. Readers who followed Miriam's fortunes could pick up the thread here, in a tale shaped by loss, duty, and change at home.
sinking-of-the-titanic-and-great-sea-dis:
Logan Marshall edited this account of the Titanic's loss, built, the title page states, from facts given by survivors. A front caption hails her as the world's grandest liner, on her first voyage with more than 2,300 souls aboard. She struck an iceberg late on Sunday, April 14, 1912, and sank within hours.

Captain E. J. Smith, praised as brave and seasoned, died with his ship. The book adds records of earlier great sea disasters, the growth of safety gear, and causes of such wrecks with means to shun them. A message of comfort by Rev. Henry Van Dyke closes the volume.
sister-songs-an-offering-to-two-sisters:
Francis Thompson published this long poem with Burns and Oates in London in 1908, as an offering to two sisters, Monica and Madeline Meynell. A preface dated 1895 states that Thompson wrote the poem some four years before that printing push, in the same season as The Hound of Heaven.

Thompson owns one borrowed image in the proem, taken without intent from Coventry Patmore's St. Valentine's Day. He leaves it in place, with thanks to a poet wealthy enough to lend to a poorer one. Boyhood, sisters, and lost youth sing through Thompson's dense, glowing verse.
sisters:
Ada Cambridge wrote this Australian novel around Guthrie Carey, a sailor who began life young. Not yet twenty-one and between voyages, Carey marries Lily Harrison, a poor, pretty, homeless girl worn down as a lady-help in hard posts at Sandridge. He wins her father's glad consent and a parson's blessing in sailor haste.

A fortnight of snatched honeymoon ends in a year's parting. Carey returns a father and a first mate with a master's ticket and better pay, ready to make a home. Cambridge traces young love's costs across sea years, in a tale of devotion strained by distance.
sketches-of-the-covenanters:
J. C. McFeeters, minister of the Second Church of the Covenanters in Philadelphia, wrote these sketches of Scotland's covenanting past. A picture of the modern Covenanter church at Greenock stands among the plates. Chapter heads open with the land of the covenants, then the battlefield of Presbyterianism and its flag.

Early martyrs follow, with George Wishart named, then Knox in the field of conflict. Foundation stones and Mary, Queen of Scots, come next in the contents. McFeeters writes to pass the tale to generations following, as his title verse urges, honoring men who held worship and liberty dearer than life.
some-diversions-of-a-man-of-letters: Edmund Gosse wrote Some Diversions of a Man of Letters. William Heinemann printed the London book in 1920. It first came out in October 1919. New printings followed in November 1919 and February 1920. The opening pages list Gosse's other works. They run from Northern Studies of 1879 onward. His Life of Gray came in 1882. Lives of Congreve, Donne, and Jeremy Taylor stand in the list. A short history of modern English letters appears there too.
some-roundabout-papers:
William Makepeace Thackeray writes the Roundabout Papers in a loose, chatty vein, and the 1908 T. N. Foulis edition opens with On Some Carp at Sans Souci. The first paper turns to an old lady of ninety who has spent twenty-five years in the workhouse of the parish of Saint Lazarus. She came out once, some twenty-three years back, to earn a bit by hop-picking.

The work broke her. Nights lying out gave her a palsy that stopped all later labor and still shakes her poor old limbs. She must share a workhouse bed each night with some other old woman, like it or not. A gentleman gave her brandy-and-water, and Queen Charlotte, who loved snuff herself, left snuff to some poorhouses. A pinch of it in her wakeful nights, the old woman says, is a true comfort.
songs-out-of-doors: Henry Van Dyke wrote Songs Out of Doors, dated 1923. The contents sort the poems under heads, and the first head, Of Birds and Flowers, names the veery, the song-sparrow, and the Maryland yellow-throat. The whip-poor-will, wings of a dove, the hermit thrush, sea-gulls of Manhattan, and the ruby-crowned kinglet follow, with an angler's reveille, a November daisy, and the lily of Yorrow. A second head, Of Skies and Seasons, opens with If All the Skies.
stand-by-for-mars:
Carey Rockwell wrote Stand By for Mars, a Tom Corbett Space Cadet adventure, with Willy Ley as technical adviser. Grosset and Dunlap of New York printed the book under a 1952 copyright held by Rockhill Radio. Chapter 1 opens at the monorail station of Space Academy. A harsh, bull-throated roar, stand to, you rocket wash, stills the chatter and laughter of more than a hundred boys at once.

Out of the gleaming monorail cars the boys tumble and freeze to attention. Down the main exit ramp comes a short, squat, heavily built man in the scarlet uniform of the enlisted Solar Guard. His fists sit on his hips, his feet spread wide, and his sharp eyes flick over the silent clusters. Then he saunters down with a strangely light, cat-like tread and barks the order: form up, column of fours.
stanton-eighty-years:
Elizabeth Cady Stanton published Eighty Years and More in 1898, her reminiscences of a life spent fighting for women's rights. Stanton was the chief philosopher of the American suffrage movement. She looks back from 1815 to 1897, the span in her subtitle.

She recalls her girlhood, the Seneca Falls convention of 1848, and her long partnership with Susan Anthony. Debates over the vote, marriage law, and the church fill the middle years. Her wit is sharp even when her allies fall short of her hopes. The book is both a memoir and a history of the movement she helped found.
stories-by-english-authors-africa-select:
Stories by English Authors: Africa, one of Scribner's picked sets, holds The Mystery of Sasassa Valley by A. Conan Doyle, Long Odds by H. Rider Haggard, King Bemba's Point by J. Landers, Ghamba by W. C. Scully, Mary Musgrave by an unnamed writer, and Gregorio by Percy Hemingway.

Doyle's tale opens with the riddle of Lucky Tom Donahue, whose nickname and fortune came from one strange stretch of time at Cape Colony. The teller swears men still living there can back every word. The set as a whole draws on diamond fields, bush camps, and colonial posts for tales of luck, danger, and strange turns.
stories-by-english-authors-france-select:
France, in Scribner's Stories by English Authors set, brings together five tales. It holds Stevenson's A Lodging for the Night and Ouida's A Leaf in the Storm. It also holds Collins's A Terribly Strange Bed and Hesba Stretton's Michel Lorio's Cross. A Perilous Amour by Stanley J. Weyman closes the set.

Stevenson's tale drops into Paris in late November 1456, with snow falling thick and silent over the city. The poet Francis Villon, a poor Master of Arts, jokes at a tavern window about the snow while the cold city sleeps. From there the set moves through storm, gambling terror, and risky love, all on French ground.
stories-by-english-authors-germany-selec:
Germany and Northern Europe, in the Stories by English Authors set, contains five tales. It holds Harraden's The Bird on Its Journey and John Strange Winter's Koosje, a study of Dutch life. Ouida's A Dog of Flanders and Stevenson's Markheim follow. Queen Tita's Wager by William Black closes the set.

Harraden opens in a small Swiss hotel, where a young girl comes in soaked at four in the afternoon, owning no luggage but a knapsack and no companions at all. She has walked from far off, yet sits at the piano and plays sad, sweet music. The tales that follow range from Dutch village life to a Flemish dog and a murderer's haunted conscience.
stories-by-english-authors-italy-selecte:
Stories by English Authors: Italy holds A Faithful Retainer by James Payn, Bianca by W. E. Norris, Goneril by A. Mary F. Robinson, The Brigand's Bride by Laurence Oliphant, and Mrs. General Talboys by Anthony Trollope.

Payn begins with the Luscombes, a county family settled since the time of Charles II and respected mostly for having lasted. Spendthrifts and misers have traded turns in the line, and the present owner, Roger Luscombe, leans careful after his father's losses at dice, cards, and race-horses. Old families, kept servants, brigands, and English folk living in Italy give the volume its mix of loyalty and pride.
stories-by-english-authors-london-select:
Stories by English Authors: London lists The Inconsiderate Waiter by J. M. Barrie, The Black Poodle by F. Anstey, That Brute Simmons by Arthur Morrison, A Rose of the Ghetto by I. Zangwill, An Idyl of London by Beatrice Harraden, The Omnibus by Q, and The Hired Baby by Marie Corelli.

Barrie's opener mocks a club man who holds that waiters are mere fittings, yet cannot forget his waiter William, who kept him a window seat and heard his small troubles for years. When William brings his own distress forward, the member's whole view shifts. The set roams London from clubs to the Jewish quarter and the omnibus.
stories-by-english-authors-scotland-sele:
Scotland, in Scribner's Stories by English Authors set, collects The Courting of T'nowhead's Bell by J. M. Barrie, The Heather Lintie by S. R. Crockett, A Doctor of the Old School by Ian Maclaren, Wandering Willie's Tale by Sir Walter Scott, The Glenmutchkin Railway by Professor Aytoun, and Thrawn Janet by R. L. Stevenson.

Barrie opens with a village courtship watched by all: Sam'l Dickie the weaver has thought for two years of courting Bell, while Little Sanders the coal-carter may prove a strong rival. Scots speech, kirk talk, and small-place pride run through the set, which closes with Stevenson's dark tale of a haunted minister.
stories-by-english-authors-the-orient-se:
Orient, in the Stories by English Authors set, holds The Man Who Would Be King by Rudyard Kipling, Tajima by Miss Mitford, A Chinese Girl Graduate by R. K. Douglas, The Revenge of Her Race by Mary Beaumont, King Billy of Ballarat by Morley Roberts, and Thy Heart's Desire by Netta Syrett.

Kipling's tale is told by a newsman who once came near kinship with a king and was promised a share of a kingdom, army, law courts, and all. It begins on a train bound for Mhow from Ajmir, in a hard third-class carriage. The set ranges across India, Japan, China, and Australia.
stories-of-achievement-volume-iii-orator:
Asa Don Dickinson edited Stories of Achievement, Volume III: Orators and Reformers, copyrighted in 1916 by Doubleday, Page and Company and reprinted at Garden City, New York, in 1925. It is the third of six volumes telling how notable people overcame hard starts.

The subjects are Demosthenes, Elihu Burritt, John B. Gough, Frederick Douglass, Henry Ward Beecher, Booker T. Washington, and Judge Ben B. Lindsey, with Beecher as frontispiece. The contents bill Demosthenes as the orator who stammered and Burritt as the learned blacksmith. Each life stresses practice, courage, and public speech put to work for reform causes.
strange-pages-from-family-papers:
T. F. Thiselton Dyer, author of The Ghost World and Church Lore Gleanings, published Strange Pages from Family Papers at London in 1895. The book mines old family records and household traditions for the odd, the grim, and the ghostly.

The opening chapters treat fatal curses, the screaming skull, and eccentric vows. Dyer gathers tales that families kept about their own houses and ancestors: deaths foretold, skulls that would not rest, and promises kept at strange cost. The frontispiece shows a blast of death on a heath and a grave yawning for a child of Moy, which sets the book's flavor of folklore mixed with dread.
studies-and-essays-concerning-letters:
Concerning Letters gathers six of John Galsworthy's studies and essays. It holds A Novelist's Allegory and Some Platitudes Concerning Drama. It holds Meditation on Finality and Wanted: Schooling. On Our Dislike of Things As They Are and The Windlestraw close the set. An Anatole France motto on the evil of excess fronts the set.

The allegory opens like a tale. The Prince of Felicitas rides at dusk through a dark quarter of his city. The quarter is called the Vita Publica. His horse picks its way among unseen scuttling things. Galsworthy uses story, complaint, and reflection to press writers and readers on honesty in fiction, the state of the drama, and schooling that leaves minds unready for life as it is.
studies-and-essays-quality-and-others:
Quality and Others, one of John Galsworthy's Concerning Life sets, holds Quality, The Grand Jury, Gone, Threshing, That Old-Time Place, Romance in three gleams, Memories, and Felicity. The title piece is his famous sketch of a German bootmaker in London's West End.

Galsworthy knew the man from boyhood, since he made boots for his father from two little shops let into one in a small by-street, with no sign above the door. The portrait honors a craftsman who would not cheapen his work, and it has become a byword for the price of true quality in a world drifting toward the shoddy. The other pieces mix story and meditation on English life.
studies-and-essays-the-inn-of-tranquilit:
Ten pieces fill The Inn of Tranquillity and Others, from Galsworthy's Concerning Life essays. The title sketch leads. Magpie over the Hill, Sheep-Shearing, and Evolution follow. Riding in the Mist, The Procession, and A Christian come next. Wind in the Rocks, My Distant Relative, and The Black Godmother close the set.

The title piece starts under a burning blue sky on an Italian coast of pines, cypresses, and olives, where the writers come on a pink house lettered Osteria di Tranquillita. A skittle alley cut from the olive grove, a gramophone's song, and a stout gentleman in yellow boots show change reaching even quiet places. Galsworthy's travel sketches blend scene, character, and gentle argument about what progress does to old ways.
susan-clegg-and-her-neighbors-affairs:
Anne Warner followed her first Susan Clegg book with Susan Clegg and Her Neighbors' Affairs, printed at Boston by Little, Brown, and Company in 1906. The frontispiece shows a garment admired as brand-new, with the price tag still hanging on the back.

A prefatory note tracks the stories' first homes. Mrs. Lathrop's Love Affair ran in The Century Magazine in 1905. The Wolf at Susan's Door ran in The Reader Magazine early in the present year. A Very Superior Man ran in The Red Book. Old Man Ely's Proposal appears here for the first time. Susan again watches her neighbors' courtships, debts, and proposals with a dry tongue, and Mrs. Lathrop again supplies the wondering questions.
swirling-waters:
Max Rittenberg's novel Swirling Waters was first published on July 3, 1913, by Methuen and Company of London, and reached a second edition by August of the same year. Rittenberg had already written The Mind-Reader and The Cockatoo, and he dedicates the book to his mother, whose advice and criticism helped greatly in the making of it.

The contents open with The Whirlpool, then a five-million-pound deal, then a chapter called Shadowed. The titles promise a story of high finance, where a young man is pulled into deep water by big money, watchers, and rivals. Rittenberg wrote city novels of business and speculation, and the whirlpool of the first chapter names the force that drags at his hero throughout.
table-talk-essays-on-men-and-manners:
William Hazlitt's Table-Talk: Essays on Men and Manners gathers his familiar essays in two volumes. The first volume opens with On the Pleasure of Painting. It moves through On the Past and Future and On Genius and Common Sense. A character of Cobbett follows. On People with One Idea and On the Ignorance of the Learned come next.

The second volume ranges wider. It runs from a landscape of Poussin to Milton's sonnets. It runs to On Going a Journey and coffee-house politicians. It ends with On Familiar Style. In that essay Hazlitt sets out his own plain, talkative manner. Later pieces weigh patronage and puffing, the knowledge of character, and the fear of death. Few English essayists pack so much gusto, quarrel, and shrewd portraiture into the short essay form.
tanakh-jps-1917-numbers:
Numbers, fourth book of the Torah, is given in the Jewish Publication Society's English rendering of 1917, from the Masoretic Text. God speaks to Moses in the desert of Sinai, in the second year after the escape from Egypt.

Moses and Aaron are told to count all Israel by family and tribe, each male from age twenty who can go to war. A chief for each tribe is named to stand with them, from Reuben to Naphtali. Readers get counts, camp rules, and march orders, then tales of doubt, spies, and revolt as a slave-born crowd is shaped into a people fit for the promised land.
the-actress-in-high-life-an-episode-in-w: Sue Petigru Bowen wrote The Actress in High Life. Its subtitle is An Episode in Winter Quarters. Derby and Jackson printed it in New York in 1860. It was entered that year at the district court of South Carolina. Lines from Shakespeare stand at the head. They tell how war has smoothed his wrinkled front. Chapter one opens under verses from Wordsworth. They sing of a happy traveler on the moor.
the-ambassadors: James' 1903 Ambassadors sends Strether to Paris to retrieve Chad. Consciousness deepens. The Tower library holds the full text. It ambassadord Strether. Paris seduced. Duty called. Awareness dawned. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
the-angel-and-the-author-and-others:
Jerome K. Jerome, named as author of Idle Thoughts of an Idle Fellow and Paul Kelver, published this set of pieces with Hurst and Blackett of London in 1908. The first chapter starts with a vexing dream about a fortnight after Christmas. The dreamer flies out of his window in his nightshirt, rising glad to be noticed at last.

London shrinks below him to a line of lamps along the Embankment, then to a faint glow under darkness. Behind him comes the slow beat of wings. He turns and finds the Recording Angel, weary with his work. Jerome builds the title piece on that meeting, mixing jokes about his own goodness with a shy fear that a little less virtue might have bought a longer life.
the-art-of-letters: Robert Lynd's The Art of Letters, printed at New York in 1921, opens with a letter to J. C. Squire dated from Steyning on August 30, 1920. Lynd calls Squire godfather to many chapters. They were first printed in the London Mercury, the New Statesman, and the British Review. Others ran in the Daily News, the Nation, the Athenaeum, the Observer, and Everyman. He offers Squire the whole brood in the name of a friendship of many midnights. The contents begin with Mr. Pepys, John Bunyan, Thomas Campion, and John Donne.
the-aspern-papers:
Henry James's tale is shown here in its first American book edition, from Macmillan and Company in 1888. Its narrator has taken Mrs. Prest into his confidence, and with reason: the fruitful idea in the whole business, he admits, dropped from her friendly lips. She cut the knot he had been picking at.

Her plan was simple: ask the Misses Bordereau to take him in as a lodger. To grow close to them, first live in their house. The narrator confesses he would never have risen to so bold a scheme alone. He had come from England with a few firm facts about the two women, which he now bends toward his hunt for a dead poet's papers.
the-bible-king-james-version-book-4-numb:
Numbers in the King James rendering, begins in the wilderness of Sinai, in the tabernacle, on the first day of the second month in the second year after leaving Egypt. God tells Moses and Aaron to take the sum of all Israel.

Men from twenty years old upward, able to go to war, are to be numbered by families and fathers' houses. A man from each tribe is to stand with them. Names follow: Elizur for Reuben, Shelumiel for Simeon, Nahshon for Judah, Nethaneel for Issachar. Census and army order give the book its name and its first task.
the-blockade-runners:
Jules Verne's novella, translated by N. D'Anvers, follows the fast ship Dolphin. An editor's note says it first appeared with A Floating City, about the huge Great Eastern, in early editions. Another translation by Henry Frith came out in 1876.

Contents name the Dolphin, getting under sail, and things not being what they seem. Crockston's trick, a shot from the Iroquois, and Miss Jenny's arguments follow. A Sullivan Island channel, a southern general, an escape, and being between two fires lead to St Mungo. Chapter one recalls the Clyde in 1812, when the steamer Comet first ran between Glasgow and Greenock.
the-boy-allies-with-uncle-sam-s-cruisers:
Ensign Robert L. Drake wrote The Boy Allies with Uncle Sam's Cruisers. The first chapter is called Jack's Adventure. It opens at Lord Hastings's London home. Frank Chadwick jumps from a chair by the front glass and runs to the door. A man has come up the drive, and Frank flings the door wide to greet Jack with a handshake.

Frank feared harm had come to Jack, gone so long with no word. Jack laughs and says he is whole, and gone less than two weeks. Frank says the house sails the next night, so a day more would have lost him the trip. Jack asks where they are bound. Frank thinks it is America. The United States, he has heard, is about to make war on Germany, and troops will soon cross the sea. Convoys for those troop ships will be the work, he believes.
the-boy-scout-aviators:
George Durston wrote The Boy Scout Aviators. The first chapter, Serious News, pairs two boys of two lands. Harry Fleming, an American, says that if he can't be at home, he'd rather be here than any place on earth. Dick Mercer, his English friend, laughs that it must be funny to be an American.

The talk turns to scouting itself. Dick admits he was shocked when Mr. Grenfel let Harry into their troop at once, and when he learns scouts thrive in America too. Both boys praise Baden-Powell, whom school boys once called Bathing-Towel, a name that stuck through the army and past Mafeking. Harry then makes a bold claim. Starting the scout movement, he says, did England more good than the famed defense of Mafeking. Dick asks him to prove it, and the debate is on.
the-boy-scouts-with-the-motion-picture-p:
Robert Shaler wrote The Boy Scouts with the Motion Picture Players. Its chapters start with a haunted make-believe castle and a panic made on purpose. Scouting at midnight, a startling surprise, and guests at the camp fire come next. Days of chivalry, a clash of swords, and thrills for the town of Oakvale close the list.

The tale opens on a fall Friday, as five lads in faded khaki rest on a mossy log by a cold spring. Their leader is Hugh Hardin, assistant scout master of the Oakvale troop. With him are Alec Sands, stout and rosy Billy Worth, slim Arthur Cameron, and Monkey Stallings. Monkey earned his name by hanging by his toes from telegraph poles and tree limbs. Arthur's gift, the tale notes, is amateur surgery, at which he is a marvel.
the-boy-with-the-u-s-foresters: Francis Rolt-Wheeler wrote The Boy with the U.S. Foresters, put out in Boston by Lothrop, Lee and Shepard Company in 1910. The book stands in the U.S. Service Series. Its thirty-eight plates come from photos taken by the U.S. Forest Service. The chapters start with Entering the Service. Putting a Stop to Gun-Play and The Fight in the Coulee come next. A wild-cat fight and In the Heart of the Forest come later.
the-bridge-builders:
Rudyard Kipling opens The Bridge-Builders with Findlayson of the Public Works Department. For three years he has borne heat and cold, danger and disease, with a load of charge near too heavy for one pair of shoulders. Day by day the great Kashi Bridge over the Ganges has grown under his care. In less than three months, if all goes well, the Viceroy will open it in state.

Kipling gives the work in hard figures. With its approaches it runs one mile and three-quarters. A lattice-girder bridge, trussed with the Findlayson truss, stands on twenty-seven brick piers. Each pier is twenty-four feet across, capped with red Agra stone, and sunk eighty feet below the shifting sand. A railway line of fifteen feet runs on top. Red brick towers at each end are loopholed for muskets and pierced for big guns.
the-british-association-s-visit-to-montr:
The British Association's Visit to Montreal, 1884 holds letters by Clara Lady Rayleigh, printed for private circulation. Its first word is a piece reprinted from The Times of 1884. It may seem early, the piece says, to speak of plans for the next meeting, but Montreal is a far cry, and a long start must be made before the final leap.

All, it reports, is ready. The Dominion Government and the Canadian savants have thrown themselves into the work. Presidents, vice-presidents, and secretaries of sections are all chosen. Much is owed to the zeal of Sir Charles Tupper, the High Commissioner, and his secretary Mr. Colmer. The decision, taken at Southampton, drew grumbles and doubt of its rightness. The piece answers that this Imperial Parliament of Science could do no better work than to foster science in a great part of the dominions.
the-caesars:
Thomas De Quincey opens The Caesars with a claim on Rome's scale. The condition of the Roman emperors, he says, has never yet been fully grasped. In what respects it was unique has not been sufficiently perceived. There was but one Rome: no other city of ancient or modern times has rivalled it in the grandeur of magnitude. Few, if any, match it in architectural display.

A million and a half of souls justify the larger name for London. Rome, counted from horn to horn of its mighty suburbs, held not less than four millions of inhabitants, and very probably half as many more. As was the city, such was its prince: mysterious, solitary, unique. Each was the other's perfect mirror, he says. Rome has not been repeated; neither has Caesar. The old maxim runs: where Caesar is, there is Rome.
the-camp-fire-girls-at-school-or-the-woh:
Hildegard G. Frey wrote The Camp Fire Girls at School, or The Wohelo Weavers, dated 1916. Frey had three more Camp Fire books in print by then. Chapter I, Chronicles in Color, opens at a work meeting. Gladys Evans spreads out a bead band, a yard or more long, in which she has worked in colors the main events of the summer's camping trip.

Sahwah Brewster cries out the sights: Shadow River, the canoe floating upside down, and Ed Roberts serenading Gladys, though it turned out to be Sherry serenading Nyoda. It is a crisp October evening at the Bradford house, with Dorothy Bradford, or Hinpoha, as host. Seven girls and their Guardian, Miss Kent, called Nyoda, sit round a cheerful wood fire. Sahwah tats, the quiet girls work their symbols in crochet, and Hinpoha pops corn over the glowing log on the floor.
the-cheerful-cricket-and-others:
Jeannette Marks wrote these tales for children, with pictures by Edith Brown, and inscribed them to her nephew Henry Douglas Bacon and to other children, good and bad, big or little. The contents name a cast of small creatures: a cheerful cricket, a slothful toad, a sullen caterpillar, a mean spider, an honest ant, and more.

The title tale opens on Mrs. Cricky, who has run about the grass all morning with her head down, hunting food for Chee, Chirk, and Chirp. When she runs she scuttles, and when she stops she holds still but for her bright eyes. Mr. Cricky usually brings the food home, but he sings with the Marsh Grass Vesper Quartette. That quartette, with Miss K. T. Did, Mr. Frisky Frog, and Mr. Tree Toad Todson, was out very late, so she lets him sleep.
the-chessmen-of-mars:
Edgar Rice Burroughs sends John Carter to Mars again in this adventure, which opens with a prelude in which Carter comes to Earth. The contents promise Tara in danger, headless humans, a perfect brain, pits, and a play to the death. Chess, in a Martian form, stands at the heart of the tale's later chapters.

The prelude begins after a chess game on Earth. Shea has beaten the narrator, as usual, and the narrator teases him with a pet theory: that the finest chess players are children under twelve, adults over seventy-two, or the mentally defective. Shea goes to bed, and Carter's arrival follows in the night. From that frame the tale moves to Tara, daughter of Carter's line, swept by a gale, captured, and held for a deadly game. Burroughs mixes Earth humor with Barsoomian peril in his established manner.
the-chignecto-isthmus-and-its-first-sett: Howard Trueman wrote this history of the Chignecto Isthmus and its first settlers, issued as a Project Gutenberg text in June 1998. Only the Gutenberg header and title lines are present here, with the standard notes on copyright and keeping the file for later readers.The chapters themselves remain out of view.
the-cliff-climbers-a-sequel-to-the-plant:
Captain Mayne Reid wrote this adventure as a sequel to The Plant Hunters, dated 1853 in its heading. Chapter One turns at once to the Himalayas. Those mountains, Reid says, stand between the hot plains of India and the cold table lands of Thibet.

He calls them a worthy barrier between two great empires, the Mogul and the Celestial. Any beginner in geography, he notes, can say they are the tallest mountains on earth. A half-dozen summits rise more than five miles above the sea, and more than thirty pass twenty thousand feet, carrying eternal snow. A skilled geographer could fill volumes with their animals, forests, and plants. Reid promises only the salient points, enough to give readers a sense of that grandeur. On those heights his plant hunters' companions face the climbing tale that follows.
the-climbers: Clyde Fitch wrote this play in four acts, copyrighted in 1905 by Little, Brown, and Company and reprinted by Samuel French of New York and London. Only the front matter is present here, including a strict notice that no performance, professional or amateur, may be given without written leave from the owner of the acting rights. Fitch dedicates the printed play to Charles T. Mathews, in grateful recognition of true friendship. No act text follows.
the-colonel-of-the-red-huzzars: John Reed Scott wrote this novel, copyrighted in 1905 and published in June 1906, with pictures by Clarence F. Underwood, and dedicated to his wife. Only the front matter and contents are present here. A frontispiece line has a lady asking, suddenly, whether the hero is a soldier and an American officer. The chapters promise a picture and a wager, ancestors, a return to Dornlitz, the laws of the Dalbergs, and a princess royal sitting as judge. No chapter text follows.
the-comedy-of-errors: Only an editor's notes are present for this Shakespeare comedy. The notes explain the old spelling kept in the text. They quote the first lines of Hamlet as an example. Forms such as long liue the King appear there. Printers once ran short of letters, the notes say. They packed common words into cliches. They also swapped u for v, and v for u. No scene text from the comedy follows.Nothing inside the book follows its front matter.
the-coming-of-the-friars:
The Rev. Augustus Jessopp, D.D., a canon of Norwich Cathedral and a fellow of Worcester College, Oxford, and of St. John's College, Cambridge, gathered these historic essays in a fourteenth impression. The pieces first appeared in The Nineteenth Century and are reprinted with alterations and additions. He offers the volume to Francis Whalley Harper, canon of York, his friend and sometime tutor.

The contents join the coming of the friars with village life in Norfolk six hundred years ago and daily life in a medieval monastery. Two essays treat the Black Death in East Anglia, and others cover the building up of a university and the prophet of Walnut-Tree Yard. The title essay opens under a line from Tennyson wishing St. Francis of Assisi were here again. It begins with King Richard the Lion-hearted.
the-complete-short-works-of-georg-ebers:
Georg Ebers's complete short works open with a contents list of five tales: In the Blue Pike, A Question, The Elixir, The Greylock, and The Nuts. The first tale follows in full, translated from the German by Mary J. Safford. Chapter I drops readers into a rough Nuremberg crowd scene.

A swearing fellow points out of doors and shouts a curse, yet only two people near him grasp his meaning. His speech is mangled because the Nuremberg magistrates had Cyriax's tongue cropped for gross blasphemy. A fading, sickly girl understands him, and so does the red-haired woman who leads him by a chain, like a tame bear. She drops her knife, which had been slicing bread and onions into a pot, and looks at him with anxious questions. Cyriax snatches her shawl over his unkempt head and addresses the crowd as Nuremberg honourables.
the-conquest-of-new-france-a-chronicle-o: George M. Wrong wrote The Conquest of New France as volume 10 of the Chronicles of America series, edited by Allen Johnson and printed at Yale University Press in 1918. Its contents run from Frontenac and Phips and the fight for Quebec through the loss of Acadia, Louisbourg, the Ohio valley, and the expulsion of the Acadians. It ends with Montcalm, Pitt's strategy, and the fall of Canada. A short list of sources and an index close the book. Only the front matter and full contents are present here.
the-cornet-of-horse-a-tale-of-marlboroug:
G. A. Henty's The Cornet of Horse, dated 1914, tells a tale of Marlborough's wars. Its contents promise a long campaign: chapters on Venloo, a duel, the Battle of the Dykes, Blenheim, Ramilies, Oudenarde, and the sieges of Lille and Tournai. Malplaquet closes the war. A spell as a prisoner and a visit to the court of Versailles come along the way.

Chapter 1, Windthorpe Chace, opens not on a battlefield but at a dancing lesson. A master counts the steps aloud, corrects his pupil's grip on his lady's fingertips, and demands a deeper bow. The boy is improving, the master allows, but he must grow lighter, more graceful, and more courtly in his air.
the-crayon-papers: The Crayon Papers, by Geoffrey Crayon, Gent., gathers sketches under heads such as Mountjoy, or Some Passages out of the Life of a Castle-Builder, The Great Mississippi Bubble. Don Juan: A Spectral Research follows. Further pieces treat Broek, or the Dutch Paradise, sketches in Paris in 1825 from Crayon's traveling note-book, Seminole subjects including the conspiracy of Neamathla, a letter from Granada. A Creole village sketched from a steamboat closes the list. Only the title page, the full list of pieces, and the heading of Mountjoy are present here.
the-cross-of-berny-or-irene-s-lovers:
The Cross of Berny, or Irene's Lovers, carries four names on its title page: Madame Emile de Girardin, Theophile Gautier, Jules Sandeau, and Mery. A preface to the American edition notes that literary partnerships are often tried and rarely succeed, and that groups of more than two writers have almost always failed.

Against that record, the preface claims, this book stands nearly alone: a harmonious joint work of four minds and, beyond the novelty, a great book on its own merits. Rivalry among the four sharpened the wit of its letters, while tact kept the tone whole. The tale takes the form of letters among four characters whose names are the pen names of the four authors, letting each keep a distinct voice and style.
the-danvers-jewels-and-sir-charles-danve: Mary Cholmondeley wrote The Danvers Jewels and its sequel, Sir Charles Danvers, published in New York by Harper and Brothers in 1890. Cholmondeley dedicates the story to her sister Di, who helped her write it. A contents page places The Danvers Jewels at page 9 and Sir Charles Danvers, labeled the sequel, at page 93. Only the title page, dedication, and contents are present here, so the tales themselves do not appear.
the-delight-makers: Adolf F. Bandelier wrote The Delight Makers, published in New York by Dodd, Mead and Company with an introduction by Charles F. Lummis and a portrait of the author at the front. The copyright pages show dates of 1890 and 1916 for the publisher and 1918 for Mrs. Fanny R. Bandelier. A dedication panel gives Santa Fe, New Mexico, under the author's name, and a note begins after the copyright matter. Only the front matter through the head of that note is present here.
the-disentanglers:
Andrew Lang's The Disentanglers came out from Longmans, Green, and Company in 1903 in a second impression, with illustrations by H. J. Ford. Lang dedicates these studies of life and character to Herbert Hills, Esq. Chapter I, The Great Idea, opens in a dusky, shabby little room in Ryder Street.

Such caves, Lang says, draw men whose days are passed in the clubs of Pall Mall nearby. Logan sprawls on a sofa covered with horsehair cloth, a historic piece, while Merton, the tenant, takes the arm-chair in a Zingari cricketing coat. A glass-doored bookcase holds first editions in faded blue boards. Merton is fair, slim, and active. He coxed his college eight as a freshman, rowed bow later, won the hurdles, and took a fair second in Greats. His most obvious vice, Lang notes, is a thirst for general information.
the-doctor-s-dilemma-preface-on-doctors:
Bernard Shaw's Preface on Doctors, dated 1909, fronts his play The Doctor's Dilemma with a fierce attack on paid medicine. Shaw says the fault lies not with doctors but with a system that pays a surgeon most when the cut is worst. A man who trims a toenail earns shillings; one who cuts out your insides earns hundreds of guineas.

When the man paid to judge is the man paid to cut, Shaw warns, needless work will follow. He presses for a public health service paid by salary. The essay is witty, harsh, and still much quoted.
the-federalist-papers:
Alexander Hamilton, John Jay, and James Madison wrote The Federalist Papers to urge New York to back the new plan for the United States. The first paper, signed by Hamilton, ran in the Independent Journal on October 27, 1787.

Hamilton opens with a stark claim: the choice will decide if men can build good rule by thought and choice, or must trust to chance and force. He warns that state office holders and bold men seeking gain will fight the plan. Paper by paper, the set then defends a strong union, split powers, and a frame built to guard both order and freedom.
the-first-1000-euler-numbers: Simon Plouffe edited this list of the first one thousand Euler numbers, number twenty in a series of math constants, dated April 2001. Only the old Project Gutenberg header is present here. It names Plouffe, of the University of Quebec at Montreal, and his Plouffe's Inverter site. No table of the numbers themselves shows up in these pages, so the values and their form cannot be described from the front matter alone.
the-first-1001-fibonacci-numbers: Simon Plouffe edited this list of the first one thousand and one Fibonacci numbers, number twenty-one in a series of math constants, dated April 2001. Only the old Project Gutenberg header is present here. It names Plouffe, of the University of Quebec at Montreal, and his Plouffe's Inverter site. No table of the numbers themselves can be read in what is present, so the values and their growth cannot be stated from this front matter alone.
the-first-498-bernoulli-numbers: Simon Plouffe edited this list of the first four hundred and ninety-eight Bernoulli numbers, number twenty-two in a series of math constants, dated April 2001. Only the old Project Gutenberg header is present here. It names Plouffe, of the University of Quebec at Montreal, and his Plouffe's Inverter site. No table of the numbers themselves appears in these opening pages, so the values and their form cannot be judged from the front pages alone.
the-fitz-boodle-papers:
William Makepeace Thackeray wrote The Fitz-Boodle Papers as comic pieces told by George Fitz-Boodle, a club man of London. Confessions and professions make up the set.

In his preface Fitz-Boodle writes to his editor, Oliver Yorke, from the Omnium Club in May 1842. He calls himself the third-best whist player in Europe, whose card winnings long swelled his income. Then a French rival, Monsieur Lalouette, joined the club, and luck turned: Fitz-Boodle lost two-and-thirty nights of play. Tales of his loves, Dorothea and Ottilia, and of his odd trades follow, all told with a bachelor's sly wit.
the-flyers:
George Barr McCutcheon wrote The Flyers as a light novel that starts at a country club on a raw spring night. Six chapters carry the tale from the Faraway Club to a road to paradise.

Cold drizzle and a biting wind keep most members home, but a dozen loyal sports folk lounge by a great fire. Young women in sweaters trade talk with the men while stewards mix up drink orders. McCutcheon, author of Graustark, builds a comedy of crossed trains, missed meets, and young love in a storm, where two pairs catch the wrong flyer and land in one fix.
the-foolish-lovers:
St. John G. Ervine wrote The Foolish Lovers as a novel of Ulster pride, printed at New York in 1920. He gives the book to his mother and to Mrs. J. O. Hannay, with two sly thanks.

His mother had asked for a tale with no bad words, and Mrs. Hannay for one with no sex in it. The tale opens by asking who the proudest folk in Ireland are, and lands at last on the folk of Ballyards. Ervine mocks that fierce town pride while he tells of young love in such a place, where each street holds its worth above the whole wide world.
the-forest-lovers:
Maurice Hewlett wrote The Forest Lovers as a romance of the old forest, given to Mrs. W. K. Clifford with the author's homage. Prosper le Gai rides out in the first chapter.

The contents name a dead knight, a holy thorn, Dom Galors, a woman called La Desirous, and a virgin marriage. Galors abjures, rides hunting, and fights through broken sanctuary and high march. Hewlett builds a dream-like tale of knights, hermits, and forest folk, where love and vows clash with pride and the sword. The old tale style, half ballad and half prose poem, is the book's chief charm.
the-four-feathers:
A. E. W. Mason wrote The Four Feathers as a novel of honor lost and won, printed at New York in 1903. Harry Feversham stands at its heart, a young officer who quits the army on the eve of war.

The contents open with a Crimean night, a telegram, and a ball at Lennon House. Feversham's plan follows, then a last reconnaissance and a tempter's plea. Three white feathers, sent by fellow officers as a mark of shame, drive the tale. To wipe out the charge, Feversham goes in disguise to the Sudan war, doing brave deeds in secret while his friends think him a coward.
the-garotters:
William D. Howells wrote The Garotters as a short comic play, printed in his author's edition at Edinburgh in 1897. Mrs. Roberts and her husband Edward stand in the first scene.

The play opens at the window of Mrs. Roberts' rooms in the Hotel Bellingham on a night of driving snow. She hears quick steps, runs to the door curtain, and calls out in the dark. Howells builds a farce on a fad of the day: garotting, the choke-hold robbery that scared city folk. Mistakes, fright, and drawing-room talk turn a crime scare into light sport for two acts.
the-gate-of-the-giant-scissors:
The Gate of the Giant Scissors is a tale for young readers built around Joyce, a twelve-year-old American girl sent to live in France. A bunch of chapter heads pairs home scenes with French lessons and holidays.

Joyce sits crying in Monsieur Greville's pear tree, sick for home. She is tired of the high stone wall, of French verbs and strange faces, and of France itself. Snow, she thinks, lies at home where Jack, Holland, and the baby shell corn by the fire. A gate held by giant scissors, a new fairy tale, and a letter home start her cure, as the Greville house slowly turns from prison to home.
the-gods-of-mars:
Edgar Rice Burroughs wrote The Gods of Mars. A contents list has twenty-two chapters. They run from The Plant Men and A Forest Battle to Victory and Defeat. They name Thuvia, The Black Pirates of Barsoom, and Issus, Goddess of Life Eternal. A foreword by the narrator frames the tale.

The narrator says twelve years have passed. In that time he laid his great-uncle in a strange tomb. The great-uncle was Captain John Carter of Virginia. The tomb stands in an old Richmond cemetery. Carter left odd orders for it. He was to lie in an open casket. The vault door was to work only from inside. Carter claimed he remembered no childhood. He could not guess his own age. The foreword sets up Carter's return to Mars.
the-gold-stealers:
Edward Dyson wrote The Gold Stealers. Chapter I opens not with gold but with a schoolhouse. The school stands at Waddy, a Victorian mining town. It was no trim state building. Local folk built it by subscription. They acted after Mr. Joel Ham arrived and made clear he would not leave.

The town, Dyson jokes, could make nothing else of Ham. So it made a schoolmaster of him. A meeting at the Drovers' Arms passed the plan. No one gave cash. Each man gave labor and timber of every sort. Miners from each shift worked on the walls in their off hours. Each man was his own architect. The rough, comic start grounds a tale of a gold town. It shows the town's folk and their makeshift ways.
the-governors: E. Phillips Oppenheim wrote The Governors. It is dated 1909. Pictures are by Will Grefe and Howard Somerville. Oppenheim is named as author of A Maker of History and The Missioner. Only front matter is present here. It gives the title page and a contents list for Book I. The heads open with Mr. Phineas Duge and Cousin Stella. They name Storm Clouds, A Meeting of Giants, and Treachery. They name A Professional Burglar, Firearms, and Conspirators. They end with Stella Succeeds and The Warning. No chapter text is present.
the-grafters: Francis Lynde wrote The Grafters. Pictures are by Arthur I. Keller. Only front matter is present here. It gives the title page and a contents list of thirty chapters. The heads run from Ashes of Empire and A Man of the People. They run through The Flesh-Pots of Egypt and Of the Making of Laws. They end with The Night of Alarms and The Relentless Wheels. The names point to a tale of politics, rail deals, and graft. No chapter text is present.
the-grammar-of-english-grammars: Goold Brown wrote The Grammar of English Grammars. It has a historical and critical introduction. Only front matter is present here. It gives a transcriber's note and the long title page. That page promises the whole methodically arranged and amply illustrated. It promises forms of correcting and parsing, and improprieties for correction. It promises questions for examination and exercises for writing. It adds observations for the advanced student and proofs for disputed points. Four appendixes cover the four parts of grammar. No grammar rules or lessons are present.
the-great-book-collectors: Charles Isaac Elton and Mary Augusta Elton wrote The Great Book-Collectors. Kegan Paul, Trench, Trubner and Company printed it in London in 1893. Only front matter is present here: the title page and the start of a contents list. The chapters begin with Classical collectors, then Ireland and Northumbria, then Italy in the age of Petrarch. Later heads name Oxford and Duke Humphrey's books. They name the library of the Valois, Italy in the Renaissance, and the books of Corvinus. No chapter text is present.
the-great-german-composers: George T. Ferris wrote The Great German Composers. D. Appleton and Company held its copyright of 1878. Only front matter is present here: the title page, the author's note, and the start of a contents list. The contents open with Bach and Handel, then Gluck, Haydn, Mozart, and Beethoven. In his note Ferris explains his choices. Space is given by a man's tie to great art-epochs, not by rank alone. Chopin, a Pole, is included because his early training was in the German school.
the-grimke-sisters:
Catherine H. Birney wrote The Grimke Sisters. The book is dated 1885. Its title page calls Sarah and Angelina Grimke the first American women advocates of abolition and woman's rights. Birney's preface tells how the book was made. The sisters' diaries and letters were placed in her hands. She had lived nearly two years under the same roof with them. The work, she says, is a labor of affection as well as of duty.

The contents open with Sarah's childhood: practical teachings, teaching slaves, Sarah as godmother, and their mother. The second chapter turns to her thirst for knowledge and religious impressions. It tells of their father's death-bed and of Sarah and slavery. It tells of the Friends and of Sarah resisting the call. It ends with Sarah leaving Charleston. Its motto runs: the glory of all glories is the glory of self-sacrifice.
the-half-brothers:
Elizabeth Gaskell wrote The Half-Brothers, a story told by a narrator whose mother was married twice. The opening explains that the mother wed her first husband at about seventeen, that he rented a small farm in Cumberland, and that his affairs failed before he died of consumption. She was left a young widow with a small child, debts, and a lease still to run.

Grief deepens as the account goes on. A little girl sickens with scarlet fever and dies shortly before a son, Gregory, is born. The mother, silent and dry-eyed through the funeral, weeps at last after the birth. Gaskell builds the tale on family memory, told in part through the narrator's aunt Fanny.
the-hand-of-ethelberta-a-comedy-in-chapt:
Thomas Hardy wrote The Hand of Ethelberta, subtitled a comedy in chapters. In a preface dated December 1895, Hardy calls the tale a somewhat frivolous piece set between stories of a more sober design. He warns that he did not aim for strict likelihood in the incidents, and he asks the reader to meet the book in a light mood.

Hardy also explains a bold choice in the telling. Servants matter as much as, or more than, their masters, and drawing-room scenes are often seen from the servants' hall. The contents move from a street in Anglebury to Sandbourne pier, a ballroom, and a butler's pantry, keeping that shift of view in place throughout.
the-happy-adventurers: Lydia Miller Middleton wrote The Happy Adventurers. The book is dedicated to Alastair and Margaret. A short verse from Kipling stands before the contents. It speaks of how little things have changed in the building trade. Chapter headings pair a group name with a place or puzzle. Examples include The Builders, or The Little House. Later headings name The Treasure-Hunters and The Aeronauts. What is present here stops with the front matter. The tales themselves do not appear.
the-harvest-of-years:
M. L. B. Ewell wrote The Harvest of Years, published in New York by G. P. Putnam's Sons in 1880. In a letter dated at New Haven, Conn., in June 1880, Ewell dedicates the recital of her life to her family. She says old friends and other days rose around her as she wrote, and that the people in the account feel as real to her as living hands.

Ewell states her purpose in plain words. She wrote as the story runs, with no effort at dressing it up, to show how a little leaven can leaven the whole lump. She hopes the book will greet old friends from her years of mission work like a familiar hand, not a stranger.
the-haunted-and-the-haunters:
Edward Bulwer-Lytton wrote this tale of a haunted house in 1859. Its full name runs on with the words 'The House and the Brain' as a second title. Bulwer-Lytton was a star of his age, and his ghost tale set the form for all that came next.

A man takes a house in London that no tenant can bear to stay in for one night. He sits up with a friend and a dog to face its dread in a calm, planned way. The tale founds the line of the psychic quest tale, in which men hunt ghosts with method.
the-historical-romances-of-georg-ebers:
Georg Ebers wrote the historical romances gathered under his name. The contents list runs to more than twenty titles. It names Uarda and An Egyptian Princess. It also names The Sisters, Joshua, and Cleopatra. Later titles include The Emperor, Serapis, and Arachne. The volume opens with Uarda, a romance of ancient Egypt. Clara Bell translated Uarda from the German.

A dedication in verse begins Uarda. A preface follows the dedication. Ebers recalls the winter of 1873. He spent weeks in a tomb of the Necropolis of Thebes. He studied the monuments of that city of the dead. Long rides in the silent desert planted the germ of the book.
the-house-behind-the-cedars: Charles W. Chesnutt wrote The House Behind the Cedars. The contents list thirty-three chapters. Early titles include A Stranger from South Carolina. Later titles include An Evening Visit and The Old Judge. The list goes on to The Tournament. It also names The Queen of Love and Beauty. Later titles include Doubts and Fears and Tryon Goes to Patesville. Only the title page and contents are present here. The heading of chapter one also appears. The novel itself does not appear.
the-house-of-atreus-being-the-agamemnon-:
Aeschylus, the earliest of the three great Greek tragedians, wrote the three plays gathered here: Agamemnon, The Libation-Bearers, and The Furies. E. D. A. Morshead translated them into English. An introductory note sketches the playwright's sparse biography: born at Eleusis near Athens in 525 B.C., a competitor for the tragic prize before he was twenty-five, a soldier reported at Marathon, Salamis, and Plataea, and dead in Sicily in 456 B.C.

The note explains why these plays matter together. They form the Oresteia, described here as the only complete Greek tragic trilogy that survives, out of the seventy or eighty plays Aeschylus is said to have written. Readers also get his place in theater history: before him, tragedy used a chorus and one actor, and he added the second actor, which widened what dramatic dialogue could do.
the-house-of-whispers: William Le Queux published this novel in 1910. Only the title page and contents are present here. The story itself does not appear.
