The chapter headings sketch a Scottish mystery. The book opens with the Laird of Glencardine. It moves through material concerning James Flockhart. The Muries of Connachen follow. A secret belongs to Gabrielle. Later chapters reach the whispers themselves. They promise curious confidences and bait being cast. A mysterious business appears. Final headings say Flockhart foresaw events. A woman's love will also be declared.
the-inheritors:
Joseph Conrad and Ford M. Hueffer wrote this story together. Hueffer later became Ford Madox Ford. McClure, Phillips and Company published it in New York in 1901. Heinemann issued it in London. An epigraph sets the tone of decay. Let us eat, drink and sleep, for tomorrow we die. Chapter One opens in banter about ideas. The narrator walks with a woman through an old gateway. Saints' effigies and fretted canopies line it. Grime and bird-droppings mark the stone.

He points at the masonry and asks a question. Does it suggest nothing to her? She answers with a shake of her head. Contempt mixes with refusal in it. He stammers about associations and historical ideas. The mismatch drives the scene. His reverence for the past meets her cool dismissal. Behind the comedy sits their premise. A coming race stands ready to inherit the earth.
the-inner-sisterhood-a-social-study-in-h: Douglass Sherley, who also wrote The Valley of Unrest, published this social study in high colors with John P. Morton and Company of Louisville, Kentucky, in 1884. Only the title pages, copyright notice, and a dedication to one of the sisterhood are present here, so the study itself does not appear. The contents promise just three numbered sections, marked simply I, II, and III, with no titles to reveal how Sherley framed his look at the inner circle of women his title names.
the-intriguers: Harold Bindloss, author of Ranching for Sylvia and Alton of Somasco, published this novel with A. L. Burt Company of New York in February 1914, by arrangement with Frederick A. Stokes Company, with a frontispiece in colors by D. C. Hutchison. Only the title pages and contents are present here, so the story itself does not appear. The chapter headings sketch a northern adventure: the Blake affair, a river boat, cornering the bobcat, the muskeg, a kidnapping, a fever patient, the frozen north, and the trail of the caribou.
the-last-of-the-huggermuggers: Christopher Pearse Cranch wrote a giant story for young readers about a boy called Little Jacket who wants to go to sea. Only the title page and contents are present here, Seventeen chapters trace his luck at sea and his life in a giant boot. Later chapters cover escape from Kobboltozo shop and travel using Huggermugger himself. The tale itself does not appear in this record, so the chapter list alone traces his visit to the giant island and the sorrows of its last giant.
the-life-of-captain-matthew-flinders:
Ernest Scott, a history professor at the University of Melbourne, published his life of Captain Matthew Flinders at Sydney in 1914. His preface notes that his subject died one hundred years earlier. Flinders charted a large part of what became Australia within a forty year life.

Scott lists war, perilous voyages, unknown coasts, shipwreck, and imprisonment among the career elements. He also claims no full biography of Flinders existed before his book, despite the explorer rank. Readers get a life built from footnoted material, aimed at giving a wronged and gifted navigator his due.
the-life-of-st-frances-of-rome-and-other:
Lady Georgiana Fullerton wrote lives of Saint Frances of Rome, Blessed Lucy of Narni, Dominica of Paradiso, and Anne de Montmorency, with an introductory essay by J. M. Capes. Opening pages name her chief source for Frances. Her confessor Mattiotti kept a daily record of her visions for years, under obedience.

After her death Mattiotti wrote a full biography, later placed in the Bollandist collection at Venice in 1735. A Jesuit named Ursinus added a life early in the seventeenth century. Readers get Roman and Italian holy women told through confessor records and early printed lives.
the-light-of-egypt-or-the-science-of-the: Henry O. Wagner, Belle M. Wagner, and Thomas H. Burgoyne share credit in catalog entries for The Light of Egypt, a work on the science of the soul and the stars. Only a Project Gutenberg header for volume two is present here, and its own note admits the author entries are rather strange. The header also says no plan exists to add volume one. The occult text itself remains outside this record at all.
the-light-of-the-western-stars:
Zane Grey sets his western romance at El Cajon, New Mexico, near midnight. Madeline Hammond steps off a late train into huge dark space, cool wind, and blinking white stars. No brother waits to meet her, and the conductor worries aloud on her behalf.

Contents promise a roundup, a rancho ruled like a queen court, Don Carlos and his vaqueros, guerrillas, bandits, and a lost mine of the padres. Madeline, an eastern heiress, enters a border ranch world of cattle, raids, and hard riding. Her brother reckless life and a foreman quiet strength shape the tale ahead.
the-little-lame-prince-rewritten-for-you: Dinah Maria Mulock's The Little Lame Prince was rewritten for young readers by Margaret Waters. Barse and Hopkins of New York issued it in the Pleasant Hour Series, with pictures by Hugo von Hofsten. Only the title pages and part of the contents are present, so the rewritten tale itself does not appear. One frontispiece caption quotes a regent's oath to do his duties and take care of His Majesty. The contents list chapters with page numbers, reaching chapter four in what is shown.
the-logbooks-of-the-lady-nelson-with-the:
Ida Lee edited The Logbooks of the Lady Nelson, first published in 1915, pairing the ship's logs with the journal of her first commander, Lieutenant James Grant of the Royal Navy. The volume carries sixteen charts and illustrations taken from originals in the Admiralty Library. Lee's preface stresses that the Lady Nelson was essentially an Australian discovery ship, employed exclusively in Australian waters across her successive commissions.

Her logbooks record early discoveries in Victoria, exploration of the Queensland coast, and surveys of King Island and the Kent Group. They also cover visits to New Zealand and the founding of settlements at Hobart, Port Dalrymple, and Melville Island. Lee warns that some logbook handwriting is already so faded it is hard to decipher, making publication urgent.
the-lost-naval-papers: Bennet Copplestone's The Lost Naval Papers is dated 1917. The record holds only a title page and contents, leaving the stories themselves unread. The contents divide the book into parts: Part I, headed William Dawson, runs through chapters titled A Story and a Visit, At Close Quarters, An Inquisition, Sabotage, Baffled, and Trehayne's Letter. Part II, headed Madame Gilbert, begins with The Woman and the Man, A Progressive Friendship, and At Brighton, suggesting linked naval intrigue tales from wartime.
the-loves-of-great-composers: Gustav Kobbé wrote The Loves of Great Composers, published by Thomas Y. Crowell and Company in September 1905, with a frontispiece photogravure of Mozart. Only the title page and contents are present here, so the chapters do not appear. The contents pair composers with the women in their lives. Mozart appears with his Constance, Beethoven with his "Immortal Beloved," and Mendelssohn with his Cécile. Chopin follows with the Countess Delphine Potocka. Robert and Clara Schumann, Franz Liszt and his Carolyne, and Wagner and Cosima close the list.
the-messengers:
Richard Harding Davis opens The Messengers with a rich idler named Ainsley buying Lone Lake Farm in Connecticut. The farmer who sold it had abandoned the place as worthless, and Ainsley's friends ask how a man who cannot tell a plough from a harrow hopes to make it pay. Ainsley answers that he bought the farm as a retreat and a test of true friendship. Friends who travel six miles of execrable wood road to see him, he argues, are friends indeed.

On a rocky, forested tract by a pond hardly larger than a city block, Ainsley builds a red brick house. He names the pond's rocky points the Needles, St. Helena, and the Isle of Pines. In truth he waits there until Polly Kirkland makes up her mind to marry him. Many men love her, and friendly opinion favors Ainsley, yet his persuasion has so far failed.
the-moneychangers:
Upton Sinclair's novel The Moneychangers, published in New York in 1908 and dedicated to Jack London, opens inside wealthy society talk. Reggie Mann declares himself beside himself to meet Lucy Dupree. Allan Montague, lounging in a leather chair, smiles at his friend's excitement.

People exaggerate when they talk about Lucy, Montague warns. Reggie, exquisitely groomed and perfumed, with a scarlet orchid in his buttonhole, has come to take Alice to church. Montague privately pictures Reggie treating Lucy as a new kind of flower to parade down the Avenue. Alice enters in a new spring costume, springs the talk back to earth, and notes that she went to school with Lucy.
the-motor-boys-on-the-pacific-or-the-you:
Clarence Young's boys' adventure The Motor Boys on the Pacific, also titled The Young Derelict Hunters, lays out thirty chapters in its contents. Bad news and a desperate race open the tale, followed by Professor Uriah Snodgrass, a strange conversation, and a party hemmed in. Later headings promise a motor boat, fog, rocks, a brig, and a mysterious influence, ending with The End of Blowitz.

A preface addressed Dear Boys follows the contents. Young writes that most readers already know the Motor Boys from earlier books in the series, so no introduction is needed for them. For newcomers picking up this volume first, he says he takes pleasure in presenting the boys properly before the story starts.
the-mound-builders:
George Bryce's lecture The Mound Builders was printed at Winnipeg by the Manitoba Free Press as Transaction 18 of the local Historical Society, season 1884-85, priced at 25 cents. Bryce, a professor at Manitoba College, presided over the society. An illustration shows a cup found in a mound at Rainy River in August 1884.

Opening his address, Bryce claims that Manitoba's mounds form the only distinct mound region on Canadian soil. Settlers who migrated there inherit a far wider field of study than the lakeshore fringe of Ontario offered, he argues. A thousand miles of prairie stretch before them. Where an Ontario geologist studies rocks in garden plots, the north-westerner can roam the age of reptiles at the Rockies' feet.
the-mystery-of-the-four-fingers:
Fred M. White's The Mystery of the Four Fingers, dated 1908, is present here only in title page and a partial contents list, so the mystery does not appear. White is billed as author of The Midnight Guest and The Crimson Blind. Nineteen chapters are listed before the pages end, and their titles turn on fingers counted off one by one.

The Black Patch opens the book, and The First Finger follows in Chapter II. A lost mine, a scene in a lift, and A Puzzle for Venner build toward The White Lady. The Second Finger does not arrive until Chapter X. Phantom Gold closes the visible list at Chapter XIX, with a house next door and a man named Felix Zary among the middle headings.
the-neapolitan-lovers:
Alexandre Dumas's The Neapolitan Lovers is present here only through a contents list, so the novel itself does not appear. The record heading credits Robert Singleton Garnett as editor and translator, with a date of 1917, and a translator's introduction is listed at page 9. The contents lettering in these pages is rough, with several headings and page numbers misread by the scanner.

Eighteen chapters are listed. The Hero of the Nile opens the book, followed by The Envoy from Rome and The House of the Palm Tree. The King and Queen, a council of state, Luisa and Salvato, and General Championnet fill the early list. A chapter in which the king washes his hands while the queen instructs her inquisitors stands at Chapter XII.
the-necromancers:
Robert Hugh Benson's novel The Necromancers, first published in 1909, is present here only as a list of Benson's other books and a reprint title page, so the story does not appear. Wildside Press of Doylestown, Pennsylvania, issued the reprint whose pages are shown. No chapter, character, or line of the novel is included.

The book list runs to more than thirty titles and maps Benson's range. Lord of the World, By What Authority? and The King's Achievement stand among the novels. The Religion of the Plain Man, Confessions of a Convert, and Paradoxes of Catholicism show his religious writing. Sermon Notes, Poems, and Spiritual Letters to one of his converts complete the catalogue.
the-new-book-of-martyrs:
Georges Duhamel's The New Book of Martyrs was translated by Florence Simmonds. It collects nine pieces named in its contents. Throughout Our Land, The Story of Carre and Lerondeau, and Memories of the Martyrs open the list. The Death of Mercier, Verdun, The Sacrifice, The Third Symphony, Grace, and Nights in Artois complete it. The martyrs are the wounded soldiers of the First World War.

The opening piece surveys a wounded country. From the disfigured regions where cannon reign, the cry of wounded men echoes to the mountains, the ocean, and the inland sea. No French town, Duhamel writes, is free of battlefield wounds bleeding within its walls, and every town accepts its share of the suffering and the mourning. In white beds with spotless bandages, stricken men await the verdict of fate.
the-origin-and-nature-of-the-emotions-mi: Only the Project Gutenberg header is present here for The Origin and Nature of Emotions by George W. Crile. The header gives the etext number 1233 and a date of March 1998. No title page, contents, or chapter text appears in what is present, so the papers themselves cannot be described. The rest is standard header matter on copyright laws, donations, and public domain editions. Title and author are the only facts about the book that these pages supply.
the-perils-of-certain-english-prisoners:
A Christmas tale from the 1894 Chapman and Hall edition of Christmas Stories tells The Perils of Certain English Prisoners. No author is named in the pages present. The narrator, Gill Davis, a private in the Royal Marines, dictates his account to a lady who writes it word for word, since he cannot read or write. The lady keeps correcting his name to Gilbert, though he insists he was always called Gill.

The tale is set in 1744, aboard the armed sloop Christopher Columbus off the Mosquito Shore in South American waters. Davis, a foundling who once frightened birds for a living, leans on the bulwarks as his adventure begins. His rough voice and her tidy pen frame the story together.
the-peterkin-papers:
Lucretia P. Hale wrote The Peterkin Papers, comic stories of the Peterkin family, first told to Meggie, daughter of the lady from Philadelphia. A preface to the second edition explains their printing. The first story appeared in Young Folks, later ones in St. Nicholas, and this edition adds a new paper, The Peterkins at the Farm.

The family debated publishing by postcard, so that everyone along the way would read the question and help it on. Solomon John proposed it, Elizabeth Eliza praised its cheapness, and each member signed, the little boys with sketches of their india-rubber boots. The preface itself shows the family's solemn silliness.
the-philanderers:
A. E. W. Mason, author of The Courtship of Morrice Buckler, published The Philanderers in 1897. The prologue opens at a camp fire in a forest clearing in mid-Africa. Five Englishmen sit silent against logs, smoking, while dying fires dot the floor and rifles glint among sleeping troops. One man points east as the purple fades from the sky.

Drake, their captain, rises. The eldest urges him to delay an execution until they return, since a village stood a week ago where the camp now is. Drake answers quietly that he too has thought all night, and there is no choice for him. He speaks of keeping up the prestige of the white man. The novel opens on a grim colonial decision.
the-pickwick-papers: Charles Dickens's The Pickwick Papers, formally The Posthumous Papers of the Pickwick Club, appears here through its contents alone. Only the chapter list is present, so the novel itself does not appear. Early chapters include The Pickwickians and the first day's journey with its consequences. Others promise a stroller's tale, a field day and bivouac, and an old-fashioned card party. Later entries name a discovery and a chase, an account of Eatanswill, and a pleasant day with an unpleasant ending.
the-potato-child-others:
Mrs. Charles J. Woodbury's The Potato Child and Others collects three stories: the title piece, A Story That Never Ends, and A Nazareth Christmas. The first story opens on Elsie, a tender-hearted girl at The Home, an orphan institution more than full. Miss Amanda Armstrong, the leading dressmaker of the city and a woman of some money, selects her from among the girls. The motherly matron is sorry to see her go.

Elsie lives in Miss Amanda's kitchen. She waits on the door, washes dishes, cleans vegetables, sets the table, sweeps on Fridays, and sleeps in a back attic room. Her new clothes are to last six months, and she needs no light to go to bed by. Miss Amanda never strikes her or speaks much at all. Everything comes as commands, and the loving child is driven into herself.
the-pothunters: P. G. Wodehouse's The Pothunters, dated 1902, is dedicated to Joan, Effie, and Ernestine Bowes-Lyon. Here only the title page, dedication, contents, and the heading of Chapter I appear, so the story itself is absent. Eighteen chapters are listed with playful titles. They include Thieves Break in and Steal, Barrett Explores and then Barrett Ceases to Explore, Enter the Sleuth-hound, and Mr. Thompson Investigates. Later entries promise the sports, the long run, and the disappearance of J. Thomson. A search for the missing Thomson follows.
the-potiphar-papers:
George William Curtis's The Potiphar Papers opens with a fan of epigraphs and a prefatory letter addressed to the Reverend Cream Cheese. Goldsmith's Deserted Village supplies the motto about the parlor splendors of a festive place. Burke's first letter on a regicide peace supplies a passage on manners. Manners, it says, work on us like the air we breathe. Walton's Angler and the Memoirs of Grammont add their voices.

The letter, playful and pointed, explains that the leading essay's title is itself a quotation. It was taken from the lips of Mrs. Potiphar. Curtis flatters his correspondent as an astute observer and austere critic whose judgment needs no prompting on that point. The frame promises a satire of fashionable society life. It is conducted through essays named for the formidable hostess whose words gave the volume its title.
the-profiteers:
E. Phillips Oppenheim's The Profiteers, dated 1921, opens at the Marchioness of Amesbury's Kensington garden party. Stockbrokers Roger Kendrick and Maurice White have escaped the City early and found a shady seat with iced drinks. White is sick of B. & I. shares, all his clients ask about, and he cannot advise on them honestly. Kendrick, ten years older and well preserved, has made money and kept it. They say Rockefeller backs the shares, White says, but who can prove it?

White turns to the board itself, starting with Peter Phipps, called Dreadnought. Phipps was ruined on the New York Stock Exchange, made a million or so in Montreal, then returned to New York and the copper crowd. Everyone on the Exchange, Kendrick agrees, is interested in B. & I.'s. He settles down to hear his younger friend's account of the directors.
the-range-dwellers: B. M. Bower, writing also as B. M. Sinclair, published her western with Grosset and Dunlap at New York in 1906, illustrated by Charles M. Russell. Contents promise a reward of folly, a white divide, a renewed quarrel, and a road through King's Highway into the lion's mouth, with a dance asked of Beryl King along the way. Here only the title pages and opening of the chapter list are present, so the range story itself does not appear.
the-rifle-rangers:
Captain Mayne Reid published his Mexican adventure in 1850, opening with a rhapsody on the land of Anahuac across the Atlantic. Emerald land, sapphire sky, and a golden sun greet the traveler who turns west instead of toward Greece or the Alps.

Reid scolds poets, painters, tourists, and novelists for chasing hackneyed Italian bandits while ignoring Mexico's forests, mountains, and table-plains. The narrator urges readers to land, climb, and traverse with him like Columbus. Frontier romance here begins as travel writing, with scenery praised warmly before any rifles are raised at all.
the-rough-riders:
Theodore Roosevelt published The Rough Riders in 1899. He dedicated the book to the officers and men of five regular regiments. Together with his own regiment, they formed the cavalry division at Santiago. His first chapter concerns raising the regiment.

Roosevelt recalls his year as Assistant Secretary of the Navy. That year preceded the outbreak of the Spanish War. He had preached intervention in Cuba with fervor. He wanted Spain driven from the Western World. He also resolved to go to the front himself if war came. The opening describes his work readying the navy. He consulted officers such as Commodore Dewey. They discussed ammunition, coal, and squadrons. Marksmanship and target practice also occupied them.
the-royal-game-of-the-ombre-written-at-t:
Printed in London for Thomas Palmer in 1665, The Royal Game of the Ombre was written at the request of divers honourable persons. No author is named on its title page. Palmer's shop was at the Crown in Westminster-Hall. The transcription preserves original spelling and punctuation. Its copy is held in the British Library.

The text explains L'Ombre, a Spanish game at cards. The name means the man. A player declares himself the man when he undertakes the game. Only three can play at it. Each is dealt nine cards. The eights, nines, and tens are discarded first. Thirteen cards remain in the stock. No trump is turned up. The player chooses the trump himself. Stakes are counted with greater and lesser marks.
the-satyricon-volume-05-crotona-affairs:
Volume five of W. C. Firebaugh's unexpurgated Satyricon translation is titled Affairs at Crotona. It opens at chapter the one hundred and twenty-fifth. The set's bracket code still flags the text. Forgeries of Nodot and Marchena and additions of De Salas are marked.

At Crotona, Eumolpus basks in success. He brags that no one can resist any wish of his. He even claims criminals in his suite would escape punishment through his friends. Encolpius grows fat on good things, yet he broods. A wily legacy hunter might send an agent to Africa, he thinks. Their lie could be caught. A hireling servant might also give the scheme away. Flight and fresh poverty would follow.
the-scalp-hunters:
Captain Mayne Reid's The Scalp Hunters is dated 1860. Its first chapter is called The Wild West. Reid invites the reader to unroll the world's map. The eye should travel toward the setting sun. It should rest where golden rivers rise among snowy peaks.

The narrator then stands in an open plain. No rock or tree breaks the horizon's ring. As far as he can range, his eye rests only on flowers. Golden helianthus, scarlet malva, and purple monarda colour the expanse. He calls this weed prairie a misnomer. It is the garden of God, he declares. The scene shifts to a grass prairie, green as an emerald. Buffalo, antelope, and a snow-white steed cross that boundless pasture.
the-science-of-human-nature-a-psychology: William Henry Pyle wrote The Science of Human Nature, subtitled A Psychology for Beginners. Pyle was professor of educational psychology at the University of Missouri. Silver, Burdett and Company copyrighted the book in 1917. It belongs to a Teacher Training Series edited by W. W. Charters. The pages shown give the title matter and only the start of the author's preface. That preface begins by naming its audience. The book is written for young students in high schools and normal schools, Pyle says. The psychology chapters themselves do not appear here.
the-sea-lions-or-the-lost-sealers:
J. Fenimore Cooper's The Sea Lions, or The Lost Sealers, is dated 1860 and described as complete in one volume. An epigraph from Campbell heads the title page. Cooper's preface opens with a rebuke. Men live engrossed by worldly objects, he says. They stay indifferent amid sublime natural phenomena. Those phenomena speak to imagination, affections, and judgments, he argues.

Not one man in ten turns aside once a day, Cooper claims. Few contemplate the majesty and mercy of the Divine Being. A million eyes pass over the firmament on a cloudless night, he writes. Not a hundred minds feel a proper sense of the Creator's power. Familiarity breeds this disregard, he concludes. The things constantly before us become like the air we breathe. His preface builds toward the sealers' tale from that moral ground.
the-sea-raiders: H. G. Wells's The Sea Raiders appears here in a Penguin Classics front matter. Three stories are listed in the contents. They are The Sea Raiders, The Land Ironclads, and The Magic Shop. A short life of Wells follows the list. He was born in Bromley, England, in 1866, it says. He died in London in 1946. The title story was first published in 1896, the note adds. The other two stories date to 1903. No story text is present in the portion shown.
the-seven-poor-travellers:
A Christmas tale in three chapters, transcribed from the 1894 Chapman and Hall edition of Christmas Stories, opens in the old city of Rochester. No author is named in the pages shown. Strictly speaking, the narrator begins, there were only six poor travellers. Being a traveller himself, though an idle one, he brought the number up to seven.

An inscription over a quaint old door explains the count. Richard Watts, by his will dated August 22, 1579, founded a charity there. Six poor travellers, not being rogues or proctors, may receive one night's lodging free. Entertainment and fourpence each are included. The narrator stood reading it on Christmas Eve, he says. He had wandered about Rochester Cathedral and seen Watts's tomb. He joked about whether he himself counted as a rogue.
the-ship-of-stars:
Arthur Thomas Quiller-Couch, signing himself Q, published The Ship of Stars in 1899. He dedicated it to Leonard Henry Courtney, M.P., in a long letter dated St. John's Eve. The story claims the West Country, which claims Courtney with pride, he writes. Its places will be found on no map, he warns. A visitor may discover Nannizabuloe, but the lighthouse will be missing.

Much of the tale is true in a fashion, Quiller-Couch says. Things that happen to Sir Harry Vyell actually happened to a better man near Liskeard. A true account of the Samaritan's wreck lies in a chapter by Robert Stephen Hawker, he notes. The dedication rests on two texts, he explains. They are Lord, make men as towers, and all towers carry a light. Its first content entry is The Boy in the Gate-House.
the-silverado-squatters: Robert Louis Stevenson's The Silverado Squatters appears in a new impression from Chatto and Windus, London, 1906. Joseph D. Strong supplied the frontispiece, a picture of the squatters. A Latin epigraph from Cicero heads the title page. The pages shown give the title matter and contents only. No narrative follows. The contents divide into time in the valley and time with the children of Israel. The act of squatting, the hunter's family, and the sea fogs follow. Episodes in the story of a mine close the list.
the-sowers: Henry Seton Merriman published this novel in 1895. The pages present here give the title page and contents only. Nineteen chapters open with a waif on the steppe and move by the Volga through diplomatic scenes. A Talleyrand club, a Moscow doctor, and a winter city follow. The closing titles reach the Champs Élysées and the Neva, so the narrative itself does not appear.
the-space-pioneers: Carey Rockwell wrote this Tom Corbett, Space Cadet adventure, with Willy Ley as technical adviser, for Grosset and Dunlap of New York, under a 1953 copyright held by Rockhill Radio. The pages present here are front matter only. A series list shows titles such as Stand By for Mars, Danger in Deep Space, and The Revolt on Venus. Illustrations are credited to Louis Glanzman, so the cadets' adventure itself does not appear.
the-spinners: Eden Phillpotts, author of Old Delabole and Brunel's Tower, published this novel in 1918. The pages present here give the title page and contents only. A first book of thirty-one chapters is set around a mill. Its titles name a funeral, the hackler, and the foreman's garden. The warping mill and the master of the mill also appear. The heading of a second book follows, so the narrative itself does not appear.
the-spoilers: Rex Beach, author of The Iron Trail and The Auction Block, dedicated this novel lovingly to his mother. Only the title pages and contents are present here. The contents list sixteen chapters. In them Glenister errs and a mine is jumped. Sluice robbers appear, and the Bronco Kid eavesdrops. A writ and a riot fail, and vigilantes gather. The Alaskan mining story itself does not appear.
the-stories-of-the-three-burglars:
Frank R. Stockton published this comic novella in 1889. A householder narrates it. He lives in pleasant country about twenty miles from New York. His household includes his wife, a two-year-old son, servants, and, at the time of the story, his Aunt Martha, and the neighbourhood has lately been troubled by burglars as well as mosquitoes.

Houses have been entered and robbed for months without the offenders being detected, and with no police force or village organization, each household depends on itself for protection. Stockton sets that anxious scene, of fastened windows and doors and rare poultry thefts grown serious, before the three burglars of the title make their memorable visit.
the-street-of-seven-stars:
Mary Roberts Rinehart sets this novel in an Austrian city. An old stucco house stands back in a ruined garden there. The Empress Maria Theresa once kept a hunting-lodge on the spot. So tradition says. On a rainy November night the great glass chandelier is dark, and the barred garden gate, left open by a piano student named Scatchett, slams to and fro in the wind.

One stubby candle lights the disorder of afternoon coffee and cakes in the salon, where the score of a Tchaikovsky concerto lies abandoned on the uneven floor. A girl in a black dress rises from beside the tile stove. She gathers the loose sheets almost tenderly. She anchors them on the grand piano with a china dog. The keys wait ice-cold under her fingers.
the-tales-and-novels-v9-belphegor-and-ot:
Volume 9 of J. de La Fontaine's Tales and Novels gathers three verse tales: Belphegor, The Little Bell, and The Glutton. Belphegor opens with a long address to Miss de Chammelay, praised as the actress Phillis. The speaker admires her triumphs in roles such as Berenice, Phaedra, and Camilla, and confesses his own hopeless love. He then turns at last to the story he means to tell.

That story begins with old Satan, sovereign of hell, and grows into La Fontaine's comic tale of a demon sent to earth. La Fontaine writes in rhymed verse full of wit and sly asides about love and marriage. Readers who enjoy classical French storytelling in English dress will find the volume's flavor in its very first pages.
the-things-which-remain-an-address-to-yo:
Daniel A. Goodsell, a bishop of the Methodist Episcopal Church, addressed The Things Which Remain to young ministers, publishing it in 1904 with Jennings and Pye. He opens with a blunt rule: followers of Him who said 'I am the Truth' can never afford to hold or propagate what is false. No man, he argues, preaches with power unless his belief is strong. Teaching force depends on faith.

Goodsell traces Methodist preaching power to Christian experience and the doctrine that doing leads to knowing. He describes the direct call of the Holy Spirit, demanded of every candidate at ordination, and the personal surrender behind it. Young preachers get a senior bishop's case that conviction and experience, not technique, give a sermon its force.
the-three-impostors: Arthur Machen's Three Impostors, or The Transmutations, was published in 1895 by Roberts Brothers in Boston and John Lane in London. This record gives the title page and contents only. The contents promise a prologue, the adventure of the gold Tiberius, and linked episodes called novels: of the dark valley, the black seal, the iron maid, and the white powder. Machen, already known for The Great God Pan, built the book as tales nested inside tales. His horrors themselves, however, begin beyond the pages present here.
the-three-partners:
Bret Harte opens The Three Partners at sunset on the Black Spur Range, where red light eats along the pine crests like sparks in burnt paper. Night wind struggles with shadows climbing from the valley until darkness swallows cabin after cabin and tunnel after tunnel. On Heavy Tree Hill one cabin door stays open. Three men sit before the embers in profound reflection, respecting each other's silence on a shared subject.

The youngest breaks it with a boyish laugh at their glumness. While working for grub wages they speculated nightly about striking gold; now, wallowing in it, they sit like men facing a washout. They once argued over grand hotels in San Francisco and tours of London, Rome, and Japan. Harte turns a mining fortune into a study of what money does to friendship.
the-three-sisters:
May Sinclair's Three Sisters, dated 1914, opens with the village of Garth in Garthdale, crouching where the road comes down off the High Moor. Sinclair describes it as a beaten thing cowering in the dale. Its gray houses are old, small, and humble. Their stone roofs are weather-blackened, as though fire had swept across them. The village keeps the silence, darkness, and secrecy of all ultimate habitations.

Northward stands the Vicarage alone, facing the village sideways through a small shy gable window, with its garden sloping to the churchyard. Sinclair's compressed, poetic prose makes the dale itself a character pressing on the three sisters inside that house. Readers expecting a quiet clerical family story are warned by page one: this landscape breeds repression, longing, and revolt.
the-time-traders: Andre Norton's Time Traders is documented here by its publisher's pages rather than its text: the World Publishing Company of Cleveland lists Norton's science fiction, with The Stars Are Ours! and Star Born, her historical Yankee Privateer, and anthologies she edited. A Library of Congress catalog card number, 58-11154, dates this printing to 1958. No page of Ross Murdock's time-travel adventure appears in what is shown. Readers can place the edition within Norton's early career, while the traders themselves step into the past beyond this record.
the-toys-of-peace-and-other-papers: The Toys of Peace and Other Papers, transcribed from the 1919 John Lane edition, collects work by H. H. Munro, the writer known as Saki, who was killed in the war this volume follows. This record shows the dedication to the 22nd Royal Fusiliers, an editor's note thanking the Morning Post, Westminster Gazette, and Bystander, and a contents list headed by a memoir of Munro. Titles include The Interlopers, The Wolves of Cernogratz, and The Phantom Luncheon. Saki's polished tales themselves begin beyond the leaves present.
the-traitors: E. Phillips Oppenheim's Traitors was published by Dodd, Mead of New York in March 1903, copyrighted the year before. This record stops at the title page and the head of the contents list. One dramatic frontispiece caption survives: 'Marie ... shot the man through the heart.' That single line promises the Oppenheim mixture of conspiracy, romance, and sudden violence, in a story of Balkan intrigue. The chapters themselves do not appear in the pages present, so the shot is heard, as it were, from outside a closed door.
the-transvaal-from-within-a-private-reco:
J. P. FitzPatrick, author of The Outspan, published The Transvaal from Within with Heinemann in 1899, calling it a private record of public affairs. Written in August 1896, privately circulated in June 1899, and supplemented that September, the book carries an opening note about its own language. FitzPatrick warns that terms like 'the Boers,' 'the Cape Dutch,' and 'the Hollanders' are meant in the political sense only. They are never meant in the racial sense. He begs an indulgent reading of anything seeming offensive.

He adds that Transvaal officials include men who would earn public confidence in any administration in the world. The contents then run from earlier days through the Reform Committee, its dilemma, and the invasion, meaning the Jameson Raid. FitzPatrick was himself a Reform insider, and his careful note shows a participant writing history while the Boer War gathered.
the-troubadours: The Rev. H. J. Chaytor's Troubadours, printed at the Cambridge University Press in 1912, is shown here by its title page and contents, with the first chapter reached only as a heading. Nine chapters move from an introduction through the theory of courtly love and technique to the early troubadours, the classical period, the Albigensian Crusade, and Provençal influence abroad. A bibliography and index are promised. Chaytor's account of the poets of courtly love begins past these leaves, though its itinerary is visible.
the-two-brothers:
Honoré de Balzac's Two Brothers, translated by Katharine Prescott Wormeley, is dedicated to Charles Nodier of the French Academy in a long, sombre letter. Balzac describes a book of deeds screened from the law by domestic privacy, where chance, God's finger, must supply the justice men cannot. Such deeds, he argues, teach hard lessons about family and motherhood. He warns of the diminution of paternal authority, once ceasing only at a father's death, the sole tribunal for domestic crimes.

No mother, however tender, can fulfil the patriarchal function, he insists, and selfish interests indulged without restraint bring fatal results. The dedication is a conservative manifesto framing a novel of inheritance war between brothers. Balzac asks that society shudder at the law's impotence before a system that deifies success, then shows that system at work in one family.
the-upton-letters:
Arthur Christopher Benson's Upton Letters appeared in 1905, framed by a preface signed T. B. from Monk's Orchard, Upton. The letters came back to their writer after the friend who received them died suddenly. Sorting papers days before his death, the friend had refused to destroy the bulky packet and hoped for publication someday.

The widow, who had the best right to decide, wished the same, so personal details were cut and the rest printed as written. The preface admits haste and literary shortcomings, yet claims a spontaneity deliberate work often lacks. Books, education, and modern life supply the topics. Publication so soon after the death is defended as obedience to a last message of love.
the-vicar-of-tours:
Honoré de Balzac opens The Vicar of Tours in the autumn of 1826, in Katharine Prescott Wormeley's translation. Abbé Birotteau hurries home through rain across the deserted Cloister square behind Tours cathedral. Short, stout, about sixty, and prone to gout, he dreads wetting his silver-buckled shoes above almost any petty misery.

Balzac notes the small consolations: the pavement may stay dry, and Birotteau has won three francs ten sous at cards. Behind the comedy sits a twelve-year-old desire, renewed every evening and now apparently near fulfilment. A dedication to the sculptor David precedes the tale, contrasting bronze that survives nations with a book whose permanence Balzac doubts.
the-warlord-of-mars:
Edgar Rice Burroughs opens The Warlord of Mars on the River Iss, with John Carter creeping through forest shadows beside the Lost Sea of Korus. Contents chapters promise the Temple of the Sun, a secret tower, the Kaolian road, carrion caves, yellow men, and a magnet switch. Six Martian months, Carter says, he has haunted the temple's vicinity.

Inside its slow-revolving shaft, far underground, his princess Dejah Thoris lies entombed, and he cannot know whether Phaidor's blade found her heart. Six hundred eighty-seven Martian days must pass before the cell door again meets the tunnel's end. Half that span has nearly gone. Burroughs resumes the rescue exactly where suspense left it, under Mars's hurtling moons.
the-warriors:
Anna Robertson Brown Lindsay, author of What Is Worth While, signed The Warriors from Philadelphia on November 1, 1902. Her table of contents shapes the book like music: chords of awakening, a prelude on the call of Jesus, a processional of the church of God, and a world-march. That march is divided among kings, prelates and evangelists, sages, traders, and workers.

Chapter one, The Higher Conquest, opens by printing a martial hymn in full. Its verses ask who follows in the train of the Son of God going forth to war for a kingly crown. Cup of woe, cross borne patiently, lions, and tyrants' steel mark the followers. Lindsay's devotional argument plainly recasts Christian life as enlistment in a conquering host.
the-water-ghost-and-others: John Kendrick Bangs dedicates The Water Ghost and Others to his brother Francis Sedgwick Bangs. The pages present here give the contents and a long illustrations list, so the stories themselves do not appear. Eight tales are named, opening with The Water Ghost of Harrowby Hall and The Spectre Cook of Bangletop. A speck on the lens, a midnight visitor, and a quicksilver Cassandra follow. Later stories include The Ghost Club, A Psychical Prank, and The Literary Remains of Thomas Bragdon.
the-whole-family-a-novel-by-twelve-autho:
Twelve authors share The Whole Family, each writing one family member's chapter. William Dean Howells takes the father, Mary E. Wilkins Freeman the old-maid aunt, and Mary Heaton Vorse the grandmother. Henry James writes the married son, John Kendrick Bangs the son-in-law, Elizabeth Stuart Phelps the married daughter, and Henry Van Dyke the friend of the family, among others.

Howells opens the novel with news of an engagement, news the narrator decides he ought to carry to the father himself. The families are new neighbours, and a prompt word avoids both stiffness and the appearance of courting grander acquaintance. Finishing his lawn mowing in the cool evening, he leans at the fence and begins with a good-evening across it.
the-wolf-hunters:
James Oliver Curwood published The Wolf Hunters in 1908, subtitled a tale of adventure in the wilderness. He dedicates it to companions of the northern trails. Mukoki, his guide and friend, gets special thanks. Sixteen chapters follow Roderick, Wabigoon, and Mukoki. Chapter titles promise fights, skeletons, and a secret buckskin bag.

The first chapter is called The Fight in the Forest. Later chapters bring snow, rescue, and a stand against the Woongas. Curwood writes from his own years in the Canadian north. Young readers get hunting, danger, and friendship in deep woods. The story also shows respect for Indigenous skill and knowledge.
the-woman-haters:
Joseph C. Lincoln explains in a foreword how The Woman-Haters grew from a magazine story into a book. The earlier tale covered John Brown and Miss Ruth Graham only in part. Revising it, Lincoln says, taught him more about the lightkeeper's past. A housekeeper at the bungalow also came into clearer view. New figures joined, including Bennie D. and a boat named Daisy M.

Lincoln calls the result a summer farce-comedy, a yarn rather than a novel. The story more than doubled in length during revision. A famous high tide in Eastboro also earns its place. Readers can expect Cape Cod humor, romance, and seaside misunderstandings. Lincoln hopes his second telling is the more accurate one.
the-women-of-the-caesars: Guglielmo Ferrero's The Women of the Caesars, published by the Century Company in 1911, appears here through its contents alone. Six chapters move from marriage in ancient Rome to Agrippina, mother of Nero. Livia and Julia share a chapter. Caligula's sisters and Messalina's marriage come later. The chapter texts themselves are absent from the pages shown.
the-woodlanders: Hardy's Woodlanders (1887) traps lovers in Dorset's dark forests. Class divides hearts cruelly and finally. The Tower library holds the full text. It woods with Wessex gloom deeply. Nature watches human folly calmly. Fate is indifferent to love. The novel aches with beauty.
the-world-english-bible-web-numbers:
Numbers, book four in the World English Bible, begins with a census in Sinai's wilderness. God speaks to Moses in the Tent of Meeting. The date is the second year after leaving Egypt. Every male aged twenty and upward must be counted. Only those able to go to war are numbered. Aaron helps Moses organize the count by divisions.

A leader from each tribe stands with them. Reuben's Elizur and Simeon's Shelumiel are named first. Judah's Nahshon follows in the list. Wilderness journeys, rebellions, and a new generation fill the book. Readers see Israel counted as an army. Organization precedes the long march toward Canaan.
the-world-s-greatest-books-volume-09-liv: Volume nine of The World's Greatest Books, edited by Arthur Mee and J. A. Hammerton in 1910, turns to lives and letters in its contents list. Augustine's Confessions and Bunyan's Grace Abounding appear. Boswell's Life of Samuel Johnson is included. Cellini's autobiography and Chesterfield's letters to his son are listed. The love-letters of Abélard and Héloïse open the volume. The condensed lives themselves do not appear in the pages present.
the-world-s-greatest-books-volume-10-liv: A contents list for volume ten of The World's Greatest Books, the lives and letters volume edited by Arthur Mee and J. A. Hammerton, is present here. Washington Irving's lives of Columbus and Washington appear. Lockhart's lives of Scott and Burns are listed. Luther's Table Talk and Josephus's autobiography also appear. Thomas Moore's Life of Byron is included. The summaries themselves do not follow in the pages shown in this record.
the-young-buglers: G. A. Henty's The Young Buglers appears here as a contents list of twenty chapters, without the story itself. A coaching adventure opens the tale, and enlistment follows. The boys then sail for Portugal and the Peninsular War. Talavera, Albuera, and Salamanca mark their campaign. Ciudad Rodrigo and Badajos also appear. Vittoria and Toulouse close the list of battles. The chapters themselves do not appear in the pages present in this record.
the-young-carpenters-of-freiberg-a-tale-: The Young Carpenters of Freiberg, a tale of the Thirty Years' War, reached English readers in an 1880 Edinburgh edition. J. Latchmore, Jun. translated it from the German. Only the contents and illustration list appear in this record. Chapters cover a siege, an enemy before the town, and treachery. A frontispiece shows a woman tipping a robber into a chest. The story chapters themselves do not follow in the pages present here.
the-young-engineers-in-mexico-or-fightin:
H. Irving Hancock sends Tom Reade and Harry Hazelton to Mexico in The Young Engineers in Mexico. Mine owner Luis Montez opens the tale on his handsome veranda. He surveys country sweeping eastward from his home. Visitors, he declares, stand in a land of golden promise. The contents promise a mine that both did and did not exist. Don Luis will show his claws in later chapters.

Swindlers dangle golden bait before the young engineers. Sampling ore and watching midnight lights expose the fraud. Hancock pits honest engineering against mining scams. The boys must defend their professional honor abroad. Boys' series readers get geology, danger, and detective work in one package.
this-country-of-ours: H. E. Marshall, full name Henrietta Elizabeth Marshall, wrote This Country of Ours, identified in an electronic text header first posted in 2001. The header gives no chapter or title page from the book itself. It explains the volunteer text project instead. Readers can confirm the book's title and author from what is present, but none of Marshall's history writing appears here. The header alone is held in this record, so the chapters themselves are not shown.
thuvia-maid-of-mars:
Edgar Rice Burroughs opens his Martian novel in the royal gardens of Thuvan Dihn, Jeddak of Ptarth. Contents promise slavery, treachery, phantom bowmen, a hall of doom, and a glossary of Martian names. Thuvia sits on a polished ersite bench under giant pimalia blooms, tapping a sandalled foot.

Astok bends close, declaring a love that burns hotter than the cold stone bench. Thuvia springs up in anger, reminding him he has won no right to address a jeddak's daughter so. Readers get Barsoom romance and adventure, with green men, white apes, and battles ahead.
tom-of-the-raiders: Austin Bishop wrote Tom of the Raiders, illustrated by Morgan Dennis, who shows Tom feeding logs into flames again and again. Twenty-one chapters are listed, starting with the Second Ohio and the raiders starting out. Headings follow an arrest, Tom going alone, a captured train, a race, pursuit, and fighting with fire. Later chapters bring capture, escaping, the Tennessee River, and Tom reporting at headquarters. The front pages and contents are what is on these pages, so Bishop's Civil War adventure itself does not appear.
tommy-atkins-at-war-as-told-in-his-own-l:
James A. Kilpatrick compiled Tommy Atkins at War from soldiers' own letters, published by McBride, Nast at New York in 1914. An epigraph quotes a letter found on a German officer, calling English soldiers the best trained in the world and their fire worse than hell. Kilpatrick's note explains his method.

The book, he says, is the soldier's story told through vivid, intimate impressions of Europe's battlefields. Letter passages show grim realities beside chivalry, humanity, and exaltation in battle. London and provincial newspaper editors lent the passages. Readers get a First World War portrait assembled from the men's own words home.
two-summers-in-guyenne-a-chronicle-of-th: Edward Harrison Barker's Two Summers in Guyenne chronicles the wayside and waterside of southwestern France. The contents tour the upper Dordogne, the moors of the Correze, the viscounty of Turenne, and upper Perigord. Later sections follow the Vezere and Isle valleys and a canoe voyage on the Dronne. The illustration list promises abbey doorways, moorland widows, and peasants of the causse. Only the title page, contents, and illustration list are present here, so the chronicle itself does not appear.
un-doc-international-review-of-criminal-:
Moving a criminal case from one state to another is the subject of a chapter in the International Review of Criminal Policy, issues 43 and 44. That journal is a United Nations forum on crime and justice. The chapter dates from the 1970s. It deals with a hard problem of place. A crime, a suspect, and the best court for trial may sit in three different countries.

The chapter explains how one state can hand a case to another state for trial. It covers the legal steps, the rights of the accused, and the gains in fairness and speed. Readers see an early, careful attempt to make cross-border justice work in practice.
under-sealed-orders: H. A. Cody's Under Sealed Orders, published at New York in 1917, is dedicated to all spuds, all fools, and all the devil's poor, authors not forgotten. The contents open with the lure of falling water and a sale to the lowest bidder. Later chapters promise a little cabin, an unmasking, a wild nor'easter, harnessed power, and a rescue. Only the title page, dedication, and contents are present here, so the novel itself does not appear.
under-the-deodars:
Rudyard Kipling's Under the Deodars collects Anglo-Indian tales, beginning with The Education of Otis Yeere. The contents also list A Wayside Comedy, The Hill of Illusion, A Second-rate Woman, and Only a Subaltern. The Enlightenments of Pagett, M. P. closes the set of eight stories.

Otis Yeere's education is announced as the history of a failure. The narrator blames a clever woman's unretrieved blunder, since a woman's mistake, he jokes, falls outside the course of nature. The scene is Simla, where everything in station life begins and much of it ends badly. Mrs. Hauksbee arrives at her friend Mrs. Mallowe's tiffin, and the comedy of station life starts.
van-bibber-and-others:
Richard Harding Davis gathered fifteen short stories in Van Bibber and Others, dated 1892 and 1920. He dedicated the book to his father, L. Clarke Davis, his kindest and severest critic. Several tales follow Van Bibber, a young man about town. They cover his man-servant, a day at the races, and a first hunt for Mr. Travers. Others take up a hungry man fed, an experiment in economy, and a recruit at Christmas.

The first story, Her First Appearance, drops readers backstage on a nervous opening night. The first act of The Sultana has just ended. Every member of the Lester Comic Opera Company is sick with fear for the show. The fear runs from Lester himself down to the wardrobe woman's son. Davis writes with a reporter's speed and a fond eye for New York types, from chorus girls to patrons of art.
venus-in-furs:
Leopold von Sacher-Masoch wrote Venus in Furs, rendered here from the German by Fernanda Savage in an edition of 1,225 copies meant for private circulation. An introduction sketches the author's life before the tale. He was born at Lemberg, in Austrian Galicia, on January 27, 1836, studied law at Prague and Graz, and taught at Graz from 1857.

The introduction follows him out of the lecture hall into full-time writing, years editing a review at Leipzig, and a move to Paris, since he always leaned toward France. He died at Lindheim in Hesse on March 9, 1895. His wife Aurora wrote novels as Wanda von Dunajew, and Wanda is also the name of the heroine of this tale. Readers meet the man whose name later became a term for the desires his fiction describes.
violin-mastery-talks-with-master-violini: Frederick H. Martens gathered Violin Mastery, talks with master violinists and teachers, for Frederick A. Stokes Company at New York, with copyright in 1919 and sixteen portraits. Pages present here hold the title page and the start of the contents, so the talks themselves are not shown. The title page names the stars he questioned: Ysaye, Kreisler, Elman, Auer, Thibaud, Heifetz, Hartmann, and Maud Powell. Contents begin with Ysaye on the tools of mastery, Auer on a method without secrets, and Eddy Brown on technic, with hints to the student.
virginibus-puerisque-and-other-papers:
Robert Louis Stevenson's Virginibus Puerisque and Other Papers opens with an essay on marriage. This copy was transcribed from the Chatto and Windus edition of 1897. Stevenson begins with Shakespeare. With the single exception of Falstaff, he says, all of Shakespeare's people are marrying folk. Mercutio would have come to Benedick's end in the long run. Even Iago had a wife, and was jealous, which is stranger still.

Folk of Shakespeare's day, he argues, hesitated far less over marriage. They laughed more when they did hesitate. Modern heroes of comedy share Benedick's doubts. They hold them twice as much in earnest, with a quarter of his confidence. That fear, Stevenson says, proves how sincere their terror is. Snares wait about their feet, and the shadow of matrimony stands ahead. The essay turns a light, fond eye on courtship, in Stevenson's easy familiar style.
walking-stick-papers: Robert Cortes Holliday published Walking-Stick Papers in 1918. He dedicated the book, as a cat may look at a king, to three men: W. C. Brownell, Hilaire Belloc, and Royal Cortissoz. Pages present here hold the title page, dedication, and contents only, so the essays themselves are not shown. Contents promise a prologue on carrying a cane. Pieces on a fish reporter, going a journey, and art exhibitions follow. A reviewer nicknamed Cuss, Henry James himself, and the humours of the book shop all get papers.
wanderers:
Knut Hamsun's Wanderers joins two books in one volume: Under the Autumn Star and A Wanderer Plays on Muted Strings, rendered from the Norwegian by W. W. Worster, who also wrote the introduction. Worster finds a strong thread of Hamsun's own life in nearly all his work, but most of all here and in the sequel named The Last Joy. The three books belong together, he argues.

Their center is Knut Pedersen from the Northlands, through whose eyes the fates of Captain Falkenberg and his wife slowly unfold. Events come straight from Hamsun's life, Worster says, and the pages mirror his moods and thoughts so closely that they may pass for diaries of a rare intimacy. As a side gift, the reader gets a story told by indirection, with a skill Worster ranks beside Conrad's best. The volume shows a great writer watching himself wander and work.
winning-his-spurs: This record for G. A. Henty's Winning His Spurs gives the title page and a contents list that stops at chapter seventeen, with no tale text present. A line in the record dates the book to 1882, while its title page reads 1895. The contents open with outlaws, a rescue, and the capture of Wortham Hold. The Crusades, the lists, and revenge follow. Princess Berengaria, pirates, and the Holy Land fill the middle list. A twin record carries a fuller contents list and the first chapter.
wives-and-daughters: Elizabeth Gaskell wrote this novel about Molly Gibson and her widowed father's world. An editor's note here says it ran in the Cornhill Magazine from August 1864 to January 1866. Gaskell died in November 1865, before the last chapter was done. The magazine editor added remarks on how she meant the story to end. Pages present here hold that note and a chapter list, but no novel text.
woodroffe-garland-of-letters:
Woodroffe's Garland of Letters appeared in 1922 as studies in mantra-shastra. The Tantric science of sacred sound stands at the book's core. Letters and syllables, in this teaching, are far more than signs.

Woodroffe shows how sound becomes form, deity, and world in Tantra. He traces the fifty letters as powers that build all things. Ritual speech, breath, and the body join in one bold scheme. His prose mixes a scholar's rigor with a devotee's real sympathy. Readers gain the clearest English path into the thought behind mantra practice. The garland of its title strings letters like flowers on one thread.
wyndham-towers:
Thomas Bailey Aldrich wrote this long narrative poem and dedicated it to actor Edwin Booth. His note explains the method. An early sketch held the story in rough form, then got cancelled. Aldrich recast it fully for this volume. Elizabethan dramatists shaped his style on purpose. He wanted the colour of the period in which the action sits, though the tale is told later.

The poem opens in a hamlet by a slender arched bridge. A stone church, grey houses, and an old inn called The Falcon set the scene. Readers get a verse tale in an old English mood. Booth's stage art stands behind the dedication.
yesterdays-with-authors:
James T. Fields, the Boston publisher, wrote these memoirs of famous writers he knew. A preface to this edition tells his own story first. Fields clerked in a bookshop at fourteen and rose to partner in Ticknor, Reed and Fields. His firm published most great American writers of the century. He coaxed a jobless Nathaniel Hawthorne into printing The Scarlet Letter.

Fields also courted British stars on trips to England. Charles Dickens became a personal friend and host at Gad's Hill. Amusing Dickens notes appear in the volume. Readers get publishing history told through friendship, talk, and letters. The 1879 edition was the seventeenth.
